chunks.content: Background Preeclampsia (PE), an important cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality, is a multi-organ and heterogeneous disorder that occurs in 2–5% of all pregnancies [ – ]. The onset of PE can be divided into early-onset and late-onset by applying a threshold of 34 weeks of gestation [ ]. There are only options to treatments that control disease progression but no curative therapy once preeclampsia has developed. Thus, the primary clinical management strategy for PE is to prevent this condition through a variety of approaches from the outset [ , ]. Low-dose aspirin prophylaxis was demonstrated to be effective against PE in 1978 by Ngene and Moodley [ ]; this strategy is now widely used to prevent pregnancies at high risk of PE pregnancies [ , , ]. The risk of PE can be mitigated in women with moderate and high-risk characteristics using prophylactic aspirin [ ]. Aspirin increases the level of prostacyclin, a vasodilator, and antagonizes the production of thromboxane A2, a vasoconstrictor, thereby preventing PE by maintaining a balance between pro-angiogenic factors and anti-angiogenic factors [ , , ]. Accordingly, aspirin can inhibit inflammation and platelet aggregation which are responsible for the onset of PE [ ]. The current recommended daily dose of aspirin for PE prophylaxis is 75 mg; however, several studies have suggested that a higher dose of aspirin may be more effective due to the identification of a dose-response effect [ – ]. Thus, there is a clear need to further investigate the aspirin dose and the occurrence of PE. Furthermore, current guidelines recommend the initiation of aspirin prior to 16 weeks of gestation but with a discontinuation time ranging from 26 to 36 weeks [ , , , , – ]. At present, there is no uniform consensus for the duration of aspirin usage. Because different start times correspond to different exposure times, we suggest that discontinuation time should be individualized for each patient. Here, we exploratorily set a new variable, medication duration, by computing the difference between start time and discontinuation time. In addition, several studies have reported that low dose aspirin will effectively prevent up to 60–62% of early-onset or pre-term PE but may not definitively prevent late-onset PE or PE at term [ , – ]. Our objective was to investigate how aspirin regimens, including aspirin dose and duration, and maternal characteristics during early pregnancy might relate to the occurrence of early- and late-onset PE. Methods Study design and participants This study is both a retrospective case-control analysis as well as a secondary analysis of a prospective cohort study, the data of which were derived from a prospective cohort study conducted by our research team. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) pregnant persons who had been registered and delivered at Capital Medical University Affiliated Beijing Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital between the 1st of January 2023 and the 30th of June 2024, and (2) pregnant persons who had been recommended to take aspirin based on clinical evaluation. Patients were excluded for the following reasons: (1) ultrasound indicated fetal malformation; (2) in utero fetal death during pregnancy; (3) prenatal diagnosis was suggestive of fetal genetic or chromosomal abnormalities; and (4) the patient requested withdrawal from the study, or the patient did not accept medication orders during their maternity appointments. All participants completed an informed consent form before recruitment. This study was approved by the Beijing Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital, Capital Medical University Research Ethics Board (Reference: IEC-C-29-V03-FJ1). Data collection We collated the following data for each participant: maternal age, gravidity, parity, maternal height and weight, mode of conception, and history of chronic diseases (including chronic hypertension, diabetes, and antiphospholipid syndrome). The recommendation for aspirin use was decided by obstetricians in accordance with the ACOG guidelines and the 2020 Chinese Expert Consensus on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy [ , ]. The recommended dose of aspirin was determined by obstetricians based on the individual status of each pregnant person and clinical practice. A commonly used specification of aspirin in domestic clinical settings is 25 mg per tablet. Therefore, the recommended daily doses for PE are predominantly 50 mg, 75 mg, 100 mg, 125 mg, or 150 mg. The indications for aspirin discontinuation were defined as follows: (1) attainment of 36 weeks of gestation; (2) clinical onset of preeclampsia; and (3) identification of potential bleeding-associated risks (e.g., coagulation dysfunction). During prenatal check-ups and delivery, the following data were collected: aspirin start time, aspirin dosage, aspirin discontinuation time, maternal pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI), gestational weight gain (GWG), the time of diagnosis for gestational hypertension and preeclampsia, delivery method, gestational age at delivery, newborn birth weight, and adverse perinatal outcomes (including postpartum hemorrhage and placental abruption). The indications for aspirin discontinuation were defined as follows: (1) attainment of 36 weeks of gestation; (2) clinical onset of preeclampsia; and (3) identification of potential bleeding-associated risks (e.g., coagulation dysfunction). During prenatal check-ups and delivery, the following data were collected: aspirin start time, aspirin dosage, aspirin discontinuation time, maternal pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI), gestational weight gain (GWG), the time of diagnosis for gestational hypertension and preeclampsia, delivery method, gestational age at delivery, newborn birth weight, and adverse perinatal outcomes (including postpartum hemorrhage and placental abruption). Medication duration (in weeks) was calculated as the difference in gestational weeks between aspirin start and discontinuation time. Gestational age was recorded by complete gestational weeks, with all additional days assigned to the corresponding completed week for consistent statistical analysis. The primary outcome was the occurrence of PE. The diagnostic criteria for preeclampsia were according to ACOG guidelines [ ]. All cases associated with a diagnosis of PE were reviewed by an independent maternal-fetal medicine specialist to confirm the diagnosis. PE was classified according to gestational age at onset as early-onset (< 34 weeks) or late-onset (≥ 34 weeks). All collected data were entered into an electronic data capture database managed by attending physicians specializing in obstetrics. Statistical analyses Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS for Windows, version 26 (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY) and R version 4.2.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria; 2022). The normality of raw data was determined using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality test. Skewed quantitative data are expressed as medians and quartiles whereas categorical data are shown as percentages. The Kruskal-Wallis test was used to compare skewed quantitative data across multiple independent groups. Fisher’s exact probability test was used to analyze associations between categorical variables. Collinearity diagnostics via linear regression ruled out significant multicollinearity among independent variables. For multinomial logistic regression, model assumptions were validated: mean-centering of continuous variables for logit-linearity, study design-guaranteed observation independence, and linear regression-derived Cook’s distance/leverage values confirming no influential outliers. Multinomial logistic regression analysis was used for univariate and multivariate analysis and to generate crude and adjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the three groups. Univariate factors with P <0.1 were entered into the multiple logistic regression model and P < 0.05 was used to indicate a significant difference. Propensity score matching (PSM) was used to perform 1:1 matched-pair analysis to minimize group differences caused by covariates. For PSM, we used nearest neighbor matching within a caliper of 0.05. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population before and after PSM were summarized in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2. The absolute value of the standardized mean difference (SMD) was used to evaluate baseline balance between groups, with an absolute SMD < 0.1 defined as achieving satisfactory balance. Given the inherent limitations and potential selection bias of PSM, its results were only used to revalidate the conclusions of univariate and multivariate analyses, with the main study conclusions based on pre-matching data. The best exposure threshold to predict the prophylactic effect of aspirin for late-onset PE was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses. The best exposure threshold was defined as the medication duration corresponding to the optimal cutoff value, as determined using the Youden index. ROC analysis was performed with the pROC version 1.18.0 package and visualized by the ggplot2 package version 3.4.4 in the R environment. Results Characteristics of the study population A total of 975 eligible participants were included in our analysis. Of these, 725 participants were classified as non-PE (74.4%), 46 as early-onset PE (4.7%), and 204 participants as late-onset PE (20.9%). The baseline characteristics of patients in the non-PE, early-onset PE and late-onset PE are shown in Table .Daily aspirin dosage distributions were as follows: the non-PE group – 75 mg (73.5%), 100 mg (19.4%), 50 mg (6.8%), 25 mg (0.3%); the early-onset PE group – 75 mg (76.8%), 100 mg (19.6%), 50/150 mg (2.2%); the late-onset PE group – 75 mg (71.1%), 100 mg (21.6%), 50 mg (5.9%), 150 mg (1.0%), 25 mg (0.5%). The mean medication duration was 20 weeks in the non-PE group, 16 weeks in the early-onset PE group, and 21 weeks in the late-onset PE group. There were no significant differences between the three groups in terms of maternal age, gravidity, parity, GWG, mode of conception, aspirin start time, and aspirin dosage. Significant differences were, however, detected between the non-PE group and early-onset PE group for pre-pregnancy BMI, delivery method, gestational age at delivery, newborn birth weight and aspirin discontinuation time ( P <0.05). Participants in the early-onset PE group had a higher pre-pregnancy BMI and cesarean section rate, a lower newborn birth weight and an earlier gestational age at delivery and aspirin discontinuation time. Differences were detected between the non-PE group and late-onset PE group for pre-pregnancy BMI, delivery

differences between the three groups in terms of maternal age, gravidity, parity, GWG, mode of conception, aspirin start time, and aspirin dosage. Significant differences were, however, detected between the non-PE group and early-onset PE group for pre-pregnancy BMI, delivery method, gestational age at delivery, newborn birth weight and aspirin discontinuation time ( P <0.05). Participants in the early-onset PE group had a higher pre-pregnancy BMI and cesarean section rate, a lower newborn birth weight and an earlier gestational age at delivery and aspirin discontinuation time. Differences were detected between the non-PE group and late-onset PE group for pre-pregnancy BMI, delivery method and newborn birth weight ( P <0.05). Participants in the late-onset PE group had a higher pre-pregnancy BMI, cesarean section rate, and lower newborn birth weight. Risk factors for early- and late-onset preeclampsia Table shows the results of univariate and multivariate analysis in an attempt to determine the risk factors for early-onset PE. Risk factors significantly associated with the development of early-onset PE, as identified by univariate analysis, including pre-pregnancy BMI, gestational age at delivery and medication duration ( P <0.1), were then included in multivariable logistic regression analysis. First, our analysis revealed that different aspirin dosages were not significantly related with the occurrence of early-onset PE. Second, multivariable analysis revealed that pre-pregnancy BMI (adjusted OR (95% CI): 1.102(1.028–1.181), P = 0.006) and gestational age at delivery (adjusted OR (95% CI): 0.552(0.489–0.623), <0.001) were independent risk factors for the development of early-onset PE. Table shows the results of univariate and multivariate analysis; these analyses were performed to identify risk factors for late-onset PE. Risk factors significantly associated with the development of late-onset PE, as determined using univariate analysis, including parity, pre-pregnancy BMI gestational age at delivery and medication duration ( P <0.1), were then included in multivariable logistic regression analysis. Analysis revealed that different aspirin dosages were not significantly related with the occurrence of late-onset PE. Moreover, multivariable analysis revealed that pre-pregnancy BMI (adjusted OR (95% CI):1.102 (1.068–1.136), P =<0.001), gestational age at delivery (0.854 (0.781–0.933), <0.001) and medication duration (1.024 (1.000–1.049), 0.046) were independent risk factors for the development of late-onset PE. Risk factors for early- and late-onset preeclampsia after PSM Next, we performed PSM to further reduce bias and imbalances in matched covariates. Matched variables included maternal age, parity, pre-pregnancy BMI, gestational age at delivery and aspirin dosage. Following PSM, there were 35 patients in the non-PE group and early-onset PE group, respectively. Table shows the results of univariate analysis, which attempted to identify risk factors for early-onset PE after PSM. Following PSM, our analysis still indicated that different aspirin dosages were not related to the occurrence of early-onset PE ( P = 1.000). Following PSM, some of our findings differed slightly from our previous results. Gestational age at delivery was no longer related with prophylactic effects in the development of early-onset PE ( P = 0.701). Following PSM, pre-pregnancy BMI (adjusted OR (95% CI): 1.113 (1.003–1.235), P = 0.044) was identified as an independent risk factor for the development of early-onset PE. Following PSM, there were 203 patients in the non-PE group and late-onset PE group, respectively. Table shows the results of univariate and multivariate analysis, which were performed to determine the risk factors for late-onset PE after PSM. Risk factors significantly associated with the development of late-onset PE, as determined by univariate analysis, included gestational age at delivery and medication duration ( P <0.1). These risk factors were then included in multivariable logistic regression analysis. Following PSM, our findings remained in line with our previous results in that different aspirin dosages were not significantly related to the occurrence of late-onset PE ( P = 0.577). However, some of our findings differed slightly from our previous results. Pre-pregnancy BMI was no longer related with prophylactic effects for late-onset PE ( P = 0.130). Following PSM, gestational age at delivery (adjusted OR (95% CI): 0.876 (0.777–0.989), P = 0.033) and medication duration (1.031 (1.002–1.061), 0.034) were identified as independent risk factors for the development of late-onset PE. Computing the optimal medication duration by ROC curves Collectively, these results suggested that increased medication duration was associated with an increase in late-onset PE group. Therefore, we performed ROC analysis to determine an optimum threshold for medication duration. ROC curves for the prediction of medication duration and the occurrence of late-onset PE are shown in Fig. . ROC curve analysis revealed that the area under the curve (AUC) for predicting the study outcome was 0.555 (95% CI: 0.512–0.598), with an optimum threshold for medication duration of 22.5 weeks. Discussion PE is an important obstetric disorder, and low-dose aspirin prophylaxis is widely administered to pregnant persons with a high risk of PE. However, optimal aspirin regimens, including dosage and medication duration, have yet to be developed, and there has been no

to determine an optimum threshold for medication duration. ROC curves for the prediction of medication duration and the occurrence of late-onset PE are shown in Fig. . ROC curve analysis revealed that the area under the curve (AUC) for predicting the study outcome was 0.555 (95% CI: 0.512–0.598), with an optimum threshold for medication duration of 22.5 weeks. Discussion PE is an important obstetric disorder, and low-dose aspirin prophylaxis is widely administered to pregnant persons with a high risk of PE. However, optimal aspirin regimens, including dosage and medication duration, have yet to be developed, and there has been no separate investigation of its effects on early- and late-onset PE. We designed this study to investigate how aspirin regimens and maternal characteristics with early- and late-onset PE. Our analysis suggested that aspirin dosage, aspirin medication duration and GWG were not significantly associated with early- and late-onset PE. Analysis also revealed that the prevalence of early-onset PE was higher for patients with a higher pre-pregnancy BMI receiving an earlier gestational age at delivery. Pregnant persons with a higher pre-pregnancy BMI, an earlier gestational age at delivery, and a longer medication duration of aspirin were associated with a higher prevalence of late-onset PE. A post-PSM reanalysis was conducted to validate the above results, and ROC curve analysis was conducted to derive the optimal medication duration. Nearly all major obstetric organizations recommend aspirin prophylaxis in pregnant persons at high risk of developing PE. In routine clinical practice, aspirin prophylaxis at a daily dose of 75 mg is the mainstream dosage, as authenticated by several studies [ – ]. However, several recent meta-analyses and systematic reviews have reported that higher doses of aspirin (100–150 mg in early pregnancy) were associated with meaningful outcomes [ , – ]. One meta-analysis revealed that women taking 150 mg aspirin daily experienced a 62% reduction in the risk of developing PE. In comparison, those taking 81 mg aspirin daily experienced only a 30% reduction in risk [ ]. Several studies have also demonstrated a dose-response effect for aspirin at dosages between 60 and 150 mg [ , – ]. In contrast, Tapp et al. reported conflicting findings: 160 mg aspirin did not significantly reduce PE rates compared with 80 mg in at-risk [ ]. These results were consistent with our findings: we observed no significant association between different aspirin dosages and the early- and late-onset PE within the limited dosage range used in this population. There are several possible reasons underlying these findings. On the one hand, most recommendations related to higher dosing regimens are based on meta-analyses and systematic reviews. These analyses aggregate small and heterogeneous populations, varying enrollment criteria, and inconsistent definitions of PE which may have overestimated the true effects of the intervention [ ]. On the other hand, women may receive conflicting information from non-obstetric clinicians or pharmacists regarding the safety of aspirin [ ]; this may result in reduced adherence to higher doses. In addition, a recent study suggested that aspirin was associated with bleeding disorders, including placental abruption, postpartum hemorrhage and spinal epidural hematoma [ , ]. Collectively, existing data suggest that the use of aspirin in pregnancy is deemed to be safe with minimal risks, especially for aspirin doses < 100 mg [ ]. The majority of evidence still continues to support the use of aspirin at doses < 100 mg with a modest risk reduction for PE [ , , , ]. Caution is required for higher doses of aspirin (100–150 mg in early pregnancy) and evaluate the long-term effects of this treatment in large clinical studies. Meanwhile, our findings do not contradict evidence from high-dose aspirin trials but rather reflect real-world clinical practice in settings where low-dose aspirin predominates. Considering our current results, although the rarity of doses other than 75 mg limits the ability to definitively evaluate dose-related effects, we still tend to support continued recommendation of 75 mg aspirin. At present, multiple guidelines and studies recommend differences in the optimal timing of initiating and discontinuing aspirin. The FIGO guidelines (2019) recommended that women at high risk of PE should receive aspirin prophylaxis commencing at 11–14 + 6 weeks of gestation until 36 weeks of gestation, when delivery occurs, or when PE is diagnosed [ ]. The SOGC guidelines (2022) recommended aspirin prophylaxis commencing at 16 weeks of gestation until 36 weeks of gestation for women at high risk of PE [ ]. Furthermore, some clinical studies have evaluated the optimal timing. A randomized clinical trial reported that aspirin was highly effective if commenced before 16 weeks of gestation with good compliance [ ]. A meta-analysis further suggested that low dose aspirin was most effective for PE prevention when initiated at ≤ 16 weeks in pregnant persons at high risk [ ]. Some studies also suggested that the

occurs, or when PE is diagnosed [ ]. The SOGC guidelines (2022) recommended aspirin prophylaxis commencing at 16 weeks of gestation until 36 weeks of gestation for women at high risk of PE [ ]. Furthermore, some clinical studies have evaluated the optimal timing. A randomized clinical trial reported that aspirin was highly effective if commenced before 16 weeks of gestation with good compliance [ ]. A meta-analysis further suggested that low dose aspirin was most effective for PE prevention when initiated at ≤ 16 weeks in pregnant persons at high risk [ ]. Some studies also suggested that the initiation of aspirin at 11 to 13 weeks of gestation can prevent the majority of at-risk individuals from developing preterm PE [ ], and available evidence even supports initiation from 11 weeks [ ]. In contrast, some studies reported that aspirin should not be commenced before the 11th or 12th week of pregnancy for PE prophylaxis due to the lack of clear benefit [ , , , , , , ]. Considering our current findings, we identified two deficiencies in practice. First, we routinely recommend aspirin prophylaxis commencing at 11–14 weeks of gestation in clinical practice; however, different start times correspond to different exposure times. The discontinuation time for aspirin should be determined on an individual basis. Second, whether early- and late-onset PE show distinct associations with aspirin usage remains to be fully investigated. Therefore, in the present study, we exploratorily present a new variable, medication duration, by computing the difference between start time and discontinuation time and performed a series of specific evaluations. In our study, we found that reduction in early-onset PE incidence was not correlated with medication duration. Several recent findings support the prophylactic effect of aspirin use for early-onset PE [ , , ]. These studies reported that a low dose of aspirin can prevent up to 60% of early-onset PE. Combined with the results of these studies and our study, the prophylactic effect of aspirin for early-onset PE may be independent of medication duration, but this finding cannot exclude confounding by gestational age. The reason was that aspirin was immediately discontinued upon the diagnosis of preeclampsia in clinical practice, which shortens the medication duration accordingly. This speculation warrants further verification in subsequent studies. Notably, these previous results differed from our findings for late-onset PE. Previous studies recommended that a low dose of aspirin will not prevent late-onset PE [ , , ]; however, we observed that the rate of incidence for late-onset PE was positively correlated with medication duration. This implies that taking aspirin over the long-term may be associated with the occurrence of late-onset PE. Furthermore, this finding remained consistent in our post-PSM reanalysis. The divergent prophylactic effects against early- and late-onset PE likely reflect underlying pathophysiology differences between the two phenotypes. Some studies have reported that shallow trophoblast invasion and immune maladaptation are key to early-onset PE, whereas late-onset PE is strongly associated with maternal cardiometabolic variables (metabolic syndrome) [ , , ]. This offers an explanation for why aspirin results in a different prevalence for early-onset and late-onset PE; however, cannot explain why the long-term use of aspirin was associated with late-onset PE. We reviewed the mechanism of drug action and provide some hypothesis-generating explanations. First, long-term aspirin use may perturb the immune regulatory network and disrupt the delicate balance of pro- and anti- thrombotic factors, thereby inducing vascular damage and late-onset PE. Aspirin inhibits cyclo-oxygenase-1(COX-1) to reduce thromboxane A2(TXA2) production——the core mechanism for PE prophylaxis——but also potentially suppresses prostaglandin E2(PGE2), prostaglandin I2 (PGI2) synthesis; low-dose aspirin has been shown to reduce systemic PGE2 biosynthesis by 45% in healthy volunteers [ ]. Second, long-term aspirin use may effect maternal metabolism to contribute to late-onset PE: Some earlier studies reported the increased insulin resistance generated by salicylate compounds, and highlighted that the relationship between salicylate compounds and insulin sensitivity is multi-factorial [ ]. In parallel, aspirin-mediated blockade of the arachidonic acid-TXA2 pathway may shunt metabolism toward leukotriene and hydroxy eicosatetraenoic acid production——molecules, though the precise mechanisms remain undefined. However, mechanistic specifics have not been fully clarified by existing research. The above explanations are evidence-based inference and require experimental validation. In addition, aspirin intake could shift the distribution of PE to a later gestational age [ ]. Considering our current results, medication duration may potentially be incorporated into the aspirin regimens for PE prophylaxis. However, medication duration should be interpreted as a proxy marker influenced by gestational age and clinical course rather than as a causal exposure. The association between medication duration and late-onset PE is observational, it may reflect residual confounding or marginal effect and requires confirmation in prospective studies. Some studies have shown that the main drivers of late-onset PE are increased maternal pre-pregnancy BMI or GWG, along with other clinical characteristics

could shift the distribution of PE to a later gestational age [ ]. Considering our current results, medication duration may potentially be incorporated into the aspirin regimens for PE prophylaxis. However, medication duration should be interpreted as a proxy marker influenced by gestational age and clinical course rather than as a causal exposure. The association between medication duration and late-onset PE is observational, it may reflect residual confounding or marginal effect and requires confirmation in prospective studies. Some studies have shown that the main drivers of late-onset PE are increased maternal pre-pregnancy BMI or GWG, along with other clinical characteristics such as metabolic syndrome and maternal age [ ]. Pre-pregnancy maternal factors, particularly obesity, are key contributors to the pathophysiology of late-onset PE [ ]. Some studies have reported that late-onset PE is specifically, linearly and positively associated with an increased maternal BMI in pre-pregnancy [ , , ]. Our findings are consistent with these previous studies. We observed that pre-pregnancy BMI was not only an independent risk factor for early-onset PE but also for late-onset PE. For each 1 kg/m 2 increase in pre-pregnancy BMI, the odds of early- and late-onset PE increased by 10.2%. However, this result was overturned after PSM in late-onset PE. There was no significant difference between high pre-pregnancy BMI and late-onset PE. This conclusion is consistent with a previous cohort study involving a large population, which demonstrated that a high pre-pregnancy BMI did not automatically translate into a high risk of PE at term [ – ]. This study also demonstrated that obese patients could reduce their risk of PE by optimizing their GWG [ – ]. However, our analysis failed to detect a significant difference among the non-PE, early-onset PE, and late-onset PE groups in terms of GWG. In addition, a large cohort study demonstrated that increasing maternal age was a risk factor for both early-onset and late-onset PE [ ]. However, we observed that maternal age was not related to the development of PE. This was not consistent with the general consensus, perhaps due to insufficient sample size and inadequate statistical power. Thus, prudent interpretation of this result is warranted. Strengths and limitations The strengths of this study include the fact that all variables were collected prospectively. Another strength is that all data were acquired from a tertiary care academic obstetrics and gynecology specialist hospital in Beijing, using a database managed by attending obstetricians. The vast majority of participants underwent adequate pre-delivery inspections and exhibited high adherence. These factors ensured that our data were highly accurate. Furthermore, our results are highly credible because our findings remained significant even after propensity scoring. The limitations of our study include the fact that we did not include data related to dietary habits and physical activity, although these factors could contribute to the development of PE [ ]. An additional limitation included the fact that the relationship between different aspirin initiation times at the optimum medication duration and early- and late-onset PE were not performed due to sample size limitations. It is also possible that an earlier delivery for early-onset PE may limit aspirin medication duration. Another limitation is that the effect of aspirin prophylaxis for PE could be influenced by a chronic history of hypertension, medication adherence, clinical decision bias and indication bias could influence the effect of aspirin prophylaxis for PE. However, due to limitations in availability of samples, we could not include a group of patients for relevant subgroup analysis. Finally, as this was a single-center retrospective study, our results are subject to the shortcomings inherent to all single-center and retrospective studies. Although PSM was employed to balance inter-group differences, the potential association between medication duration and PE occurrence still exerted a certain degree of interference in our analyses. Our ROC analysis was restricted to a single-outcome threshold analysis, without the dual opposing outcome threshold analysis. Other analyses were not be conducted to further validate our conclusions due to sample size constraints. However, our results and conclusions can be regarded as exploratory and population-specific, thus providing valuable insights for future research. Future research Our results suggest that the aspirin dosage is not related to the occurrence of early-onset and late-onset PE. We still tend to recommend a daily aspirin dose of 75 mg for the clinical management of PE. Our analysis suggested that medication duration was not correlated with early-onset PE. The results of a previous studies confirmed the prophylactic effect of aspirin use for early-onset PE [ , , ]. However, clinical studies of the relationship between the aspirin medication duration and early-onset PE remain rare. Further large-sample prospective studies are required to confirm our findings. In addition, longer medication duration was statistically associated with increased odds of late-onset preeclampsia in our cohort. A previous study has confirmed that the aspirin use

tend to recommend a daily aspirin dose of 75 mg for the clinical management of PE. Our analysis suggested that medication duration was not correlated with early-onset PE. The results of a previous studies confirmed the prophylactic effect of aspirin use for early-onset PE [ , , ]. However, clinical studies of the relationship between the aspirin medication duration and early-onset PE remain rare. Further large-sample prospective studies are required to confirm our findings. In addition, longer medication duration was statistically associated with increased odds of late-onset preeclampsia in our cohort. A previous study has confirmed that the aspirin use not prevent late-onset PE; however, no previous study has proposed that long-term aspirin use may be associated with the occurrence of late-onset PE. Our findings provide an interesting reference base for future research, and we look forward to seeing the future relative basic and clinical research to explain and verify our discovery. Further research into the associations between aspirin use and late-onset PE would offer new insights and improve the management for aspirin use for PE prophylaxis. Here, we present a new variable, medication duration, and found the optimum medication duration was 22.5 weeks. However, this threshold is population-specific and exploratory, with low discriminatory power (AUC = 0.555), and is therefore not intended for clinical decision-making. Future research is expected to validate the optimal threshold for clinical decision making and confirm the relationship between the different aspirin start times at this medication duration and the development of early-onset and late-onset PE. Conclusion Collectively, our findings indicate that aspirin dosage and GWG were not related to the occurrence of early- and late-onset PE, although the rarity of doses other than 75 mg limits the ability to definitively evaluate dose-related effects. We found that the prevalence of early-onset PE was lower for patients with a lower pre-pregnancy BMI and a later gestational age at delivery. The prevalence of late-onset PE was lower for patients with a lower pre-pregnancy BMI, a later gestational age at delivery and a shorter duration of aspirin. Pre-pregnancy BMI was identified as an independent risk factor for the occurrence of PE, thus providing a basis for individualized perinatal care and the risk assessment of PE. Moreover, our data suggest that a longer medication duration was associated with a higher incidence of late-onset PE in this cohort. However, this finding may reflect residual confounding or marginal effect and should be interpreted cautiously. It should not guide clinical aspirin discontinuation strategies without confirmation in large prospective studies. Supplementary Information Supplementary Material 1. Supplementary Material 2.

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Use of postmenopausal hormones has varied over the past decades. Until the 1970s, estrogen formulations were most common ( , ). In 1975, an elevated risk of endometrial cancer from estrogen therapy was recognized ( – ), and postmenopausal hormone use declined ( – ). Thereafter, studies demonstrated that adding progestin to estrogen reduced endometrial cancer risk ( , ), and suggested additional benefits ( , ). The number of estrogen–progestin prescriptions grew rapidly until the early 2000s ( , ). In 2002, the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) clinical trial found that estrogen–progestin use among healthy postmenopausal women was associated with elevated risk of breast cancer, coronary heart disease, stroke, and venous thromboembolic disease ( ). Estrogen-progestin use decreased dramatically ( – ), and in January 2003, the FDA recommended that manufacturers label estrogen–progestin products with information on possible health risks ( ). Recent ecological studies showed that breast cancer incidence declined between 2001 and 2004, simultaneously with the decline of estrogen–progestin use ( – ), igniting a discussion of whether and to what extent changes in estrogen–progestin use contributed to changes in breast cancer incidence ( – ). Long term nationally representative data on estrogen–progestin use are needed to investigate the historical impacts of estrogen–progestin use on population-level trends in health outcomes related to its use. Estrogen-progestin prevalence estimates are available from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys (NHANES) since 1999 ( ). Available earlier national prescription sales counts ( – ) are only an indirect measure of prevalence ( , , ). We sought to estimate nationally representative trends in estrogen–progestin prevalence for the US female population by calendar year and age by integrating recent NHANES prevalence estimates with prescription drug statistics dating back to 1970. MATERIALS AND METHODS For our analysis, we used publications based on the National Prescription Audit 1970–2003 and NHANES 1999–2010 ( , , , , ). The NHANES data are publically available and were validated by the CDC. The National Prescription Audit is validated by the IMS Institute. From the NHANES data, we calculated odds ratios of estrogen–progestin use between age groups. Using these odds ratios, we split the aggregated prescription data into age specific data. Finally, we combined the two data sources and interpolated estrogen–progestin prevalence estimates by single year of age and single calendar year. This study was determined to be exempt from human subjects review by the University of Wisconsin Health Sciences Institutional Review Board under category 4 since the data are publicly available. We used data from six NHANES survey waves on the percentage of women aged 40 and older reporting current use of oral estrogen–progestin between 1999 and 2010 ( ). NHANES is a program designed to assess the health of the U.S. population, and has been conducted annually and published biannually since 1999, with less regular prior waves. It uses a multistage probability sampling design to select a population sample that is representative of the civilian non-institutionalized US population ( ). A more detailed description of the NHANES reproductive health module is given in Sprague et al. ( ). Sample sizes of women aged 40 and older with estrogen–progestin data during the NHANES waves in 1999, 2001, 2003, 2005, 2007, and 2009 were 1329, 1433, 1420, 1276, 1763, 1739, respectively. We calculated the prevalence of current use of oral estrogen–progestin by age (five-year age groups), in two calendar-year increments corresponding to the NHANES survey waves. The data was analyzed in the R survey package, and weighted by the provided sampling weights to account for sampling design in order to calculate nationally representative estimates. We relied on publications which reported national counts of postmenopausal hormone prescriptions based on data from the National Prescription Audit to assess the use of estrogen–progestin prior to 1999. The National Prescription Audit is an industry standard source of national prescription activity for all pharmaceutical products ( ). Data are collected from a representative sample of retail, standard mail service, specialty mail service, and long term care facilities. Several papers were identified which reported counts of non-contraceptive estrogens and/or progestins, covering the time period 1970–2003 ( , , , ). Each study sought to include all non-contraceptive estrogen and progestin preparations used at the time. A more complete description of the specific products included in each study is available in the source publications. Since information on the number of prescription of both estrogen and progestin used together was not directly available from the National Prescription Audit publications, counts of prescriptions for estrogen–progestin were estimated by multiplying the total number of non-contraceptive postmenopausal estrogen prescriptions by the reported fraction of estrogen prescriptions that were prescribed along with progestin. For years in which no published estrogen prescription data was available (1993–1994), linear interpolation was performed. Similarly, in years in which no estimate of the

at the time. A more complete description of the specific products included in each study is available in the source publications. Since information on the number of prescription of both estrogen and progestin used together was not directly available from the National Prescription Audit publications, counts of prescriptions for estrogen–progestin were estimated by multiplying the total number of non-contraceptive postmenopausal estrogen prescriptions by the reported fraction of estrogen prescriptions that were prescribed along with progestin. For years in which no published estrogen prescription data was available (1993–1994), linear interpolation was performed. Similarly, in years in which no estimate of the fraction of co-prescribed progestin was available (1970–1973, 1987–1991, 1993–2000), linear interpolation of that fraction was performed. The estrogen–progestin prescription counts were normalized to annual population denominator counts of US women aged 40 and older, as obtained from the US Census ( ). We used a weighted logistic regression model to measure the association between estrogen–progestin use and age in the NHANES 1999–2010 data, while adjusting for NHANES survey wave as a measure of calendar year. We tested an interaction term between age group and survey year, which was not statistically significant (P-value 0.35), and subsequently excluded the interaction term from the model. In addition to the odds ratios, we calculated biannual probabilities of estrogen–progestin use by age group. The estrogen–progestin use odds ratios by age were numerically applied to the normalized prescription counts between 1970 and 2003, such that the variation in estrogen–progestin use by age observed in NHANES 1999–2010 was mirrored in the prescription drug data, resulting in estimated age-specific prescription rates of estrogen–progestin use between 1970 and 2003 by five-year age group. These prescription rates were then calibrated to the NHANES data in order to produce pre-1999 estimates of estrogen–progestin prevalence. To generate single calendar year and single year of age prevalence estimates, we implemented a two-step interpolation process. First, the NHANES biannual prevalence estimates between 1999 and 2010 from the logistic regression were interpolated to annual probabilities per five-year age group, with one year knot per NHANES survey. The annual NHANES data and the calibrated prescriptions were then combined into one dataset in the cut-off year 2003. These prevalence estimates by five-year age groups that covered the entire period (1970–2010) were then interpolated to single year age groups, with one age knot per five-year-age group. RESULTS Estrogen-progestin prescriptions varied substantially over time ( ). The estimated age-adjusted prevalence of oral estrogen–progestin use was below 1% for all age groups until about 1980, began to rise in the early 1980s and grew by approximately 200% between 1990 and 1999. The absolute increase in estrogen–progestin prevalence for women aged 45–64 years old was 4.4% between 1980 and 1990, and 8.8% between 1990 and 2000 ( ). Age-adjusted estrogen–progestin prevalence in women aged 45–64 peaked at 13.5% in 1999. Increases in use were statistically significant (P<0.001) based on linear trends reported in Wysowski et al ( ). Estrogen-progestin prevalence declined by about 85% between 2001 and 2005. The relative change per year during 2000–2010 was associated with an odds ratio of 0.174 (95% confidence interval 0.087, 0.346; P<0.001). Annual change was not significantly different across age groups (P=0.35). The prevalence in 2010 was similar to that observed in the mid-1980s ( ). Estrogen–progestin use varied substantially by age. Estrogen–progestin prevalence was less than 5% across all years among women aged 45 years and younger, as well as among women aged 75 years and older. Peak use was observed among women in their late 50s ( ). Maximum usage estimates were reached in 1999, with an estimated 23.2% prevalence among 57-year-old women (12.4% among 50-year-old, 14.6% among 60-year-old, and 10.4% among 65-year-old women). Between 2002 and 2006, estrogen–progestin use decreased steeply in all age groups. Absolute changes during that time varied according to the different levels of estrogen–progestin prevalence per age group ( ), but the relative annual decline was similar in all groups, and ranged from about −43% in 2004 and 2005 to about −16% in 2006. Post-2000 usage was lowest in the mid-2000s, with the lowest prevalence for women aged 45–64 observed in 2006 at 1.7%. There is some suggestion of a very modest increase that occurred in the late 2000s ( – ). DISCUSSION Our analyses provide age- and year-specific estimates for estrogen–progestin use during 1970–2010 representative of the US female population. Our estimates of estrogen–progestin usage between 1970 and 2010 are unique in the level of detail they provide, and could help generate new hypotheses for future research around past and current health outcomes associated with estrogen–progestin use. The population-level impact of estrogen–progestin use on women’s health has likely varied according to the changes in estrogen–progestin prevalence in the past decades. Our estimates are consistent with patterns shown in previous publications amongst specific study populations during more

late 2000s ( – ). DISCUSSION Our analyses provide age- and year-specific estimates for estrogen–progestin use during 1970–2010 representative of the US female population. Our estimates of estrogen–progestin usage between 1970 and 2010 are unique in the level of detail they provide, and could help generate new hypotheses for future research around past and current health outcomes associated with estrogen–progestin use. The population-level impact of estrogen–progestin use on women’s health has likely varied according to the changes in estrogen–progestin prevalence in the past decades. Our estimates are consistent with patterns shown in previous publications amongst specific study populations during more restricted time periods ( , , – , – ). Our modeled estrogen–progestin prevalence trends are nationally representative and more comprehensive by providing estimates per calendar year and single year of age rather than aggregate estimates over time and age groups. In some cases, our estimates are slightly lower compared with previous publications, particularly when comparing them with studies conducted on enrollees of health maintenance organizations (HMOs). For example, Buist et al ( ) reported a 14.6% estrogen–progestin prevalence among women aged 40–80 in 1999 whereas the corresponding value in our study was 9.5%. This most likely reflects the elevated use of postmenopausal hormones among women enrolled in HMOs relative to use among the general population which also includes uninsured women. There is little nationally representative estrogen–progestin data in the published literature with which to compare our results more directly, and we found none that covered comparably long time periods. In a study based on NHANES data, Brett et al ( ) reported estrogen–progestin prevalence estimates in 1999 quite comparable to ours. Our study has limitations. First, NHANES data on postmenopausal estrogen–progestin use relies on self-reports. However, prior studies indicate good reliability and validity for self-reported hormone use ( – ). Secondly, we relied on prescription dispensary data from several publications. While these data may not precisely reflect actual use since some dispensed prescriptions may not be used, they arise from a broadly representative sample of prescription dispensaries across the US. In order to account for unused prescriptions, we calibrated the prescription information to the NHANES data. We did not have prescription drug data by age, and therefore applied odds ratios between age groups from the NHANES 1999–2010 data to the prescription data. This assumes that odds ratios of estrogen–progestin use between age groups were stable over time. We did not find evidence contradicting this, and the test for effect modification between age and time in the NHANES data was not statistically significant. We interpolated estrogen use in 1993/1994, and the fraction of progestin among estrogen users in years in which no estimate of that fraction was available. Notably, the fraction of progestin among estrogen users reported by other authors appears to have been relatively stable during these time periods ( , , , ). Nevertheless, our estimates only approximate true estrogen–progestin usage if our assumption of stable odds ratios holds true, and if the fraction of progestin among estrogen users did not fluctuate much in the 1990s. We only modeled estrogen–progestin estimates for age groups 40–84, but prevalence in women aged <40 and ≥85 is very low ( ). Finally, our results reflect oral estrogen–progestin use, because detailed data on use of patches, creams, suppositories, and injections were not available from NHANES throughout the duration of the study period. Notably, we previously reported that 90% of women reporting use of postmenopausal hormones in NHANES during 1999–2010 used oral preparations ( ). Our results show the evolution of estrogen–progestin use during a 40 year period in which the evidence base for benefits and harms grew from nearly no evidence, to a steadily increasing number of observational studies, and finally to randomized trial data ( , – ). While demonstrating the capacity for the clinical community to rapidly respond to new evidence, these trends also illustrate susceptibility towards elevated prescription use in the absence of definitive evidence. Future studies evaluating the use of low-dose, short duration, and other alternative postmenopausal hormone preparations will be needed to study the next chapter of hormone therapy in the US.

documents.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin Thromboembolism in Pregnancy

chunks.content: 1. Introduction Recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA) is a complex and multifactorial reproductive disorder with significant clinical and emotional implications. Traditionally, RSA has been defined as the occurrence of three or more consecutive pregnancy losses before 28 weeks of gestation with the same partner. However, recent evidence suggests that the risk of recurrence after two losses is comparable to that after three, prompting revisions in diagnostic criteria. The European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) recommends the diagnosis of RSA after two or more consecutive miscarriages, while the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) defines RSA as two or more pregnancy losses occurring before the 20th week of gestation [ , ]. RSA affects approximately 1% to 2% of couples attempting to conceive [ ]. Despite advances in diagnostic modalities, the etiology remains unexplained in nearly 50% of cases. Among the recognized causes, the four most significant are maternal immunological abnormalities (including autoimmune diseases such as antiphospholipid syndrome and alloimmune responses), thrombotic predispositions (both inherited and acquired), uterine anatomical anomalies, and endocrine dysfunctions [ ]. Although embryonic chromosomal aberrations are a common cause of miscarriage, parental chromosomal abnormalities account for only 5–7% of RSA cases [ ]. The contributions of infections and male-related genetic factors remain controversial and insufficiently elucidated [ ]. In recent years, the role of immune dysregulation has gained increasing attention, with reproductive immunology studies attributing over 60% of unexplained miscarriages to immune dysfunction [ ]. Increasing evidence suggests that inherited thrombophilias may play a role in pregnancy complications through mechanisms related to hypercoagulability and impaired placental perfusion [ ]. Cytogenetic evaluations in RSA have revealed that chromosomal anomalies in one of the partners are present in up to 7% of affected couples [ ]. While the female partner has traditionally been the focus of genetic evaluation, recent findings underscore the potential contribution of paternal genetic variants, although conclusive evidence remains limited [ ]. Among maternal genetic risk factors, SNPs in the methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase ( MTHFR ) gene are of particular interest due to their role in homocysteine metabolism. Reduced MTHFR activity, due to gene polymorphisms, can lead to hyperhomocysteinemia, which promotes endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and platelet aggregation—all of which contribute to placental insufficiency and pregnancy loss [ , ]. Two common polymorphisms—C677T and A1298C—have been extensively studied. Compound heterozygosity (C677T/A1298C) may result in a comparable clinical phenotype to homozygosity for C677T. Associations between the MTHFR C677T variant and RSA have been reported in numerous studies, though findings remain inconsistent and sometimes contradictory [ ]. In addition to MTHFR , other heritable thrombophilias such as F5 Leiden and the F2 G20210A mutation have been implicated in RSA. In pregnant women, this mutation has been associated with placental thrombosis, fetal loss, preeclampsia, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), and stillbirth. However, the association between F5 Leiden and RSA varies across studies, and the risk is considered modest in most cases [ , ]. Consequently, routine screening for F5 Leiden is not recommended in all RSA cases, but may be considered in patients with a personal or family history of thrombosis [ ]. The F2 G20210A mutation is another significant prothrombotic variant that leads to elevated plasma prothrombin levels. Although heterozygosity for this mutation is associated with a two- to three-fold increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and pregnancy complications, its precise contribution to RSA remains a subject of debate. While some meta-analyses have supported its association with pregnancy loss, especially in the second and third trimesters, clinical guidelines from ASRM and ACOG advise against universal screening due to insufficient evidence that such testing alters clinical outcomes [ , ]. While individual thrombophilic polymorphisms have been extensively studied, less attention has been given to the potential synergistic effects of multiple genetic variants in patients with recurrent pregnancy loss. Therefore, the present study aimed to evaluate the association between several thrombophilia-related polymorphisms and recurrent pregnancy loss in a cohort of affected women. 2. Results 2.1. Participant Demographics and Pregnancy Loss Data The patients included in the study were between 23 and 39 years of age, with a variance of 15.11%. The mean age was 30.45 years (SD ±3.89), which was very close to the group’s median age of 30 years, indicating a relatively homogeneous age distribution among participants. The number of pregnancy losses experienced by participants ranged from two to five. In most cases—specifically, 64% of the women—two miscarriages had occurred, highlighting a predominance of patients with fewer but recurrent losses within the study group. A Spearman correlation analysis was conducted to explore the relationship between the number of miscarriages and the participants’ age. The results indicated a very weak positive correlation (ρ = +0.111; p = 0.383), suggesting that as age increased, the number of miscarriages tended to increase slightly, although this trend was not statistically significant. Given the lack

a relatively homogeneous age distribution among participants. The number of pregnancy losses experienced by participants ranged from two to five. In most cases—specifically, 64% of the women—two miscarriages had occurred, highlighting a predominance of patients with fewer but recurrent losses within the study group. A Spearman correlation analysis was conducted to explore the relationship between the number of miscarriages and the participants’ age. The results indicated a very weak positive correlation (ρ = +0.111; p = 0.383), suggesting that as age increased, the number of miscarriages tended to increase slightly, although this trend was not statistically significant. Given the lack of significance ( p > 0.05), the observed correlation cannot be considered meaningful, nor can it be generalized to the broader population. These findings underscore the multifactorial nature of recurrent pregnancy loss, indicating that maternal age alone, at least within this age range, is not a strong predictive factor in this study cohort— . 2.2. Prevalence of SNPs The most frequently identified SNPs in the study population were the heterozygous variants of the MTHFR gene, with a prevalence of 53.1% for the A1298C polymorphism and 57.8% for the C677T polymorphism. Among the homozygous SNPs, the highest prevalence was also observed in the MTHFR C677T variant, present in 12.5% of participants, followed by MTHFR A1298C and PAI-1 4G/5G, each found in 7.8% of cases. Analysis of combined SNPs revealed several noteworthy patterns of association. Among individuals carrying the heterozygous F5 Leiden G1691A mutation, 55.6% also carried the heterozygous MTHFR A1298C mutation, 33.3% had the heterozygous MTHFR C677T mutation, and 11.1% had the homozygous MTHFR C677T mutation. This suggests a significant overlap between thrombophilic and folate pathway SNPs in this subgroup— . PAI-1 and factor XIII had no statistical relevance. Furthermore, both of the participants identified with the heterozygous PTM G20210A mutation also carried the heterozygous MTHFR C677T mutation, and one of them also presented with a heterozygous MTHFR A1298C mutation. These findings highlight a pattern of co-occurrence between SNPs involved in coagulation (such as FVL and PTM) and those affecting homocysteine metabolism (such as MTHFR), which may contribute cumulatively to the risk of recurrent pregnancy loss. Such associations underscore the importance of evaluating combined genetic risk factors in the assessment of thrombophilia-related pregnancy complications— . 2.3. Factor V Leiden (G1691A) Mutation and Association with Pregnancy Loss The median age rank was slightly higher among women who were heterozygous for the F5 Leiden (G1691A) mutation (mean rank: 38.11) compared to those with other types of SNPs (mean rank: 31.58). However, this difference was not statistically significant ( p = 0.327), indicating that age alone is not a major differentiating factor between carriers of the F5 Leiden mutation and other participants in the study. In contrast, the number of pregnancy losses appeared to be more strongly associated with the presence of the heterozygous F5 Leiden mutation. The Kruskal–Wallis test revealed a statistically significant difference ( p = 0.001), with women carrying the heterozygous mutation experiencing, on average, 3 to 4 miscarriages. This was notably higher than the average of 2 to 3 miscarriages among women without this mutation. These findings suggest a potential link between the F5 Leiden mutation and increased susceptibility to recurrent pregnancy loss— . The impact of heterozygous F5 Leiden SNPs (OR) on the occurrence of 4–5 pregnancy losses was 55.6%. 2.4. Prothrombin Gene Mutation (Factor II—G20210A) and Pregnancy Loss The Kruskal–Wallis test revealed that the patients carrying the heterozygous F2 G20210A gene mutation experienced a higher number of pregnancy losses (four miscarriages each), in contrast to the average of 2–3 losses observed in women with other types of SNPs. This difference was statistically significant ( p = 0.030), suggesting a potential association between the G20210A mutation and an increased risk of recurrent pregnancy loss. These findings support previous studies indicating that the G20210A mutation may contribute to a hypercoagulable state, potentially affecting placental circulation and increasing the likelihood of miscarriage, particularly in women with a history of multiple pregnancy losses— . 2.5. MTHFR A1298C Mutation and Recurrent Pregnancy Loss The Kruskal–Wallis test showed that the number of miscarriages tended to be higher in women with the MTHFR A1298C homozygous mutation, who experienced on average 3–4 pregnancy losses, compared to those with either no mutation or a heterozygous mutation, who experienced an average of 2–3 losses. This difference was statistically significant ( p = 0.012), indicating a potential association between the homozygous MTHFR A1298C genotype and increased risk of recurrent pregnancy loss. These findings suggest that the homozygous variant of MTHFR A1298C may have a more pronounced impact on pregnancy outcomes, possibly due to its effect on folate metabolism and homocysteine levels, both of which are critical for placental and fetal development— . The odds ratio (OR) analysis further emphasized the clinical impact of the MTHFR A1298C mutation: Among women

those with either no mutation or a heterozygous mutation, who experienced an average of 2–3 losses. This difference was statistically significant ( p = 0.012), indicating a potential association between the homozygous MTHFR A1298C genotype and increased risk of recurrent pregnancy loss. These findings suggest that the homozygous variant of MTHFR A1298C may have a more pronounced impact on pregnancy outcomes, possibly due to its effect on folate metabolism and homocysteine levels, both of which are critical for placental and fetal development— . The odds ratio (OR) analysis further emphasized the clinical impact of the MTHFR A1298C mutation: Among women with the homozygous mutation, the predicted probability of experiencing four miscarriages was 80%. Among those with the heterozygous mutation, the probability of experiencing 4–5 miscarriages was 27.6%. These findings support the hypothesis that the homozygous MTHFR A1298C genotype may contribute more significantly to severe forms of recurrent pregnancy loss. 2.6. MTHFR C677T Mutation and Age Correlation Analysis of mean rank values revealed that women with the homozygous MTHFR C677T mutation tended to be significantly younger compared to those with the heterozygous or wild-type genotypes. The Kruskal–Wallis test indicated that this difference reached the threshold of statistical significance ( p = 0.050). This result may suggest an earlier onset or earlier detection of pregnancy loss in women with the homozygous C677T genotype, although further studies are needed to explore the biological mechanisms behind this trend— . The Kruskal–Wallis test demonstrated that the number of pregnancy losses was significantly higher among women with the homozygous MTHFR C677T mutation. On average, these women experienced 3–4 miscarriages, compared to an average of 2 miscarriages among those with the heterozygous mutation, and approximately 3 miscarriages in women without this mutation. The difference in the distribution of pregnancy loss across these three groups was statistically significant ( p = 0.001), indicating a strong association between the homozygous MTHFR C677T genotype and a higher frequency of miscarriage. These results reinforce existing evidence that the homozygous form of the C677T mutation in the MTHFR gene may significantly impair folate metabolism, leading to elevated homocysteine levels and subsequent vascular complications, including impaired placental function. This disruption may contribute to early pregnancy loss, particularly in women with the TT genotype— . The odds ratio (OR) analysis suggests a strong association between the MTHFR C677T mutation and the number of pregnancy losses. Notably, all women in our cohort who were homozygous for the C677T mutation experienced 3–4 miscarriages, indicating a possible link between this genotype and increased miscarriage burden. In contrast, among women with heterozygous SNPs, the probability of experiencing 3–4 miscarriages was considerably lower, at 16.2%. While these observations support the potential clinical relevance of the homozygous MTHFR C677T genotype in the context of recurrent pregnancy loss, they must be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size. Further studies with larger cohorts are warranted to confirm these findings and determine their generalizability. Nonetheless, our results underscore the potential utility of targeted genetic screening, particularly in women with idiopathic RSA and suspected thrombotic or metabolic predispositions. 2.7. Multivariate Analysis of Mutation Combinations and Risk of Pregnancy Loss The multivariate analysis revealed that when the most frequently encountered SNPs— MTHFR A1298C, MTHFR C677T, F5 Leiden—are analyzed in combination, the resulting model supports the possibility that these associations may contribute cumulatively to an increased risk of recurrent pregnancy loss. The model does not exclude any of these combined SNPs as potential contributing factors, underlining the complexity and multifactorial nature of early pregnancy loss. Of particular interest is the prognostic impact of specific mutation combinations: When homozygous MTHFR C677T SNPs are combined with heterozygous MTHFR A1298C SNPs, the predicted probability of experiencing four miscarriages rises to 96.2%. In cases where both MTHFR C677T and MTHFR A1298C SNPs are present in the heterozygous form, the probability of having four miscarriages is substantially lower, estimated at only 4%. However, if these two heterozygous MTHFR SNPs are combined with the heterozygous F5 Leiden mutation, the risk increases significantly, with a 76.3% probability of experiencing four miscarriages. These findings emphasize the synergistic effect of co-existing genetic SNPs, which may substantially alter the reproductive prognosis and should be considered when evaluating patients with a history of recurrent spontaneous abortions— . This data supports the hypothesis that combinatorial genetic screening—rather than evaluating individual SNPs in isolation—may be more informative in predicting reproductive risk and guiding clinical management for women with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss— . Our comprehensive analysis of the relationship between combinations of gene polymorphisms— F5 Leiden (G1691A), MTHFR C677T, and MTHFR A1298C—and the number of pregnancy losses, using both observed and predicted frequencies, showed the likelihood of spontaneous abortion. Each combination was assessed for its likelihood to be associated with 2, 3, 4, or 5 miscarriages. The analysis reveals several patterns that highlight the
