These methods have similar acceptable performances and therefore it may be advantageous for clarity and ease of application to adopt the double false discovery method, which is simple to apply and performs better than just the false discovery method. The most important step after the statistical analysis is a process of expert prioritization of the signals produced [ , ], involving expert opinion, review of the literature, biological plausibility, strength of the signals, and further analysis of the data. The potential for conducting signal‐detection studies in the distributed database is to be explored, but is likely to be complex and initially lengthy until replicable processes are established and tested. 3.5 <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CA</styled-content> Case Series for New Medications Where a medication is new to the market, there are no previous signals to test, and, initially, there are not enough exposed pregnancies for a full study, an annual case series of exposed cases may allow an evaluation in the early years of whether any specific CA (or combination of CAs) stands out in unusual proportions. The potential for these population‐based case series to be evaluated alongside spontaneous adverse event reports has not yet been realized. 3.6 Prevalence and Ecological Studies Evaluating Population‐Level Exposures Prevalence studies can be used to evaluate preventive interventions e.g., the EUROmediCAT central database has been used to monitor the prevalence of valproic acid syndrome over time [ ]. Ecological studies of CA prevalence in relation to pandemics (the H1N1 flu pandemic [ ], and more recently the Covid‐19 pandemic) can consider the overall impact on CA prevalence (all and specific CA) of population exposure to infection, treatment, and vaccine. 3.7 Medication Utilisation Studies Medication utilization studies can only be conducted using the EUROmediCAT distributed database, as data on all pregnancies/births is required. Such studies do not require the CA registry data and thus can include other databases also [ , , , ]. These studies can be used to evaluate regulatory actions, for example, changes in prescription of valproic acid in pregnancy before and after the change in advice from EMA in 2014 [ , ]. We also recommend that medication utilization studies be twinned with risk studies [ , , ] to assess expected levels of exposure, differences between countries, changes in prescribing over time, prescribing patterns prior to and during pregnancy, and potential confounders such as maternal age. New approaches to characterizing medication utilization in pregnancy could in future lead to CA risk studies with a more sophisticated exposure classification [ ]. 4 Strengths and Limitations The impact of the research arising from EUROmediCAT demonstrates the value of this long‐standing collaboration, combining high quality standardized CA data with a large population size and multidisciplinary expertise. For example, research on valproic acid [ ], lamotrigine [ ], and metformin [ ] using the central database, and SSRIs [ ] using the distributed database, has contributed to prescribing guidelines for pregnancy [ , , , ]. As well as addressing the evidence gap concerning existing medicines, EUROmediCAT can continue to meet new challenges, such as pandemics [ , , ], new medicines, and new vaccines. CA registries are an essential data source contributing to both the EUROmediCAT central database and distributed database, since the quality of data on CA in healthcare databases is poor for many types of CA. Studies based on healthcare databases alone suffer from a number of limitations which include small population sizes; lack of data on TOPFA or restriction to livebirths; lack of data on CA diagnosed after the neonatal period; incomplete diagnostic information so that specific CA subgroups cannot be reliably studied and genetic syndromes cannot be excluded; and poorly validated coding of CA in healthcare databases, with low sensitivity and low positive predictive value for many conditions [ , , ], poor distinction between suspected and confirmed CA diagnoses, and incomplete and biased ascertainment from surgical procedures. Medication exposure ascertainment incompleteness or inaccuracy (particularly with regard to timing) may lead to bias, depending on study design, and/or loss of statistical power. Case‐malformed control study design mitigates against bias as similar levels of underascertainment are expected in both cases and malformed controls. Exposed cases and controls are individually checked by registries for each study using the central database to verify exposure timing in the first trimester. To the extent that inaccuracies remain, this non‐differential bias would lead to dilution of odds ratios. Cohort studies using the distributed database, containing linked prescription data, may also have some bias linked to the recording of medications which were not taken, or taken at a different time, or prescriptions issued outside the time window for analysis but taken within the time window

Exposed cases and controls are individually checked by registries for each study using the central database to verify exposure timing in the first trimester. To the extent that inaccuracies remain, this non‐differential bias would lead to dilution of odds ratios. Cohort studies using the distributed database, containing linked prescription data, may also have some bias linked to the recording of medications which were not taken, or taken at a different time, or prescriptions issued outside the time window for analysis but taken within the time window of exposure. Given the prospective nature of the exposure data, the bias is expected to be non‐differential leading to dilution of odds ratios. While the EUROmediCAT network covers a large population, both with the central database and the distributed database, there is potential for expansion, both in the size of the European population covered (by both EUROCAT registries and healthcare databases), and its geographical and socioeconomic diversity. Several new CA registries are expected to join in 2026. There is also potential for improvement in the sources of exposure data available, for example, improved recording of medication exposure in antenatal records, and the inclusion of in‐patient hospital prescriptions in healthcare databases. Linkage between healthcare databases with the use of civil identification numbers or healthcare identification numbers is now possible in many countries, although accurate linkage of mothers and babies is lagging behind. Some countries have provided safe ways of accessing anonymized data, but processes to obtain permission and access may be lengthy and need to be streamlined for pharmacovigilance using the distributed database. The establishment of European data safe havens where individual patient data (IPD) from all European countries can be accessed needs to occur to enable the optimum analysis of IPD across Europe. 5 Conclusions EUROmediCAT presents a unique data and expert resource for tackling the enormous evidence gap regarding the safety of medication during pregnancy, contributing to the prevention of congenital anomalies, and to the opportunity for optimal treatment of pregnant women balancing the benefits and harm of medication. chunks.content: Introduction More than 20% of US mothers experience depression during pregnancy and the postpartum period, which is consistent with global rates [ ]. Untreated depression can contribute to long-term health problems [ ], including cognitive and emotional challenges for children and unhealthy maternal behaviors, such as alcohol or drug use, insufficient physical activity, and poor diet [ ]. Furthermore, 1 in 5 women with perinatal depression expresses thoughts of self-harm, with suicide being a leading cause of maternal death [ ]. While 40% to 50% of women with perinatal depression have a history of depression, the remainder experience depression onset for the first time during their pregnancy or in the early postpartum period [ ]. Currently, the United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends early identification of perinatal women at risk of developing depression to facilitate preventive rather than reactive care [ ]. However, implementing this recommendation requires accurate identification of risk prior to depression onset. This identification is particularly challenging for those without a history of depression, who may not recognize and self-report the onset of early symptoms. There are documented factors associated with perinatal depression, including pregnancy-related stressors (eg, financial instability, fear of the birth experience, and body image concerns); psychosocial stressors (eg, lack of social support, adverse life events, history of anxiety, and food insecurity); physical health conditions (eg, gestational diabetes and hypertension); and race or ethnicity (eg, Black and Latinx individuals). Nevertheless, little is known about which combination of factors most accurately predicts future risk of developing perinatal depression. Moreover, current perinatal depression screening tools administered during prenatal care are designed to quantify active depression symptoms and do not identify risk factors for future depressive episodes [ ]. In response to this gap, we developed an interpretable machine learning–based predictive screener that can be administered directly to patients in the first trimester to identify those at risk of developing depression for the first time during pregnancy [ ]. This 6-question predictive screener was designed to identify individuals who will develop new-onset depression among those who are currently asymptomatic and have no history of depression. The screener was co-designed with clinicians and people with lived experience through an iterative process, including focus groups with providers (eg, obstetricians, family medicine physicians, and behavioral health professionals) and virtual community engagement studios with pregnant and postpartum women, the details of which are described in a prior publication [ ]. The predictive screener was shown to have a high degree of accuracy (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve=0.93), sensitivity (0.90), and specificity (0.81) [ ]. However, the ultimate usefulness of this risk screening tool will be in its adoption into clinical workflow and its acceptability to the patients completing it. To fully close the loop, successful implementation also requires the provision of preventive care in response to a positive screener score. A review encompassing 19 systematic reviews and meta-analyses and 152 randomized controlled trials across 26 countries identified therapy-based or physical activity interventions as having a small to moderate effect on the severity of perinatal depression symptoms [ ]. Interpersonal and cognitive behavioral therapy are similarly effective for perinatal depression prevention [ ]. Earlier therapeutic intervention can more effectively address perinatal mental health risk. With developments in predictive screening, there is an opportunity to tailor preventive care to address immediate, pressing risk factors (eg, food insecurity, labor and delivery fears, or lack of social support), while also developing strategies for long-term resilience to manage new and ongoing stressors. However, to date, patient-preferred preventive care options for those at risk of developing perinatal depression have not been documented. The majority of women receiving prenatal care in our clinical setting access their health care information through a patient portal. As such, deployment of prenatal risk screeners through the patient portal is our standard workflow and is increasingly common in obstetric practices nationally [ ]. Here, we examined the feasibility of deploying our predictive depression screener through our digital patient portal, as well as patients’ receptivity to completing it. To do this, we deployed the screener to women receiving first-trimester prenatal care in our health care system, followed by a survey on their experience with completing it. We also solicited their preferences for preventive care resources. Methods Study Design and Setting Participants were women (aged ≥18 years) receiving prenatal care from 1 of 4 University of Pittsburgh Medical Center obstetric practices. Electronic health records in the participating practices were screened for study eligibility on a weekly basis between October 2024 and January 2025. Eligibility criteria included being in the first trimester of pregnancy and screening negative for active first-trimester depressive symptoms using the Patient Health Questionnaire–9 [ ]. Eligible pregnant women were sent an invitation via their patient portal to complete the 6-question predictive screener and subsequent survey questions related to the screener.

preventive care resources. Methods Study Design and Setting Participants were women (aged ≥18 years) receiving prenatal care from 1 of 4 University of Pittsburgh Medical Center obstetric practices. Electronic health records in the participating practices were screened for study eligibility on a weekly basis between October 2024 and January 2025. Eligibility criteria included being in the first trimester of pregnancy and screening negative for active first-trimester depressive symptoms using the Patient Health Questionnaire–9 [ ]. Eligible pregnant women were sent an invitation via their patient portal to complete the 6-question predictive screener and subsequent survey questions related to the screener. The invitation contained a unique survey link that expired at the end of the first trimester. Upon accepting the link and completing informed consent, a pregnant woman was considered a study participant. Participants were not provided with a risk score. This allowed for independent validation of the screener in this population through passive observation of depressive symptoms and diagnoses over the course of the pregnancy. However, mental health and other pregnancy resources were provided to all participants, regardless of risk, to reflect best clinical practice. Measures Feasibility of screening was assessed by measuring (1) the proportion of pregnant women eligible from the larger clinical population ( eligibility rate ), (2) the number of eligible individuals who engaged with the screener study invitation ( reach ), and (3) the number of completed surveys among those who accessed the survey ( completion rate ). Acceptability was assessed with a series of Likert-scale questions (1=strongly disagree to 5=strongly agree), which included participant evaluations of screener question clarity (“The screener questions were clear”), ease of completion (“The screener was easy to complete”), and comfort with and honesty in disclosing responses (“I would be comfortable sharing my answers with my provider” and “I would have no concerns about answering the questions honestly,” respectively). Participants were asked about the usefulness of the screener as part of routine prenatal care, including the benefits of knowing the results of the screener (“What would be the benefit(s) to you personally of knowing you are likely to develop depression at some point during your pregnancy?”), their preferred method of receiving screener results (“If you completed a screener like this as part of your prenatal care, how would you prefer to receive your results?”), perceived helpfulness of knowing depression risk (“How helpful would it be to know whether you are likely to develop depression at some point during your pregnancy?”), and any concerns they might have if they were to learn that they were likely to develop depression at some point during their pregnancy (“What concern(s) would you personally have about knowing you are likely to develop depression at some point during your pregnancy?”). Participants were also asked to endorse from a prespecified list and/or offer open-ended options for desired preventive care resources (“If you learned you were likely to develop depression at some point in your pregnancy, which of the following resources would you be most likely to use if available to you at low or no-cost ?”) and offer any additional thoughts or comments they have about the survey or depression prevention (“We welcome any other thoughts you have about your participation in this survey or preventing depression in pregnancy.”). Deployment feasibility and acceptability of the screener were the primary outcomes of this study. Secondary analyses examined differences in attitudes between high- and low-risk pregnant women. Statistical Analysis Descriptive analyses used means and SDs for continuous variables (eg, maternal age), medians and IQRs for ordinal variables (eg, Likert-scale responses), and distributions for categorical variables. The study sample was stratified by screener score into those with and without risk of developing moderate to severe depression symptoms. Differences in survey responses by risk category were assessed using chi-square tests for categorical and binary responses. The distributions of continuous and Likert-scale responses were assessed for normality using the D’Agostino-Pearson test. Differences between normally distributed responses were evaluated using 2-sample 2-tailed t tests, and nonnormally distributed responses were evaluated using Mann-Whitney U tests. Effect size was calculated using Cliff d , a robust nonparametric method appropriate for ordinal data such as Likert-scale data [ ]. An α level of .05 was used for statistical significance. All respondents completed every survey item, resulting in no missing data. Analyses were performed using Python (version 3.12.4). Rapid inductive thematic coding was applied to open-ended survey responses by 2 coders, each with qualitative coding experience and one with formal training in rapid qualitative analysis. After reading all open-ended survey responses, the coders cocreated a codebook. Responses were then independently coded. Once independent coding was complete, codes were compared, and discrepancies were discussed until consensus (ie, consistent classification) was reached. We conducted pretests of the survey with pregnant or recently pregnant colleagues, gathering feedback on the design and clarity of the instructions and survey questions. Participants provided digital consent for study participation and were informed that they could withdraw their consent at any time. They received a US $20 gift card for completing the screener and follow-up survey, which took approximately 10 minutes. All participant data were stored in a confidential and secure manner and access was restricted to authorized members of the research team. Results Survey Participants: Reach and Risk During the study period, 1925 women received prenatal care at one of the participating obstetric practices. Of these 1925 women, 810 (42.1%) had an active patient portal, were at a gestational age of <14 weeks, and had scored <5 on the Patient Health Questionnaire–9 measure of active depression symptoms ( eligibility rate ). Of the 810 sent an invitation through their patient portal, only 2.8% (n=23) did not access it. In total, 36.7% (289/787) who accessed the invitation opened the study link ( reach ) and, of those, 88.2% (255/289) completed it ( completion rate ). All participants were female with a mean age of 32 (SD 4.5) years. Most were White (217/255, 85.1%) and non-Hispanic (232/255, 91%), married (196/255, 76.9%), and had commercial insurance (196/255, 76.9%). Full demographic information is available in . Participants were demographically representative of the larger eligible population. On the basis of established cutoff scores [ ], 80% (204/255) of participants were identified by the predictive screener as having no or minimal depression risk and 20% (51/255) were identified as at risk of developing moderate to severe depression at a later stage of pregnancy. Acceptability The predictive screener demonstrated high acceptability among participants. Most agreed or strongly agreed (236/255, 92.5%) that the screener questions were clear (median 5, IQR 4-5), and 97.3% (248/255) reported that the questions were easy to complete (median 5, IQR 5-5). Most (236/255, 92.5%) agreed or strongly agreed that they would feel comfortable sharing the results of the screener with their obstetric care team providers (median 5, IQR 4-5). Similarly, the majority (247/255, 96.9%) agreed or strongly agreed that they would have no concerns about answering the questions honestly (median 5, IQR 5-5). presents acceptability metrics stratified by depression risk category, with those at risk of developing moderate-to-severe depression symptoms being less likely to endorse strong agreement with comfort and ease of honesty in responding to the screener. Perspectives on Receiving Depression Screening Scores Overall, 80% (204/255) reported that the screener was helpful or extremely helpful (median 4, IQR 4-5). Participants largely voiced a preference for receiving screener results through the patient portal (150/255, 58.8%), compared to receiving results in person (76/255, 29.8%) or by phone (13/255, 5.1%). Perspectives did not differ by depression risk. Perceived Benefits and Risks of Depression Risk Screening When asked about potential benefits of receiving their depression risk screening score, participants most frequently cited seeking appropriate preventive resources and/or treatments (63/204, 30.9%) and the opportunity to receive education from their obstetric health provider (53/204, 26%). One survey participant wrote that the feedback could help them “reduce risk factors associated with postpartum depression and postpartum psychosis.” Despite generally positive attitudes toward score disclosure, participants also expressed concerns. The most frequently reported concerns included increased anxiety or worry about developing depression (71/204, 34.8%) and worry about the inability to prevent depression (34/204, 16.7%). Several open-ended responses were offered, including concern about parenting ability and emotional connection to children if depression were to occur, premature medication use, and false positives. Participants at risk of developing moderate to severe depression were significantly more likely than those with no or minimal depression risk to endorse the concern “fear that your health care provider will view you negatively” (5.9% vs 0.5%; P =.03). However, at-risk participants were also more likely to cite the ability to identify factors that might be affecting their mood as a benefit (17.6% vs 5.9%; P =.01). presents the complete breakdown of perceived benefits and risks. Desired Preventive Care Resources When asked about desired preventive health resources, participants endorsed multiple options. Preferred resources included counseling (197/255, 77.3%), with 61.8% (126/197) endorsing in-person therapy and 41.6% (82/197) endorsing app-based delivery. Mind- or body-based interventions (166/255, 65.1%) were frequently endorsed, with “yoga, exercise classes, or gym membership” (114/166, 68.7%) being a highly desired intervention, followed by prenatal classes or support groups (81/255, 31.8%). Participants (n=61) shared several resources not otherwise listed in open-ended responses. From most to least frequently listed, these included mental health resources for their spouse or support person (eg, “Education for family/spouses so they can possibly help the individual battling depression”), self-care opportunities (eg, “massage”), practical support such as cleaning services or meal preparation (eg, “A service similar to task rabbit that is geared towards pregnancy needs. Perhaps people that could help identify inexpensive sources of second hand furniture/items, assembly help, specific errand support, meal prep/planning for once baby arrives, etc.”), parental leave, increased medical touchpoints during pregnancy, additional mental health education (eg, books and fact sheets), medication for depression prevention, structural changes (eg, improved health care access and transportation), access to a live mental health support person (“Mental health support chat forums with a licensed counselor”), a more holistic approach to health care, and additional faith or spiritual support. shows preferred resources stratified by depression risk. Notably, less than 10% (20/204) of those with no or minimal depression risk expressed interest in childcare support compared to more than 25% (14/51) of those at risk of developing moderate to severe depression ( χ 2 1 =9.52; n=255; P =.002). Although highly endorsed by both risk groups, participants with no or minimal depression risk expressed greater interest in exercise opportunities ( χ 2 1 =3.94; n=255; P =.05). Open-Ended Feedback After completing the survey, 55.3% (141/255) of participants shared optional thoughts about screener participation and about preventing depression in pregnancy. The most frequent open-ended comments expressed appreciation for the study or confirmed that participants would find a screener of this kind helpful. Additional responses ranged from suggestions for the screener or resources (eg, “A big area of concern for working moms is their jobs. I felt that the questions did not address the concern as much.”) to specific stressors (eg, “I think one of the biggest stressors that can contribute greatly to mood in the first trimester is the viability and health/wellness of the baby, i.e., risk of miscarriage or is there any genetic or chromosomal issue?”) and barriers to care (“I feel like cost is one of the biggest barriers to seeking help, just ahead of the stigma that still exists.”). One participant reported feeling that a discussion of depression may exacerbate depressive symptoms. Those at risk of developing moderate to severe depression more frequently expressed the need for help and social support during pregnancy, while those with no or minimal depression risk largely highlighted the need for depression- and anxiety-specific resources. Discussion Principal Findings This study demonstrates the acceptability of a machine learning–based predictive screener designed to support perinatal depression prevention. Predictive screening is an emerging field, and, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to examine receptivity to a predictive mental health screener, to query pregnant women about their desired preventive care options, and to examine differences in desired resources by predicted risk level. While machine learning algorithms are being newly applied to mental health prediction, their ultimate success depends on adoption into clinical workflow, which requires patient engagement and a feasible implementation process [ ]. Here, we highlight an approach to evaluating receptivity to such predictive screeners while testing the feasibility of sending the screener through our health care system’s digital patient portal. In this study, pregnant women who completed the screener largely reported positive screener experiences, with over 90% agreeing that it was clear, easy, and comfortable to respond to and that they had no concerns about responding honestly. More than 80% thought it would be helpful to know their risk of developing depression symptoms during pregnancy, regardless of their risk score. Those at risk of developing moderate to severe depression were slightly more likely to report feeling uncomfortable sharing their honest responses with an obstetric health care provider, suggesting that the screener questions touch on risk factors

system’s digital patient portal. In this study, pregnant women who completed the screener largely reported positive screener experiences, with over 90% agreeing that it was clear, easy, and comfortable to respond to and that they had no concerns about responding honestly. More than 80% thought it would be helpful to know their risk of developing depression symptoms during pregnancy, regardless of their risk score. Those at risk of developing moderate to severe depression were slightly more likely to report feeling uncomfortable sharing their honest responses with an obstetric health care provider, suggesting that the screener questions touch on risk factors that are challenging to disclose. Perceived benefits and risks of the screener were similar between the no- or minimal-risk and at-risk groups, with 2 exceptions: those at risk of developing depression reported greater value in the screener for helping them understand contributors to their mood. They also reported greater fear about being judged by their provider. These anticipated challenges may be grounded in stigma and prior experiences of discrimination [ ]. Deploying the screener through the patient portal reached a little more than one-third of the eligible pregnant women receiving prenatal care in the participating obstetric practices. This suggests that in-person screening may need to be offered as part of a clinical workflow to deploy the screener effectively to a majority of the patient population. However, among those who initiated the screening survey, engagement was encouraging, with almost 90% of participants completing the entire screening process. Thus, if the eligible patient reach is optimized through multiple outreach channels, the screener could have a high completion rate. Survey participants identified specific perceived benefits and concerns associated with learning about being at risk of developing depression symptoms. The desire for therapy, whether in person or through an app, is reflective of the current best practices for preventive care, which include cognitive behavioral therapy and interpersonal therapy. Notably, participants also reported a desire for exercise opportunities and support groups, echoing research showing the protective effects of physical activity and social support on depression [ ]. Child care was highly desired among the study population at risk of developing moderate to severe depression, suggesting that direct tangible support may impact the trajectory of depression risk. Financial stressors during pregnancy have previously been associated with poor outcomes for both mothers and infants. Findings from recent studies of guaranteed income programs for perinatal women show promising evidence of improvements in maternal mental health and infant developmental outcomes associated with alleviating financial stress [ ]. This study contributes to a burgeoning literature on the importance of providing preventive mental health care during pregnancy and the postpartum period [ ]. The perinatal period is uniquely vulnerable to depression due to a combination of hormonal changes, novel stressors (eg, pregnancy-related anxiety), and environmental factors [ ]. However, up to half of the cases remain undiagnosed [ ]. Although women without a psychiatric history are at lower baseline risk, they are more likely to be overlooked when they do experience depression, with lower rates of both depression screening and referral to care [ ]. One solution to address the lack of diagnosis is more frequent, routine depression screening [ ]. Care navigators dedicated to monitoring mental health symptoms throughout pregnancy, for example, have been shown to improve depressive symptoms among the patients they serve [ ]. However, to date, there have been no screening tools available to support those professionals in identifying risk among individuals not actively reporting depressive symptoms [ ]. If successfully implemented, predictive screeners could make the work of such care navigators more targeted and efficient. Limitations This study has several limitations. Eligible participants were limited to those who could be contacted through an active patient portal. Although most of our prenatal patients have an active patient portal account, it is possible that these portals are not frequently accessed. Other studies suggest that individuals with limited health literacy are less likely to use patient portals to access health information [ ]. Thus, the moderate response rate may introduce selection bias if individuals more familiar with portal-based screening were more likely to participate, whereas those with lower health literacy were less likely to engage. There were some differences in responses by participant risk level. Although these differences seem intuitive (eg, participants with greater depression risk were more likely to find the screener helpful in identifying influences on mood yet were more concerned about potential stigma from providers), they should be interpreted with caution given the modest sample size of the at-risk group and the number of comparisons conducted. The study sample was generally representative of the patient population of the academic medical system in which it was conducted, and the survey was developed using a patient-centered design approach with a diverse population. However, the results cannot be generalized

in responses by participant risk level. Although these differences seem intuitive (eg, participants with greater depression risk were more likely to find the screener helpful in identifying influences on mood yet were more concerned about potential stigma from providers), they should be interpreted with caution given the modest sample size of the at-risk group and the number of comparisons conducted. The study sample was generally representative of the patient population of the academic medical system in which it was conducted, and the survey was developed using a patient-centered design approach with a diverse population. However, the results cannot be generalized to other health care systems in the United States or to clinics with more diverse patient populations. While the screener showed high accuracy within the sample on which it was built [ ], further work is needed to establish independent external validation. Additional research must address how to best implement this screener within our health care system, including a testing workflow to fully close the loop on preventive care. A future goal would be to conduct validation and acceptability research of the screener in non-US populations. Conclusions This study is a first step toward understanding how a machine learning–based prevention-focused predictive depression screener can be integrated into a clinical workflow for preventive care. We found that only one-third of the eligible pregnant women in our clinics completed the screener via their digital patient portal. Ultimately, deploying preventive screening tools will require a hybrid digital and in-person screening approach to comprehensively screen all pregnant women who may be at risk of developing perinatal depression. Our risk screener was designed to identify individuals who may need additional evaluation and care from a trained provider. As such, it is intended as a supplement to current prenatal care, allowing for earlier identification of those at risk rather than serving as a replacement for professional mental health evaluation. Our findings suggest that the screener was acceptable to those who completed it. Moreover, participants voiced clear preferences for certain forms of preventive care in response to learning their risk. Participants’ preference for receiving predictive depression screening results through the patient portal suggests a promising approach to expanding access to mental health assessment among individuals already engaged with digital health platforms. Our findings also suggest some next steps on how to inform the clinical workflow to support a more personalized approach to preventive care in pregnancy, leveraging the most endorsed preventive care resources (eg, counseling, peer support groups, exercise, and childcare support) to address the individual risk factors identified by the predictive screener.

chunks.content: Introduction Cervical cerclage is the recommended treatment for patients diagnosed with cervical insufficiency. , Although a cerclage can prevent preterm birth in cases of cervical insufficiency, the mechanism of cerclage efficacy is not clear. Investigators have hypothesized that cerclage success relates to improved compressive support for cervical tissue. - Additionally, investigators have posited that a cerclage prevents ascending intrauterine infection (IUI) by improving the immunological barrier between the fetal compartment and vaginal microbes. , It is likely that increased cervical compression leads to improved barrier function. However, statements about cervical barrier function are based on inferences from clinical studies in humans. There is no animal model of cervical insufficiency that permits study of the cervical barrier. Patients who present with cervical insufficiency often have coexisting intraamniotic infection or inflammation. - Bacteria gain access to uterine cavity via multiple paths, but the most common path is ascending from the vagina through the cervix. Prior studies using amniocentesis have documented that for patients presenting with cervical dilation in the midtrimester, the prevalence of intrauterine infection and intrauterine inflammation was 51% and 81%, respectively. , Ascending IUI and inflammation provoke an inflammatory response leading to preterm contractions and preterm birth. The murine model of ascending IUI has been used to study the natural history of ascending IUI by inoculating the vagina of the pregnant mouse with pathogenic and non-pathogenic bacteria. - The model has revealed important aspects of cervical barrier function. Investigators have reported that increased ascending IUI was associated with co-existing viral infection in the cervix ; with hyaluronan depletion in the cervical epithelium ; with Gardnerella vaginalis infection ; and with virulence factors associated with Streptococcus agalactiae. , Using bioluminescent bacterial strains, investigators have demonstrated the time course, dose dependency and fetal effects of ascending IUI. , However, improvement of the cervical barrier with cerclage has not been studied using this murine model of ascending infection. Motivated by 1) the lack of clarity for the mechanism of cerclage efficacy, 2) the observation that ascending IUI is a common cause of preterm birth and 3) the presence of intrauterine infection in cases of cerclage failure, our purpose was twofold. First, we tested the hypothesis that cerclage improves cervical barrier function leading to decreased ascending intrauterine infection in the mouse model. Second, we studied whether cerclage prevents intrauterine inflammation associated with preterm birth in the mouse. An intraabdominal cerclage was placed because a vaginal cerclage was not feasible in the mouse model. Materials and Methods Bacterial strains Two Escherichia coli ( E. coli ) bacterial strains were used in the study. E. coli K12 MG1655 and E. coli K1 (serotype 018ac:K1:H7) were purchased from ATCC. The bacteria were cultured aerobically at 37°C in sterile, non-selective LB broth. Nonpathogenic E. coli K12 were used for bioluminescent imaging while pathogenic E. coli K1 were used to provoke preterm birth and intrauterine inflammation. E. coli K1 contains the K1 capsular polysaccharide antigen, which is associated with meningitis in newborn infants. Animals Animal care and the experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with National Institute of Health guidelines and approved by the Tufts Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. The C57BL/6 mice were obtained from the Jackson laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME). All mice were kept in a temperature and humidity-controlled facility with 12:12-h day/night light cycle. Standard laboratory food and water were provided ad libitum. Abdominal cerclage An abdominal cerclage was used because a vaginal cerclage is not feasible in mice. Female adult mice (12 to 14 weeks) were housed with males and pregnancy was detected by the presence of a vaginal plug (considered day 0). At E10, a suture (6-0 silk, #1639G, Ethicon) was placed around the cervix via laparotomy ( ). A video showing the surgery can be seen in the . The cerclage was placed just below the junction of the two uterine horns. The cervix was transilluminated to assure the cerclage enclosed the entire cervix while avoiding uterine vessels. The cerclage knot was tied such that the cerclage compressed the cervical lumen ( , ). The anatomical position of the cerclage in the mouse was analogous to an abdominal cerclage in humans. The abdominal cerclage was chosen because it was not possible to place a cerclage using a vaginal approach. Sham control mice received the same laparotomy surgery except no cerclage was placed. Following surgery, mice were placed in individual cages and monitored daily for three days. Construction of bioluminescent <italic toggle="yes">E.coli</italic> K12 The bacterial lux operon from Photorhabdus luminescence (pAKlux2.1 plasmid) was used to genetically modify E. coli K12, a non-pathogenic laboratory strain according to a previous protocol. The pAKlux2.1 plasmid was a gift from Attila Karsi (Addgene plasmid # 14081; http://n2t.net/addgene : 14081 ; RRID:Addgene_14081), and expresses lux genes under the lacZ promoter. The pAKlux2.1 plasmid was isolated from its growth

place a cerclage using a vaginal approach. Sham control mice received the same laparotomy surgery except no cerclage was placed. Following surgery, mice were placed in individual cages and monitored daily for three days. Construction of bioluminescent <italic toggle="yes">E.coli</italic> K12 The bacterial lux operon from Photorhabdus luminescence (pAKlux2.1 plasmid) was used to genetically modify E. coli K12, a non-pathogenic laboratory strain according to a previous protocol. The pAKlux2.1 plasmid was a gift from Attila Karsi (Addgene plasmid # 14081; http://n2t.net/addgene : 14081 ; RRID:Addgene_14081), and expresses lux genes under the lacZ promoter. The pAKlux2.1 plasmid was isolated from its growth strain E. coli DH5alpha by QIAprep Spin Miniprep Kit (Qiagen). Then pAKlux2.1 plasmid was transformed into E.coli K12 by electroporation. E.coli K12 containing lux genes was obtained by plating cells on LB agar containing ampicillin (100μg/mL) and incubating them at 37 °C for 24 to 48 h. Ampicillin resistant E.coli K12 colonies were checked for light emission using IVIS Spectrum Imaging System (peak emission 490 nm). The bioluminescent E.coli K12 colonies (E.coli K12-lux) were used for bioluminescence experiments. Bacterial Administration Bacterial inocula were prepared by growing E.coli K12-lux in 200 ml LB broth containing 50 μg/ml ampicillin and E.coli K1 in 20 ml LB broth overnight at 37°C with shaking at 200 rpm. Cultures were harvested by centrifugation (4,000 x g for 10 min) and washed three times with PBS. The correct cell concentration for vaginal inoculation was calculated by measuring an OD600 in the last washing step. After centrifugation, the bacterial pellet was resuspended in a predetermined volume of PBS and introduced to the mice. The timeline for the experiments is shown in . On E15, mice were anesthetized with inhalation of isoflurane. Twenty microliters of mid-logarithmic-phase E.coli was inoculated into the vagina of mice using a 200-μL pipette tip. The concentration and strain of bacteria depended on the experiment (see below). For controls, the same volume of PBS was administered the same way._Following inoculation, mice were placed back to the cages and monitored twice daily. Bioluminescence imaging with the IVIS system For the bioluminescence experiment, mice with abdominal cerclage (N=6) were compared to control mice without abdominal cerclage (N=6). Whole-body bioluminescence imaging was performed 0.5 hours and 24 hours after inoculation with bacteria E.coli K12-lux (20 microliters of 1x10 9 ). Pregnant mice were anesthetized deeply with inhalation of isoflurane and were imaged using IVIS SpectrumCT In Vivo Imaging System (PerkinElmer). After whole-body imaging for 24 hours, the animals were euthanized and the whole intact uterus, including the embryos, were removed and imaged. After imaging the uterus, embryos were removed from the uterine cavity and the placenta, fetal membrane and embryo were imaged separately with IVIS. Preterm Birth Dose-Finding Study One aim of our study was to examine whether abdominal cerclage decreases intrauterine inflammation associated with preterm birth. To study intrauterine inflammation associated with preterm birth, it was necessary to use pathogenic E. coli K1 because E.coli K12-lux does not cause preterm birth. We performed a preliminary dose-finding study with E. coli K1 to determine the inoculum of E. coli K1 that provokes preterm birth. On E15, bacterial inoculums of E. coli K1 (20 microliters of 1x10 4 and 1x10 6 bacteria) were vaginally administered. There were N=6 mice for each inoculum. The mice were followed twice daily until delivery and the viability of pups were determined. It is important to note that preterm birth was studied with no cerclage in place. If a cerclage was placed, the animals were sacrificed prior to preterm birth ( ). Intrauterine inflammation The timeline for the experiment is shown in . Like the bioluminescence experiment, abdominal cerclage or sham control surgery was performed on E10. Based on the experience with the preterm birth dose-finding study, bacterial inoculums of 20 microliters of E. coli K1 1x10 4 or PBS controls were vaginally administered on E15. Gene expression of inflammation-related proteins was compared between three experimental groups: 1) Sham control surgery + inoculation of PBS (N=4) ; 2) Sham control surgery + inoculation of 10 4 pathogenic E.coli K1 (N=4); 3) Abdominal cerclage surgery + inoculation of 10 4 pathogenic E.coli K1 (N=4). Tissue was collected 24 hours after intravaginal inoculation. At harvesting, a laparotomy was performed using general anesthesia and uterus, placenta and fetal membranes were collected and snap frozen in liquid nitrogen for quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis. Care was taken when removing the placenta, uterus and fetal membranes. The uterus was incised at the cervix and the incision was continued superiorly. The uterus was incised such that the fetal sac was exposed intact. While grasping the fetal membranes with the tweezers, the sac was ruptured and the placenta was separated from the fetal membranes. Uterus, placenta, and fetal membranes were collected at the same position uterine position for all three groups.

Care was taken when removing the placenta, uterus and fetal membranes. The uterus was incised at the cervix and the incision was continued superiorly. The uterus was incised such that the fetal sac was exposed intact. While grasping the fetal membranes with the tweezers, the sac was ruptured and the placenta was separated from the fetal membranes. Uterus, placenta, and fetal membranes were collected at the same position uterine position for all three groups. Isolation of RNA and Quantitative RT-PCR Total RNA was isolated using the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. One microgram of RNA sample was used for reverse transcription and synthesis of cDNA using the High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems), as per the manufacturer's guidelines. Quantitative real-time PCR was performed on a QuantStudio 7 Flex (Applied Biosystems) using SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Qiagen). All genes were normalized by the housekeeping gene β-actin. Quantification was expressed as fold change relative to gene expression in the sham surgery + PBS control group using the 2 −(ΔΔCt) method of analysis. Predesigned SYBR Green primers for mouse inflammatory target genes (IL1β, TNFα, IL6, Cxcl1, Cxcl2 and Cxcr2) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Statistical Analysis Data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Mean values were calculated from 4 replicates. Comparisons between means were performed using one way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparison test (GraphPad Prism ver.9.04, Graphpad Software). Results were considered significant at P < 0.05. Results Abdominal Cerclage Abdominal cerclage was performed in N=14 mice and was well tolerated. No cases of preterm birth or maternal adverse effects were seen. Cerclage prevents ascending infection of <italic toggle="yes">E.coli</italic> K12-lux in pregnant mice Whole body bioluminescent imaging performed 0.5 hours post inoculation showed a strong luminescence signal in the vaginal region of mice in both control and experimental groups indicating successful bacteria inoculation ( ). Twenty-four hours after inoculation, bioluminescent signal was seen ascending into the uterine horns in all control mice (n=6). However, in mice with abdominal cerclages (n=6), no bioluminescent signal was seen after 24 hours. When the reproductive tissues were imaged separately, strong bioluminescence signal was detected in the placenta, fetal membranes, and uterus but not in the fetus ( ). These results suggested that abdominal cerclage prevented E.coli K12-lux from invading from the vagina through the cervix to the uterus. Vaginally administered pathogenic <italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic> K1 induces preterm birth Pathogenic E. coli K1 caused preterm birth and delivery of non-viable pups. The time to delivery after administration of two doses of E. coli K1 showed shorter latency periods with the larger inoculum of bacteria. Administration of 10 4 E. coli K1 induced 100% preterm birth within 72 hours (n=6), whereas 10 6 E. coli K1 induced 100% preterm birth within 48 hours (n=6). All cases of preterm birth produced non-viable pups regardless of dose. It was decided to use 10 4 E. coli K1 in the subsequent study of intrauterine inflammation. Cerclage decreases uterine inflammation induced by <italic toggle="yes">E. coli</italic> K1 in pregnant mice In the uterus, placenta and fetal membranes, ascending infection with E. coli K1 significantly increased expression of all inflammatory cytokines compared to PBS controls ( ). When an abdominal cerclage was placed, expression of all inflammatory cytokines was decreased compared to no cerclage. In the fetal membranes, there was no difference in inflammatory gene expression between controls and mice treated with cerclage. In the uterus, expression of inflammatory genes was increased in mice treated with cerclage, compared with controls. In the placenta, expression of IL1β, CXCL2 and CXCR2 was increased in mice treated with cerclage, compared with controls; however, expression of TNFα, IL6 and CXCL1 was no different between controls and mice treated with cerclage. Comments Principle findings In this mouse model of ascending intrauterine infection, abdominal cerclage prevented ascension of E.coli from the vagina through the cervix. In contrast to sham controls, mice treated with abdominal cerclage showed no evidence of ascension of vaginal inoculums of bioluminescent E. coli K12. In addition, abdominal cerclage decreased gene expression of inflammatory cytokines in the uterus, placenta, and membranes after vaginal inoculums of pathogenic E.coli K1. Results in the Context of What is Known Although cerclage prevents preterm birth in cases of cervical insufficiency, - there is no consensus about the mechanism of preterm birth prevention. It is known that the most common bacteria found in the uterus associated with preterm labor originate in the vagina. Clinicians suspect cerclage prevents preterm birth, in part, by improving the barrier between the pregnant uterus and lower tract. , The present study in mice supports this hypothesis. We found that compression of the cervical canal with a

Results in the Context of What is Known Although cerclage prevents preterm birth in cases of cervical insufficiency, - there is no consensus about the mechanism of preterm birth prevention. It is known that the most common bacteria found in the uterus associated with preterm labor originate in the vagina. Clinicians suspect cerclage prevents preterm birth, in part, by improving the barrier between the pregnant uterus and lower tract. , The present study in mice supports this hypothesis. We found that compression of the cervical canal with a suture improves the cervical barrier and decreases intrauterine infection and inflammation in mice. The permeability of the cervical barrier during pregnancy is a complex function of not only anatomical factors but also cervical mucus and components of the innate immune system such as natural antimicrobial peptides (NAMPs). Cervical mucus is composed of mucin fibers that form a cross-linked mesh filter that excludes particles larger than the mesh spacing. Mucus permeability is also regulated by chemical properties of the mucin fibers, such as glycosylation, pH and ion charge. The gel forming mucins MUC5B and MUC5AC were specifically studied in mouse pregnancy using the model of ascending infection. E.coli was shown to be trapped in the MUC5B and MUC5AC expressing mucin in the cervical canal. NAMPs are small antimicrobial peptides produced by epithelial cells in response to stimulation by microbes and inflammatory cytokines. , During human pregnancy, low levels of beta-defensin-2, a cervical NAMP, was associated with spontaneous preterm birth. Also, in mice pregnancy, gene delivery of the antimicrobial peptide human beta-defensin-3 in the cervical mucosa reduced bacterial ascent of bioluminescent E.coli and increased pup survival. Although cervical mucus and NAMPs are undoubtedly important for normal barrier function, the present study demonstrates that anatomical variables such as cervical compression can also affect ascending infection. Clinical implications An abdominal cerclage in women is the recommended treatment for patient with a failed vaginal cerclage. In a recent randomized trial, women with a history of failed vaginal cerclage were randomized to transabdominal cerclage versus high vaginal cerclage versus low vaginal cerclage. Women with an abdominal cerclage showed improved clinical outcomes. Compared with vaginal cerclage, abdominal cerclage decreased fetal loss and decreased the incidence of preterm birth prior to 32 weeks. The authors of this study hypothesized that an abdominal cerclage may improve the cervical barrier to infection and prevent the infective and inflammatory changes associated with cervical shortening. An animal model of cerclage performance could provide insight into the mechanisms of cerclage success and failure in patients. Although cerclage is the recommended treatment for cervical insufficiency, cerclage is not a cure. The risk of preterm birth before 34 weeks with a cerclage in place ranges from 13% for a first trimester cerclage to 50% for an exam-indicated cerclage. , An animal model of ascending infection and cerclage could improve our understanding of how a cerclage permits ascending infection in cases of cerclage failure. Clinical efforts to prevent ascending infection are perhaps most clearly exemplified by cervical occlusion surgery. Developed by Dr. Erich Saling, cervical occlusion is designed to create a physical barrier that prevents microbes in the lower tract from reaching the fetal compartment. A less invasive version of Dr. Saling’s procedure combines a cerclage with a cervical occlusion suture, where the anterior cervical lip is sutured to the posterior lip of the cervix. However, a randomized trial of cervical occlusion showed no significant benefit for preventing preterm birth. Research implications Animal studies are critically important for research that is not possible with human subjects. Although it is known that a short or dilated cervix is associated with intrauterine infection and inflammation, determining the natural history of intrauterine infection and inflammation is challenging with human studies. Patients who present with a dilated cervix or a short cervix in the second trimester often have coexisting inflammation and/or intra-amniotic infection. - The present study supports the hypothesis that ascending intrauterine infection is prevented when the cervical barrier is improved with a cerclage. The study also provides a blueprint for future studies that aim to investigate cervical barrier function and cerclage. Strengths and limitations The primary strength of the study is that the mouse model shows a clear relationship between cerclage placement and infection prevention, which is a relationship that is difficult to establish with studies in humans. However, there is a wide gap between the mouse model and cerclage in human pregnancy. In the current study, the cerclage was placed prior to vaginal inoculation, making it most similar to a history-indicated cerclage. It is unclear if the mouse model can be adapted to reflect an ultrasound-indicated cerclage or an exam-indicated cerclage. To do so, intrauterine inflammation would need to be present before cerclage placement, which was not

the study is that the mouse model shows a clear relationship between cerclage placement and infection prevention, which is a relationship that is difficult to establish with studies in humans. However, there is a wide gap between the mouse model and cerclage in human pregnancy. In the current study, the cerclage was placed prior to vaginal inoculation, making it most similar to a history-indicated cerclage. It is unclear if the mouse model can be adapted to reflect an ultrasound-indicated cerclage or an exam-indicated cerclage. To do so, intrauterine inflammation would need to be present before cerclage placement, which was not attempted in this study. Additional limitations are important to note. Although cerclage failure is associated with complex alterations in the vaginal flora, , the present study was limited in that only E.coli was studied. The present study was also limited in that preterm birth could not be studied because an abdominal cerclage precludes normal labor. A further limitation was that only bioluminescence and gene expression were examined for evidence of ascending infection. Future studies could examine other readouts such as bacterial culture and immunohistochemistry to gather additional information about ascending infection. Last, the present study does not permit study of cerclage mechanical support, which is a postulated mechanism by which the cerclage prevents preterm birth in humans. Conclusions Although cerclage has been used for decades, the mechanism of cerclage success is not known. The present mouse model demonstrates that compression of the cervical canal decreases ascending intrauterine infection and inflammation. The study adds important insight into cerclage success in human pregnancy. Supplementary Material 1 2

chunks.content: Introduction Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) is a major obstetric complication defined as the rupture of fetal membranes before the onset of labor and prior to 37 weeks of gestation [ ]. It affects approximately 2–3% of all pregnancies and is responsible for 30–40% of preterm births, contributing significantly to perinatal and neonatal morbidity and mortality [ – ]. The etiology of PPROM is multifactorial, involving infection, inflammation, malnutrition, mechanical stress, and structural membrane weakness. Among these, inflammation is recognized as a central mechanism in both the initiation and progression of membrane rupture [ , ]. Infectious and inflammatory processes disrupt the structural integrity of the amniotic membranes, facilitating their premature rupture and potentially leading to adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. In addition to inflammation, maternal nutritional status is increasingly acknowledged as a critical factor influencing both the risk and prognosis of PPROM [ ]. Malnutrition can impair immune function, alter the synthesis of structural proteins, and increase susceptibility to infection and inflammation, thereby further compromising membrane integrity. In this context, evaluating both inflammatory and nutritional parameters is essential for understanding the pathogenesis and prognosis of PPROM [ ]. In recent years, several albumin-based inflammatory indices have gained prominence in obstetric research due to their accessibility and potential prognostic value in pregnancy-related complications. These indices, which incorporate albumin as a key component, offer insight into both the inflammatory and nutritional status of patients. Among them, the leukocyte-to-albumin ratio (LAR) provides additional information, as white blood cell counts are sensitive to inflammatory conditions, while albumin levels are indicative of nutritional status [ ]. The neutrophil-to-albumin ratio (NAR) reflects both increased neutrophil levels and reduced albumin, serving as a marker of inflammation severity and nutritional status [ ]. Similarly, the monocyte-to-albumin ratio (MAR) may indicate chronic immune activation in the context of reduced protein reserves, thereby capturing the interplay between persistent inflammation and malnutrition [ ]. The fibrinogen-to-albumin ratio (FAR) combines the acute-phase reactant fibrinogen—which increases during inflammation—with albumin, which typically decreases, thus reflecting both systemic and local inflammatory activity [ ]. The systemic immune-inflammation index-to-albumin ratio (SII/Alb), which integrates neutrophil, lymphocyte, and platelet counts relative to albumin concentration, reflects both innate immune activation and nutritional status. This composite index has been associated with disease severity and prognosis in various inflammatory and metabolic conditions, offering a broader view of systemic immune burden and nutritional compromise [ ]. Similarly, the systemic inflammation response index-to-albumin ratio (SIRI/Alb)—calculated from neutrophil, monocyte, and lymphocyte counts divided by albumin—captures chronic inflammatory activity and host immune dysregulation in the context of malnutrition. SIRI/Alb has shown prognostic utility in predicting adverse outcomes in malignancy, infections, and cardiovascular disorders, highlighting its potential relevance in pregnancy-related inflammatory states [ ]. The neutrophil percentage-to-albumin ratio (NPAR), a newer marker, incorporates the proportion of neutrophils in the leukocyte count relative to albumin concentration, and has been shown to reflect the severity of systemic inflammation and nutritional risk, as well as to predict adverse outcomes in various clinical settings [ ]. The C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR) similarly indicates the overall burden of systemic inflammation while also serving as an indirect indicator of nutritional reserve, as low albumin may reflect poor nutritional status [ ]. In the context of PPROM, these albumin-based indices may be valuable for assessing both maternal and fetal inflammatory status, as well as underlying nutritional health, thereby improving risk prediction and clinical management. The timing of delivery following PPROM is closely linked to perinatal and neonatal outcomes. The duration of the latency period—the interval between membrane rupture and birth—is influenced by various maternal and fetal factors [ , ]. Accurately estimating this interval is essential for optimizing prenatal management, guiding the administration of medications such as corticosteroids and antibiotics, and preparing for appropriate neonatal care. Given the challenges of prediction, there is a clear need for novel markers that can reliably identify women at risk of imminent delivery. Therefore, the aim of this study is to evaluate the utility of inflammatory indices in predicting delivery within the first 48 hours (h) among pregnant women diagnosed with PPROM. In addition, we assessed the predictive value of these indices for latency periods of 72 h, 96 h, and 7 days in patients who did not deliver within 48 h. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 311 pregnant women diagnosed with PPROM and followed at the Perinatology Department of Ankara Etlik City Hospital between January 2023 and December 2023. Patients were divided into two groups based on delivery timing: those who delivered within 48 h of PPROM diagnosis ( n = 152) and those who delivered after 48 h ( n = 159). Inclusion criteria were a singleton pregnancy, diagnosis of PPROM between 24 and 34 weeks of gestation, and complete medical records regarding delivery and fetal outcomes. Exclusion criteria included multiple

who did not deliver within 48 h. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 311 pregnant women diagnosed with PPROM and followed at the Perinatology Department of Ankara Etlik City Hospital between January 2023 and December 2023. Patients were divided into two groups based on delivery timing: those who delivered within 48 h of PPROM diagnosis ( n = 152) and those who delivered after 48 h ( n = 159). Inclusion criteria were a singleton pregnancy, diagnosis of PPROM between 24 and 34 weeks of gestation, and complete medical records regarding delivery and fetal outcomes. Exclusion criteria included multiple gestations, fetal congenital or chromosomal anomalies, maternal history of chronic disease, pre-existing chronic medication use, signs of active cervicovaginal infection, uterine anomalies, placenta previa, allergies, and a history of smoking or alcohol consumption. PPROM was diagnosed based on either the observation of active amniotic fluid leakage during speculum examination and/or a positive placental alpha-microglobulin-1 (PAMG-1) protein test (AmniSure ® ROM, Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). Clinical and demographic data obtained from hospital records included maternal age, obstetric history, body mass index (BMI), presence of comorbidities, gestational age at hospitalization and delivery, mode of delivery, birth weight, APGAR scores, neonatal outcomes, and need for neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission. For all participants, laboratory tests—including complete blood count, albumin, fibrinogen, and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels—were retrospectively reviewed; all samples were collected after hospital admission and prior to the initiation of any treatment. Based on these laboratory parameters, inflammatory indices such as the leukocyte-to-albumin ratio (LAR), neutrophil-to-albumin ratio (NAR), monocyte-to-albumin ratio (MAR), fibrinogen-to-albumin ratio (FAR), systemic immune-inflammation index-to-albumin ratio (SII/Alb), systemic inflammation response index-to-albumin ratio (SIRI/Alb), neutrophil percentage-to-albumin ratio (NPAR), and C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR) were calculated and compared between the two groups. The formula for calculating is LAR = leukocyte (white blood cell) count (×10 9 /L)/albumin (g/dL), is NAR = neutrophil count (×10 9 /L)/albumin (g/dL), is MAR = monocyte count (×10 9 /L)/albumin (g/dL), is FAR = plasma fibrinogen level (g/dL)/albumin (g/dL), is NPAR = neutrophil percentage (in total white blood cell count) (%)×100/albumin (g/dL), is CAR = CRP (mg/L)/albumin (g/dL), is SII/Alb = [neutrophil count (×10⁹/L) × platelet count (×10⁹/L))/lymphocyte count (×10⁹/L)]/albumin (g/dL), and is SIRI/Alb = [neutrophil count (×10⁹/L) × monocyte count (×10⁹/L)/lymphocyte count (×10⁹/L)]/albumin (g/dL). Pregnant women in the cohort who did not deliver within 48 h were further stratified into additional subgroups according to latency periods: ≤72 h and > 72 h, ≤ 96 h and > 96 h, and ≤ 7 days and > 7 days. For each time interval, inflammatory indices were analyzed independently to determine their utility as prognostic markers for predicting delivery timing in PPROM cases. All patients received management in accordance with the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) guidelines [ ]. All patients received antibiotic prophylaxis (azithromycin 1 g plus intravenous ampicillin 2 g every 6 h for 48 h, followed by oral amoxicillin 875 mg every 12 h for 5 days). A standard corticosteroid protocol (betamethasone 12 mg intramuscularly, two doses 24 h apart) was administered to promote fetal lung maturation. Neuroprotective magnesium sulfate was provided for pregnancies less than 32 weeks’ gestation. Specifically, we stated that for neuroprotection in, magnesium sulfate was administered according to ACOG guidelines: a 4 g intravenous loading dose was given over 20–30 min, followed by a continuous infusion of 1 g per hour for up to 24 h or until delivery, whichever occurred first [ ]. Delivery was delayed until 34 weeks whenever possible, unless chorioamnionitis or fetal distress necessitated earlier intervention. For cases of PPROM beyond 34 weeks’ gestation, immediate delivery was performed as recommended. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ankara Etlik City Hospital Ethics Committee (approval number: AESH-BADEK–2025-0035). In this study, due to its retrospective nature, informed consent was waived with the approval of the Ethics Committee of Ankara Etlik City Hospital. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Continuous data are presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range, IQR), while categorical data are reported as numbers (percentages). Comparisons between groups were conducted using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, and the Independent samples t-test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, depending on data distribution. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to determine optimal cut-off values for inflammatory indices, with area under the curve (AUC) calculated. The optimal threshold was identified using the Youden index. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. (percentages). Comparisons between groups were conducted using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, and the Independent samples t-test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, depending on data distribution. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to determine optimal cut-off values for inflammatory indices, with area under the curve (AUC) calculated. The optimal threshold was identified using the Youden index. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. Results A total of 311 patients diagnosed with PPROM were included and stratified into two groups based on delivery latency: those delivering within 48 h ( n = 152, 48.9%) and those delivering after 48 h ( n = 159, 51.1%). Table presents the maternal characteristics, perinatal and neonatal outcomes of the participants. There were no statistically significant differences between the groups in terms of maternal age, gravidity, parity, nulliparity rate, in vitro fertilization rate, and BMI ( p > 0.05, for all). Compared to patients with a latency period > 48 h, those who delivered within 48 h had significantly higher gestational age at hospitalization [33 (3) vs. 30 (5) weeks; p < 0.001], gestational age at delivery [33 (3) vs. 32 (5) weeks; p = 0.014], and birth weight (1902 ± 597 g vs. 1729 ± 608 g; p = 0.012). Furthermore, the rate of cesarean delivery was significantly lower in the group with a latency period of ≤ 48 h (49.3% vs. 66.7%; p = 0.002). There were no statistically significant differences between groups regarding neonatal outcomes, including 1st and 5th minute Apgar scores, umbilical cord artery pH, respiratory distress syndrome, continuous positive airway pressure, mechanical ventilation, neonatal sepsis, phototherapy for neonates, neonatal hypoglycemia, intracranial hemorrhage, necrotizing enterocolitis, or NICU admission rates. However, the rate of transient tachypnea of the newborn was significantly lower in the group with a latency ≤ 48 h (19.7% vs. 36.5%; p = 0.001). Table compares laboratory parameters and albumin-based inflammatory indices between PPROM patients with latency periods ≤ 48 h and > 48 h. Patients with a latency period ≤ 48 h had significantly higher hemoglobin levels [11.7 (1.6) vs. 11.5 (2.0) g/dL; p = 0.010], white blood cell counts [12.8 (5.97) vs. 12.18 (4.69) ×10^9/L; p = 0.016], neutrophil counts [10.17 (6.75) vs. 9.00 (4.54) ×10⁹/L; p = 0.006], and fibrinogen levels [530 (145) vs. 482 (111) mg/dL; p = 0.001]. However, there were no statistically significant differences between groups regarding neutrophil percentage, monocyte, lymphocyte, eosinophil, basophil, immature granulocyte, and platelet counts, immature granulocytes percentage, albumin, or CRP levels ( p > 0.05, for all). Table presents the comparative analysis of albumin-associated inflammatory indices across various latency intervals in PPROM patients. The LAR, NAR, and FAR values were significantly higher in groups with shorter latency periods across all interval comparisons (≤ 48 h, ≤ 72 h, ≤96 h, and ≤ 7 days; all p < 0.05). While MAR values did not show statistically significant differences across any of the latency intervals ( p > 0.05), SII/Alb was significantly higher in the ≤ 72-hour and ≤ 96-hour groups ( p = 0.011 and p = 0.001, respectively), but not in the ≤ 48-hour or ≤ 7-day comparisons. SIRI/Alb was significantly elevated only in the ≤ 96-hour group ( p = 0.030), with no significant differences observed in the other intervals. NPAR was significantly higher in the ≤ 72-hour, ≤ 96-hour, and ≤ 7-day groups compared to their respective counterparts ( p = 0.044, p = 0.003, and p = 0.005, respectively), while the difference was not significant in the ≤ 48-hour comparison. Similarly, CAR demonstrated statistical significance in the ≤ 72-hour and ≤ 96-hour groups ( p = 0.047 and p = 0.031, respectively), but not in the ≤ 48-hour or ≤ 7-day comparisons. Table presents the diagnostic performance of albumin-associated inflammatory indices in predicting latency periods in patients with PPROM. LAR demonstrated significant predictive value at all intervals with a consistent cut-off of >~ 0.34, yielding AUCs of 0.582 for 48 h (95% CI: 0.52–0.65, p = 0.013), 0.597 for 72 h (95% CI: 0.53–0.66, p = 0.003), 0.641 for 96 h (95% CI: 0.58–0.70, p < 0.001), and 0.646 for 7 days (95% CI: 0.58–0.71, p < 0.001). NAR was a statistically significant predictor of delivery timing across all latency intervals: >0.27 for 48 h (AUC: 0.619, 95% CI: 0.55–0.69, p = 0.002), >0.249 for 72 h (AUC: 0.612, 95% CI: 0.55–0.67, p = 0.001), >0.25 for 96 h (AUC: 0.653, 95% CI: 0.59–0.71, p < 0.001), and >0.26 for 7 days (AUC: 0.636, 95% CI: 0.57–0.70, p < 0.001). Similarly, FAR consistently showed strong predictive value: >13.65 for 48 h (AUC: 0.637, 95% CI: 0.57–0.71, p < 0.001), >13.3 for 72 h (AUC: 0.627, 95% CI: 0.56–0.69, p < 0.001), >13.34

(95% CI: 0.58–0.71, p < 0.001).
