Univariate logistic regression analysis was performed for this disorder considering the basic characteristics of pregnant women, as shown in . The results indicated that aPLs positivity after SARS-CoV-2 infection was a risk factor for placental dysfunction related disorders (OR = 3.632, 95%CI: 1.153 - 12.218, P = 0.030), with a higher risk associated with LAC positivity (OR = 6.053, 95%CI: 1.192 - 44.912, P = 0.041) ( ). 3.4 Clinical characteristics of aPLs positive pregnant women after SARS-CoV-2 infection The detailed clinical data of the 15 aPLs positive cases are summarized in . None of the patients developed thrombotic events or APS-related clinical manifestations, and no COVID-19 associated complications were observed. 4 Discussion Although relevant studies have noted transient aPLs positivity in individuals after SARS-CoV-2 infection and its correlation with thrombotic risk and pneumonia-related prognosis, research on aPLs status and its impact on pregnancy outcomes in pregnant women with SARS-CoV-2 infection remains scarce. This prospective study observed and analyzed maternal aPLs status and perinatal outcomes in healthy pregnant women infected with SARS-CoV-2 at different gestational stages with a relatively small sample size, and the key findings are discussed in the following aspects. 4.1 aPLs status in pregnant women after SARS-CoV-2 infection Studies have shown that low level aPLs positivity exists physiologically in the general population, causing no significant harm to the body ( , ). Since the COVID-19 pandemic, numerous studies have revealed a significant increase in the aPLs positive rate after SARS-CoV-2 infection, ranging from 11% to 71% ( , , ). This rate is much higher than the physiological level, and aPLs positivity is closely associated with disease severity and thrombotic diseases. The variation in the positive rate is thought to be related to differences in patient age, underlying diseases, infection severity, circulating viral strains, vaccination status, and aPLs detection conditions. The largest sample study to date is a meta-analysis reported by Taha et al. in 2025, which included 21 studies with 1159 hospitalized patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection. It showed an overall aPLs positive rate of 46.8% in these patients, with a higher rate in severe cases. Among them, the positive rates of ACL (28.8% vs. 7.10%) and aβ2GPI (12.0% vs. 5.8%) were significantly higher in severe patients ( ). To date, there is only one study on aPLs in pregnant women after SARS-CoV-2 infection. A 2022 investigation by Gozzoli et al. involved 151 hospitalized pregnant patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection, which reported an aPLs positive rate of 11.00% (16/151), including 5 cases of aβ2GPI positivity, 6 cases of ACL positivity, 9 cases of LAC positivity, and 4 cases of co-positivity for two antibodies ( ). However, the study population included pregnant women with comorbidities and complications, which cannot represent the aPLs status in healthy pregnant women after SARS-CoV-2 infection. This study is a small sample study on healthy pregnant women infected with SARS-CoV-2 at different gestational stages. The results showed that the aPLs positive rate in healthy pregnant women after SARS-CoV-2 infection reached 18.75%, which is higher than the baseline physiological level of aPLs in healthy pregnant women ( ). We also found that the aPLs positive rate increased progressively with gestational advancement, which may be related to the changes in maternal immune status during pregnancy. Regarding the duration of aPLs positivity, 10 out of 15 aPLs positive cases underwent re-examination in our study. Among them, 6 cases turned negative (at an interval of 12–42 days), and the remaining 4 cases showed a decrease in antibody titer despite non - negative results (at an interval of 14–21 days). The numerical findings of this study show that aPLs induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection were transiently positive in most cases, which is consistent with the findings reported by Gozzoli et al. In addition, only single antibody positivity for aβ2GPI (10.00%) or LAC (8.75%) was observed in our study, with no co-positivity for multiple antibodies. 4.2 Analysis of the characteristics of aPLs positivity and maternal and fetal outcomes after SARS-CoV-2 infection There is currently no clear conclusion on whether aPLs positivity after SARS-CoV-2 infection directly affects maternal outcomes ( , ). Although most reports suggest that SARS-CoV-2 infection increases the risk of adverse maternal and fetal outcomes, and an elevated incidence of placental function related pregnancy disorders such as gestational hypertensive disorders and FGR has been observed in infected pregnant women, the specific mechanism remains unclear. This study found that the incidence of gestational complications was increased in the aPLs positive group, especially in the LAC positive subgroup, particularly for placental dysfunction related adverse outcomes including gestational hypertensive disorders, oligohydramnios, and FGR. The incidences of preeclampsia, preterm birth, FGR, and gestational diabetes mellitus showed numerical differences with higher values in the aPLs positive group, with no

SARS-CoV-2 infection increases the risk of adverse maternal and fetal outcomes, and an elevated incidence of placental function related pregnancy disorders such as gestational hypertensive disorders and FGR has been observed in infected pregnant women, the specific mechanism remains unclear. This study found that the incidence of gestational complications was increased in the aPLs positive group, especially in the LAC positive subgroup, particularly for placental dysfunction related adverse outcomes including gestational hypertensive disorders, oligohydramnios, and FGR. The incidences of preeclampsia, preterm birth, FGR, and gestational diabetes mellitus showed numerical differences with higher values in the aPLs positive group, with no statistically significant difference. The underlying mechanisms may be explained as follows: On the one hand, drawing on studies on antiphospholipid syndrome, aPLs can induce pathological pregnancy through multiple pathways, with aβ2GPI and LAC specifically involved in placental dysfunction. Previous studies have suggested that aPLs elevation induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection can mediate pathological hypercoagulability and exacerbate tissue damage ( , ). Among aPLs, LAC has been proven to be the antibody most closely associated with thrombotic events ( , ), and studies on pathological pregnancy in antiphospholipid syndrome have confirmed that LAC is an independent risk factor for adverse pregnancy outcomes among aPLs ( ). In addition, the significant increase in the aPLs positive rate after SARS-CoV-2 infection has been widely observed in the general population, suggesting that SARS-CoV-2 may mediate placental dysfunction through infection induced aPLs positivity, thereby leading to adverse pregnancy outcomes. On the other hand, aPLs status after infection is associated with the maternal systemic immune status ( ), and aPLs positivity also indicates excessive activation of the maternal immune system induced by infection; the systemic inflammatory response is also a fundamental factor for adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. Stratified analysis by gestational trimester at the time of infection in this study showed that the aPLs positive rate increased progressively with gestational advancement (5.88%, 16.00%, 26.31%), with the most obvious trend observed for LAC. All cases of LAC positivity in this study occurred in pregnant women infected in the third trimester. Infection-induced LAC positivity overlaps with the physiological hypercoagulability inherent in the third trimester of pregnancy ( ). Numerical associations are observed between this overlap and elevated maternal-fetal adverse outcome rates. 4.3 Clinical management of pregnant women with SARS-CoV-2 infection With the evolutionary trend of most SARS-CoV-2 variants towards enhanced transmissibility and attenuated pathogenicity, since the implementation of normalized COVID-19 control measures, most infections have been mild or asymptomatic, and symptomatic treatment is the main approach for viral infection. However, the management of pregnant infected individuals still warrants in-depth discussion. Based on the results of this study, we believe that antenatal management should emphasize the value of aPLs screening in pregnant women with SARS-CoV-2 infection, especially those infected in the second or third trimester, as well as pregnant women with high-risk factors for gestational hypertensive disorders and other conditions that affect placental function. After infection, through aPLs screening, enhanced monitoring of placental function should be implemented for aPLs positive pregnant women to identify and intervene in adverse maternal and fetal outcomes in a timely manner. In addition, when clinical manifestations of placental dysfunction related disorders such as FGR, preeclampsia, and oligohydramnios occur, if the pregnant woman has a recent history of SARS-CoV-2 infection, active serological aPLs screening should be performed to identify potential high-risk populations. This is an observational study, and all complications identified during maternal and fetal monitoring were managed in accordance with relevant guidelines and diagnostic and therapeutic protocols, with no specific interventions based on aPLs test results. Although the overall maternal and fetal outcomes were favorable, the incidence of placental dysfunction related adverse outcomes was still higher in aPLs positive cases. For aPLs positive pregnant women after SARS-CoV-2 infection, it is essential to be vigilant about infection deterioration through vital signs and inflammatory indicators, and to closely monitor coagulation function to guard against thrombotic events. From an obstetric perspective, surveillance of placental function and maternal-fetal status for this population should be further enhanced. Therefore, to further improve maternal and fetal outcomes, the value of prophylactic intervention for pregnant women with positive aPLs on screening remains to be explored. In particular, whether low-molecular-weight heparin should be administered for prophylactic anticoagulation in LAC-positive cases to mitigate pathological hypercoagulability and reduce the incidence of placental origin disorders requires confirmation in larger-scale cohort studies. 4.4 Study limitations This is a single center prospective cohort study. All the enrolled cases are from the prenatal care population of our hospital, ensuring detailed and accurate data. Although the study was conducted during a brief period of normalized COVID-19 control in China, the sample size was limited. In addition, for pregnant women without comorbidities, there was a lack of baseline aPLs data before SARS-CoV-2 infection and continuous dynamic antibody monitoring. This may have

administered for prophylactic anticoagulation in LAC-positive cases to mitigate pathological hypercoagulability and reduce the incidence of placental origin disorders requires confirmation in larger-scale cohort studies. 4.4 Study limitations This is a single center prospective cohort study. All the enrolled cases are from the prenatal care population of our hospital, ensuring detailed and accurate data. Although the study was conducted during a brief period of normalized COVID-19 control in China, the sample size was limited. In addition, for pregnant women without comorbidities, there was a lack of baseline aPLs data before SARS-CoV-2 infection and continuous dynamic antibody monitoring. This may have limited the in depth analysis of the dynamic changes and clinical significance of aPLs. 5 Conclusions This study found that healthy pregnant women without comorbidities or complications may develop transiently increased aPLs positivity after SARS-CoV-2 infection, and aPLs positivity after infection is a risk factor for placental dysfunction related adverse perinatal outcomes. These findings suggest that in clinical practice, close attention should be paid to the history of SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy, especially infection in the third trimester. Moreover, importance should be attached to aPLs screening in infected pregnant women. For aPLs positive cases after SARS-CoV-2 infection, enhanced maternal and fetal monitoring, vigilant surveillance of infection status and coagulation function, and follow-up are necessary.

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Evidence on the positive association between lactation and maternal cardiometabolic health has been developing over the past three decades [ , , , , , , , , ]. Although women are traditionally diagnosed with cardiovascular disease (CVD) at an older age as compared with men, CVD risk factors, which are associated with lifetime CVD risk, are rising among younger women [ , ]. Given the rising burden of CVD risk among younger women, lactation may represent an effective strategy to reduce CVD incidence [ ]. Over the last decade, reproductive factors such as early and late menarche, polycystic ovarian syndrome, premature menopause, adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs), and suboptimal lactation have been recognized as CVD risk factors [ , , , , , , , , , ]. Additionally, adverse social determinants of health are barriers to optimal lactation and CV health in women. In the United States, American Indian or Alaskan Native and non-Hispanic Black women have the lowest rates of breastfeeding and the highest rates of CV-related mortality [ , ]. Persisting structural inequities continue to widen the gaps in health care quality and access that contribute to non-biological differences in CV risk [ ]. The objective of this review is to synthesize current evidence on the association between lactation and cardiometabolic outcomes. This review also addresses clinical and systemic barriers that impede lactation success. Our goal is to increase knowledge of maternal cardiometabolic benefits of lactation, and the recognition of suboptimal lactation as a cardiovascular risk factor. 2 Pregnancy, lactation, and the cardiovascular system 2.1 Cardiovascular adaptations during pregnancy During pregnancy, the maternal CV system undergoes adaptations to support both maternal and fetal needs. In the first trimester, one of the earliest changes observed is an increase in maternal heart rate (HR) mediated by estrogen-regulated increase in myocardial alpha-receptors, which progressively rises to 15–25 % above baseline by the third trimester. This change supports a significant increase in cardiac output (CO) as the systemic vascular resistance drops to maximize uteroplacental circulation [ , ]. In the second trimester, progesterone primarily induces vasodilation, which lowers the resistance in the placental bed and contributes to a gradual decrease in blood pressure (5–15 mmHg in systolic and diastolic blood pressure about 24 weeks gestation) [ ]. Concurrently, plasma volume continues to increase, reaching an approximate 40 % increase by the third trimester. This increase in plasma volume drives a 45 % increase in CO. [ ] These CV changes are vital for optimal perfusion of both maternal and fetal tissues [ ]. By the third trimester, systemic blood pressure often returns to pre-pregnancy levels [ , ]. Physical manifestations of CV adaptations can include mild tachycardia, peripheral edema, systolic flow murmur, S3 gallop, and lateral displacement of the left ventricular apex [ , ]. Immediately following delivery, there is a rapid increase in systemic vascular resistance, autotransfusion of blood from the contracting uterus, and a gradual decrease in the maternal HR to baseline by approximately 10 days postpartum [ , ]. Women who consistently lactated for 5 months had lower systolic blood pressure and heart rate compared to their counterparts who formula-fed their newborns ( ) [ ]. 2.2 Hormonal regulation and cardiovascular changes during lactation The neuropeptide hormone oxytocin, synthesized in the hypothalamus and released into the circulation by the posterior pituitary ( ) surges during lactation and causes vasodilatory effects [ ]. These vasodilatory effects promote relaxation of the vascular smooth muscle which leads to decreased peripheral resistance, HR, and blood pressure, as well as increased CO. [ ] Moreover, oxytocin has been shown to have anti-atherosclerotic properties and anti-obesogenic effects [ ]. Oxytocin moderates factors directly linked to atherosclerotic CVD such as inflammation, weight gain, food intake, and insulin resistance [ ]. Additionally, oxytocin surge with lactation initiation can promote uterine involution protecting against postpartum blood loss which can indirectly benefit CV health [ ]. Oxytocin is an important trigger for prolactin secretion [ ]. Prolactin is a hormone secreted by the maternal pituitary gland which acts on the mammary glands to promote breast milk synthesis ( ) [ ]. Prolactin secretion increases during late gestation and in the postpartum period. Prolactin can be cleaved into a vasculo-toxic product that in mice has been associated with endothelial dysfunction, microvascular disease, and myocyte death [ ]. Dysregulation of the prolactin axis in pregnancy and postpartum has been linked to impaired vascular adaptation that has been implicated in both preeclampsia and peripartum cardiomyopathy [ , ]. In obese or overweight women, lower levels of oxytocin may reduce prolactin secretion, which could lead to lactation difficulties and earlier weaning [ , ]. 2.3 Metabolic adaptations during pregnancy and lactation Weight gain and an increase in visceral adiposity during pregnancy are theorized to support the increase in caloric expenditure

into a vasculo-toxic product that in mice has been associated with endothelial dysfunction, microvascular disease, and myocyte death [ ]. Dysregulation of the prolactin axis in pregnancy and postpartum has been linked to impaired vascular adaptation that has been implicated in both preeclampsia and peripartum cardiomyopathy [ , ]. In obese or overweight women, lower levels of oxytocin may reduce prolactin secretion, which could lead to lactation difficulties and earlier weaning [ , ]. 2.3 Metabolic adaptations during pregnancy and lactation Weight gain and an increase in visceral adiposity during pregnancy are theorized to support the increase in caloric expenditure postpartum which is evolutionarily designed to support a growing infant with lactation [ , ]. Insulin resistance and glucose intolerance increase during pregnancy, resulting in greater maternal fat reserves [ ]. Significant elevations of low-density lipoprotein and triglycerides during pregnancy allow for greater transfer of fatty acids to the growing fetus while creating a more atherogenic profile in the mother that may lead to endothelial damage [ , ]. During lactation, large quantities of carbohydrates, protein, and lipids are exported through the mammary gland into the offspring via breast milk. This process is energetically expensive for the mother, and to meet the nutrient demand, increased food intake or mobilization of storage depots is required [ ]. This lipid mobilization and increased energy expenditure associated with lactation is thought to lead to a faster return to maternal pre-pregnancy homeostasis [ ]. Dietary intake and energy expenditure during lactation can be associated with weight loss [ ]. Butte et al. found a mean mobilization of 156 kcal/day from fat stores in women who exclusively lactated [ ]. Women who consumed more calories, had less weight loss [ ]. Within the first 2–3 months postpartum, multiple studies have shown that formula-feeding mothers consumed 600–800 fewer calories than lactating mothers [ , ]. Another study found that women consumed an additional 300 kcal/day during lactation and expended 200 kcal/day less in physical activity to support the estimated 480 kcal/day needed for lactation [ , ]. Women may compensate for the increased energy demand of lactation by increasing their dietary intake and reducing their energy expenditure, rather than mobilizing fat stores [ , , ]. Women who lactated beyond 3 months postpartum experienced greater weight loss compared to those who did not lactate or only lactated for 3 months [ ]. However, the association between postpartum weight loss and lactation is mixed [ , , , ]. A systemic review of 43 observational studies found insufficient evidence to suggest a relationship between lactation and postpartum weight change [ ]. Of these 43 studies, five obtained objective measurements for postpartum weight change and adjusted for key covariates such as gestational weight gain and parity [ ]. Four of the 5 studies reported a direct positive association between duration of lactation and postpartum weight loss [ ]. Moreover, there may be an association between the duration of lactation and a reduction in visceral adipose tissue [ , ]. 3 Implications of lactational history on maternal cardiovascular health Lactation has been associated with reduction in major CV risk factors such as metabolic syndrome, type II diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and hypertension ( ) [ , ]. Each added month of lactation was associated with a 1 % decreased lifetime risk of developing T2DM [ , ]. Individuals affected by GDM who lactate for >6 months had the lowest risk of developing postpartum diabetes with the reduced risk extending up to 2 years post-delivery [ , ]. This T2DM risk reduction associated with lactation can reduce the risk of CVD [ ]. Lactation is also associated with hypertension reduction ( ) [ , , , ]. Lee et al. reported that women who had never lactated showed an increased risk of premenopausal hypertension [ ]. Women with cumulative lactation of one year or more can experience a 12 % lower risk of hypertension [ , , , ]. This risk reduction appears to be dose-dependent with women who lactated for 0–6 months, 6–12 months, or > 12 months showing an 8 %, 11 %, and 12 % lower risk, respectively [ , , , ]. Compared to women who never lactated, those who lactated had a 7 % lower risk of developing hypertension, after adjusting for age, body mass index, and smoking [ , ]. Additionally, lactation intensity may influence hypertension risk [ ]. A study comparing exclusive, almost exclusive, predominant, and partial lactation showed that exclusive and almost exclusive lactation was associated with lower diastolic blood pressure [ ]. Lactation has been recognized for its long-lasting metabolic benefits, mothers who lactate were on average 8 kg lighter 6 years after cessation of lactation [ ]. Besides, lactation can improve insulin requirements, glucose tolerance, and lipid metabolism in the postpartum

Additionally, lactation intensity may influence hypertension risk [ ]. A study comparing exclusive, almost exclusive, predominant, and partial lactation showed that exclusive and almost exclusive lactation was associated with lower diastolic blood pressure [ ]. Lactation has been recognized for its long-lasting metabolic benefits, mothers who lactate were on average 8 kg lighter 6 years after cessation of lactation [ ]. Besides, lactation can improve insulin requirements, glucose tolerance, and lipid metabolism in the postpartum period [ , ]. These benefits may be associated with the 500 daily caloric deficit with full lactation [ ]. In the U.S., dyslipidemia is highest in Hispanic/Latina women (37 % with total cholesterol levels of ≥200 mg/dL) [ ]. While atherogenic lipid profiles have been shown to increase the long-term risk of CVD, lactation has been associated with improved lipid homeostasis ( ) [ , , , ]. Duration of lifetime lactation has been inversely associated with serum triglycerides, total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [ ]. A positive association between lactation and HDL metabolism has been reported at 6 weeks and 3 months postpartum, with higher HDL levels until weaning for those who lactate for 1 year [ , , , ]. In the Keiser SWIFT cohort, a greater lactation frequency was associated with higher HDL and lower LDL at 6 to 9 weeks postpartum [ ]. Prior evaluation of triglyceride levels, has shown a return to baseline 13 weeks earlier in lactating than non-lactating women [ ]. Lactation may decrease the risk of CVD by improving lipid homeostasis [ , ]. Metabolic syndrome refers to a clustering of metabolic abnormalities including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and obesity [ ]. Metabolic syndrome can increase the risk of diabetes mellitus, CVD, and major CV events [ , ]. Nguyen et al. observed that lactation can decrease the risk of developing metabolic syndrome [ ]. Several studies have reported an inverse association between the duration of lactation and the incidence of metabolic syndrome in midlife parous women, indicating that longer lactation duration showed a lower incidence of metabolic syndrome [ , ]. Moreover, Magnus et al. highlighted that lactation could improve the cardiometabolic profile by reducing lower body mass index, waist circumference, and levels of C-reactive protein, triglycerides, insulin, and proinsulin [ ]. This improved cardiometabolic profile was observed decades after cessation of lactation, further demonstrating the potential long-term metabolic benefits of lactation [ ]. 3.1 Implications of lactation history on cardiovascular health in animal studies Current animal models for lactation and CV health, focus on the effects of early weaning, exclusive feeding, overfeeding, or on the on the maternal dietary composition and its impact on long-term CVD risk and possible changes in metabolism through epigenetic mechanisms on the offspring [ , , ]. Investigators, measured regional changes in lipoprotein lipase activity as a proxy for fat deposition in the rat [ ]. Fat deposition was noted to increase during pregnancy, but with lactation, storage of lipids in adipose tissue ceased, and uptake into mammary tissue increased as lipids were transferred into milk [ ]. At 20 days postpartum, lactating animals had smaller adipose cells and lower peripheral lipoprotein lipase activity than nonlactating controls [ ]. These animal studies of longer-term lactation show similar results to human studies after longer durations of lactation [ ]. Some limitations of animal studies include the controlled nutrition in laboratory settings and sometimes separation of pups. The diverse diets and caloric expenditures of humans, mixed feeding—combining formula and lactation in differing proportions—makes it more challenging to draw direct comparisons to studies in animals. 4 Lactation's influence in mitigating sequelae of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) can present as a risk factor for developing CVD later in life [ ]. Efforts are being made to understand the cardioprotective effect of lactation in HDP [ ]. Countouris et al. compared lactating women with preeclampsia, lactating women with gestational hypertension, and normotensive lactating women and found both lower systolic and diastolic blood pressures in women with gestational hypertension [ ]. Another study assessed the impact of lactation on preeclampsia, and showed women who had lactated in previous pregnancies had a lower risk of preeclampsia than women who had never lactated [ ]. 5 Lactation's influence on future cardiovascular events 5.1 Myocardial infarction (MI) In a cohort study, an inverse association was found between lactation and MI, independent of risk factors of CVD [ ]. Women with a lifetime lactation of >23 months presented a higher risk reduction for MI compared to those with shorter lactation duration [ ]. Furthermore, a meta-analysis demonstrated that parous women who had ever lactated had a reduced

assessed the impact of lactation on preeclampsia, and showed women who had lactated in previous pregnancies had a lower risk of preeclampsia than women who had never lactated [ ]. 5 Lactation's influence on future cardiovascular events 5.1 Myocardial infarction (MI) In a cohort study, an inverse association was found between lactation and MI, independent of risk factors of CVD [ ]. Women with a lifetime lactation of >23 months presented a higher risk reduction for MI compared to those with shorter lactation duration [ ]. Furthermore, a meta-analysis demonstrated that parous women who had ever lactated had a reduced risk of MI (HR 0.86 [95 % CI 0.78, 0.95]) compared to parous women who had never lactated [ ]. 5.2 Coronary artery disease There is also a relationship between lactation and coronary artery disease (CAD). Schwarz et al. reported that mothers who had never lactated were more likely to develop aortic and coronary artery calcification compared to mothers who had lactated for at least 3 months after adjusting for CVD risk factors [ ]. However, there were no differences between exclusive and non-exclusive lactation groups [ ]. Tschiderer et al. reported that 12-month lactation duration was negatively associated with CAD risk, and longer than 12 months of lactation had a progressive decreased risk for CAD [ ]. However, another study noted a plateau of reduced CAD risk between 12 and 48 months, suggesting the unknown additional CAD risk reduction past 12 months of lactation [ ]. Even though no studies have assessed the effect of lactation on carotid flow, many have studied the relationship between lactation and carotid intima-media thickness. In a study by Augoulea et al., postmenopausal women who lactated for at least 6 months had lower carotid intima-media thickness and reduced prevalence of subclinical atherosclerosis [ ]. Perez-Roncero et al. found that women, who had lactated for 3 6 months, had a lower carotid intima-media thickness and higher HDL cholesterol levels than women who lactated for <6 months [ ]. 5.3 Stroke and cerebrovascular accidents Lactation is associated with a reduced risk of stroke and cerebrovascular accidents in parous postmenopausal women [ , , ]. A study showed that women with a lifetime lactation duration of 7 months had a lower risk of stroke (HR 0.52 [95 % CI, 0.50–0.55] to 0.64 [95 % CI, 0.59–0.69]) and intracerebral hemorrhage (HR 0.56 [95 % CI, 0.49–0.63] to 0.78 [95 % CI, 0.64–0.96]) compared to those who never lactated [ ]. However, reduced risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage was observed only with a lifetime duration of lactation >24 months (HR 0.61 [95 % CI, 0.57–0.66]) [ ]. Additionally, Jacobson et al. reported that women with a lifetime lactation of 1 month or longer had a 23 % decreased risk of stroke (HR 0.77 [95 % CI, 0.70–0.84]) compared to those who had never lactated [ ]. 6 The interplay between cardiovascular health and lactation We discussed the potential benefits of lactation on CV health, however, it is known that CV health can also influence lactation [ ]. Burgess et al. suggests that women with a history of HDP are less likely to initiate and continue lactation when compared to normotensive women [ ]. In addition, data from the All Our Families Cohort demonstrated that women with HDP had lower rates of non-exclusive lactation at 4 months and a shorter lactation duration at 12 months compared to women without HDP [ ]. The lower rates of lactation duration and exclusivity were observed in groups with an increased need for medical interventions and postpartum complications, which may present as lactation barriers [ ]. Among these, women with HDP reported that the most common reason to stop or not initiate lactation was feeling sick or that they had to stop for medical reasons [ ]. Moreover, the study notes that late-onset preeclampsia (≥34 weeks' gestation) displayed higher lactation intent than those women with early-onset preeclampsia (<34 weeks' gestation) [ ]. Women with early onset preeclampsia were more likely to have infants in the NICU highlighting increased maternal/infant separation and hindered lactation initiation and establishment of the milk supply [ ]. The maternal-infant separation from preterm birth, maternal complications postpartum, and psychosocial stressors associated with HDP diagnosis may discourage lactation initiation [ ]. Implementation of Spatz et al.'s ten steps for promoting and protecting breastfeeding for vulnerable infants during hospitalization may improve lactation support [ ]. Women with cardiac disease managed at a comprehensive cardio obstetrical program for their pregnancy demonstrated high lactation initiation rates (85 %) but low continuation rates in the acute postpartum period (40 %) [ ] highlighting the need for interventions both at the time of delivery admission in addition to continuation of resources and support postpartum. While few medications are contraindicated during lactation, there is a gap in clinician

with HDP diagnosis may discourage lactation initiation [ ]. Implementation of Spatz et al.'s ten steps for promoting and protecting breastfeeding for vulnerable infants during hospitalization may improve lactation support [ ]. Women with cardiac disease managed at a comprehensive cardio obstetrical program for their pregnancy demonstrated high lactation initiation rates (85 %) but low continuation rates in the acute postpartum period (40 %) [ ] highlighting the need for interventions both at the time of delivery admission in addition to continuation of resources and support postpartum. While few medications are contraindicated during lactation, there is a gap in clinician knowledge regarding medication compatibility with lactation [ , ]. Tigka et al. reported that 39 out of 57 lactating women were inaccurately counseled to discontinue lactation by a clinician despite medication compatibility [ ]. For instance, Colaceci et al. found medication package leaflets reported higher risk profiles than evidence-based scientific sources for the use of antihypertensive medications during lactation [ ]. Inconsistent or inaccurate information on the use of medications during lactation may lead to cautious and harmful recommendations [ ]. 7 Potential negative impact of lactation on cardiovascular health Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is defined as a decline in maternal cardiac function that occurs in the third trimester or first few months postpartum in the absence of other identifiable causes [ ]. PPCM is more prevalent among women of advanced maternal age, multi-gestational pregnancies, and HDP, however, the role of prolactin and lactation have also been linked in both the pathogenesis as well as in the recovery of left ventricular function [ , ]. During pregnancy and postpartum, an increase in oxidative stress upregulates cathepsin D which cleaves prolactin into 16-kDA prolactin fragment which in mice models has been shown to lead to endothelial damage and increase cardiomyocyte apoptosis. Therefore, bromocriptine, a D2 receptor agonist that inhibits prolactin secretion, has been shown in several studies to improve the likelihood of recovery of LV systolic function. A systematic review of 8 studies of 593 patients with PPCM demonstrated increased survival (91.6 % versus 83.9 %) and showed a higher LVEF (53.3 % versus 41.8 %) with bromocriptine treatment [ , ]. The current ACC/AHA guidelines recommend consideration of use of bromocriptine for lactation suppression in severe LV systolic dysfunction (LVEF <25 %) or cardiogenic shock in the context of PPCM but highlight the marked benefits of lactation and recommend shared decision-making until more data is available. Among the Investigations of the Pregnancy-Associated Cardiomyopathy (IPAC) study, Koczo et al. followed 100 women diagnosed with PPCM throughout their first year postpartum and assessed the lactation impact on PPCM in lactating and non-lactating women. The study found higher circulating levels of prolactin among the lactation cohort and no differences were observed in LVEF recovery between non-lactating women vs 6 and 12-month lactating women [ ]. The U.S.-based REBIRTH (Randomized Evaluation of Bromocriptine in Myocardial Recovery Therapy for Peripartum Cardiomyopathy, NCT05180773 ) comparing bromocriptine for lactation suppression versus lactation is currently ongoing and aims to determine if bromocriptine is associated with better outcomes than standard medical therapy for heart failure [ ]. 8 Optimizing lactation in socially vulnerable populations 8.1 Barriers to lactation In the U.S. the prevalence of lactation initiation is high (84.1 %) with disparities based on social determinants of health [ ]. Black women have the lowest rate of lactation initiation (75.4 %) compared to the highest rate observed in Asian mothers (92.7 %) [ ]. Differences in lactation rates are also influenced by income, language, age, parity, education, employment benefits, access to health care, and lactation support [ , , , , ]. Among 142,643 new mothers in the 2016–2019 Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS), 60.4 % reported lactating up to 3 months and 54.7 % up to 6 months. High school education or lower, Medicaid insurance coverage, and absence of lactation support from the health care team was associated with lower breastfeeding rates [ ]. Mothers who reported food insecurity, including participation in WIC (Women, Infants, and Children), were less likely to continue lactation. Participants reported that the financial burden of increased food intake to meet caloric demands of lactation, financial pressures to return to work sooner, and the cost of lactation equipment were reasons why they ceased lactation [ ]. Lower breastfeeding education and support, and lower household income was associated with lower lactation initiation among Black women [ ]. Hispanic women have slightly lower rates of lactation initiation compared to White women. However, duration and exclusivity disparities are present [ ]. Cultural factors including nativity and acculturation can present as additional elements impacting lactation rates among Hispanic women. Foreign-born Hispanic women and Spanish-speaking women had higher lactation rates compared to U.S.-born Hispanic women [ ]. Lastly, Singh et al. found that immigrant women had higher rates of

cost of lactation equipment were reasons why they ceased lactation [ ]. Lower breastfeeding education and support, and lower household income was associated with lower lactation initiation among Black women [ ]. Hispanic women have slightly lower rates of lactation initiation compared to White women. However, duration and exclusivity disparities are present [ ]. Cultural factors including nativity and acculturation can present as additional elements impacting lactation rates among Hispanic women. Foreign-born Hispanic women and Spanish-speaking women had higher lactation rates compared to U.S.-born Hispanic women [ ]. Lastly, Singh et al. found that immigrant women had higher rates of lactation initiation and longer lactation duration than U.S.-born women [ ]. Thus, lactation promotion programs should target ethnic-immigrant and social groups with lower lactation rates ( ) [ ]. 8.2 Strategies for improving lactation support Multi-level interventions including national, state legislative, and medical provider support are needed to enable breastfeeding, and to maximize the health benefit for all lactating individuals. Interventions include paid parental leave, workplace accommodations, and expansion of insurance coverage for lactation support ( ). The expansion of postpartum Medicaid for up to 12 months postpartum in up to 48 U.S. states has demonstrated improved access to lactation supplies and increased favorable lactation outcomes [ ]. Community-based peer support strategies include the engagement of community health workers, doulas, and community outreach to help reinforce lactation, particularly among historically marginalized communities with low lactation rates ( ) [ ]. Importantly, educating healthcare professionals on the effect of systemic racism and implicit bias on lactation is essential ( ). Educational campaigns surrounding the benefits of lactation and the facilitation of community peer counseling and support groups in the community are vital to addressing cultural norms, stigma, and challenges. 9 Future research directions Despite the growing evidence of the benefits of lactation in maternal CV health, there are remaining gaps in evidence [ ]. Longitudinal studies with detailed lactation history such as duration, frequency, and exclusivity, biomarkers, and maternal CV health outcomes are needed. Such longitudinal studies could enhance clinical recommendations in lactation practice to maximize maternal CV health benefits. Mechanistic investigations are crucial to understanding the biological pathways through which lactation benefits maternal CV health. Racial and ethnic differences (socially based) in metabolic and inflammatory changes may show variations in CV benefits that need to be explored [ , ]. For instance, social determinants can contribute to the observed higher rates in diabetes and hypertension in Hispanic and Black women respectively which underscores the need for tailored preventative efforts [ ]. Future studies investigating structural barriers such as inadequate maternity leave, limited access to lactation support, and healthcare inequities can aid the design of lactation interventions in diverse populations [ ]. 10 Conclusion Lactation offers a unique period, with significant implications for prevention and intervention strategies for maternal CV health. By deepening our understanding of these connections, healthcare providers can better advocate for lactation as a cornerstone of maternal health. Additionally, ensuring equitable access to lactation education and support through public health strategies can enhance maternal CV health across all populations [ ]. chunks.content: Synopsis Quad test biomarkers are significantly associated with spontaneous preterm birth, particularly early preterm birth. Introduction Preterm birth remains a leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality worldwide. The second-trimester quadruple (Quad) test, consisting of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), free beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), unconjugated estriol (uE3), and inhibin-A (IhA), was originally developed for Down syndrome screening [ ]. Emerging evidence suggests that abnormal levels of these biomarkers may also be associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, particularly preterm birth, fetal growth restriction, stillbirth, and preeclampsia [ – ]. These associations are thought to reflect underlying placental dysfunction, which contributes to adverse perinatal outcomes, including preterm birth. Theoretically, in addition to its established role in identifying the risk of fetal Down syndrome, the quadruple test may also serve as a potential tool for evaluating the risk of preterm birth. Although several studies have reported associations between abnormal serum biomarker levels and preterm birth in euploid fetuses, most have included indicated preterm births [ – ], such as those due to early-onset preeclampsia with severe features, placenta previa with active bleeding, or placental abruption in early gestation, rather than specifically examining their relationship with spontaneous preterm birth. Consequently, the association between serum quadruple markers and spontaneous preterm birth remains uncertain. Although the underlying relationship remains unclear, we hypothesize that subtle placental inflammation or dysfunction, as indicated by abnormal maternal serum biomarkers, may contribute to the pathogenesis of preterm labor. This knowledge gap is clinically important, as spontaneous preterm birth may be amenable to prevention through targeted counseling that increases awareness and promotes early recognition of preterm labor, thereby facilitating timely diagnosis and management. Accordingly, this study was undertaken to investigate the associations between serum biomarkers assessed in the Quad test and their predictive value for spontaneous preterm birth. The primary objective was to evaluate the potential utility of these biomarkers as an adjunctive screening tool, complementing their established role in Down syndrome detection, and to explore the feasibility of developing a predictive model that could report the risk of spontaneous preterm birth within the same screening framework. Patients and methods A cohort and diagnostic study was conducted using a prospectively collected database of pregnant women who underwent second-trimester Quadruple (Quad) testing as part of the national fetal Down syndrome screening program at Maharaj Nakorn Chiang Mai Hospital, a tertiary referral and academic center, and its affiliated hospitals in northern Thailand. The study period extended from January 2016 to December 2024. Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of Chiang Mai University (Research Ethics Committee Panel 5; Study Code: OBG-2568-0353; Research ID: 0353; Date of Approval4 June 2025). Participants were enrolled to the database after providing written informed consent following appropriate pretest counseling of Quad test by the research team. They underwent fetal Down syndrome screening using the Quad test, which was offered free of charge. The referral system, along with the development of counseling teams, ultrasound standardization for gestational age assessment, maternal blood collection, prenatal diagnosis, and logistic support, was facilitated by the National Health Security Office (NHSO), Thailand. The study population included pregnant women attending antenatal care at our hospital and its network hospitals at 15–21 weeks of gestation. The inclusion criteria were: (1) singleton pregnancies; (2) low-risk pregnancies, defined as no underlying medical disease (e.g., heart disease or chronic hypertension) and no high obstetric risk factors, such as placenta previa, a history of cervical incompetence, or prior spontaneous preterm birth; (3) known gestational age, determined by clinical estimation and fetal sonographic biometry at the time of Quad testing; and (4) known pregnancy outcomes. The exclusion criteria were: (1) multifetal pregnancies; (2) indicated preterm births (e.g., induction or cesarean section due to preeclampsia with severe features, placenta previa, or placental abruption); (3) fetuses with chromosomal or structural abnormalities requiring pregnancy termination; (4) fetal loss (miscarriage, stillbirth, or intrauterine fetal death) prior to 24 weeks; and (5) incomplete records or loss to follow-up. Quad testing Participants were interviewed to obtain demographic information prior to maternal blood collection, and the data were recorded in standardized forms. The collected information, which was also entered into the biomarker machine’s built-in software, included maternal age, body weight, gestational age (in weeks and days) at the time of sampling, residency, ethnicity, smoking history, and pregestational diabetes mellitus, among other variables. Blood specimens were processed according to standard protocols, with immediate transfer to the laboratory and serum separation by centrifugation. The concentrations of the four biomarkers, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), free beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), unconjugated estriol (uE3), and inhibin-A (IhA), were measured using the same fully automated bioassay system (DELFIA ® Xpress, PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA, USA) with standardized immunoassay kits. To minimize inter-assay variability, all immunoassays were performed in batches, with 78 cases per batch conducted three times per week, and results available within 1–3 days. The crude serum

Blood specimens were processed according to standard protocols, with immediate transfer to the laboratory and serum separation by centrifugation. The concentrations of the four biomarkers, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), free beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), unconjugated estriol (uE3), and inhibin-A (IhA), were measured using the same fully automated bioassay system (DELFIA ® Xpress, PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA, USA) with standardized immunoassay kits. To minimize inter-assay variability, all immunoassays were performed in batches, with 78 cases per batch conducted three times per week, and results available within 1–3 days. The crude serum concentrations of the biomarkers were automatically converted to multiples of the median using reference model embedded in the built-in software with correction for gestational age, maternal weight, ethnicity, smoking status, and diabetes. Follow-up for the final outcomes In addition to fetal Down syndrome status, participants were followed for pregnancy outcomes, gestational age at delivery, and complications, including miscarriage, preterm birth, fetal growth restriction, and preeclampsia. The primary outcome measure was spontaneous preterm birth, defined as delivery before 37 completed weeks of gestation resulting from spontaneous onset of labor or preterm premature rupture of membranes, without any indication for intentional preterm delivery. Spontaneous preterm birth occurring before 34 weeks of gestation was classified as early preterm birth. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using Stata version 16 (StataCorp, 2019; Stata Statistical Software: Release 16, College Station, TX, USA) and SPSS version 26.0 (IBM Corp., 2019; IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 26.0, Armonk, NY, USA). Baseline demographic characteristics were compared using the Student’s t-test for continuous variables and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Comparisons of preterm birth rates and other outcomes between the normal and abnormal biomarker groups were conducted using the chi-square test and relative risk analysis with 95% confidence intervals. A two-tailed p -value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Multivariate logistic regression was applied to adjust odds ratios (ORs) with corresponding 95% CIs for each significant biomarker. The predictive models for preterm birth and early preterm birth were developed using binary logistic regression, with serum biomarkers transformed into adjusted multiples of the median (MoM) as independent variables. Variable selection was performed through backward stepwise elimination. The predictive performance of the models was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values were also calculated. Internal validation was conducted using bootstrapping methods, and model calibration was subsequently assessed. Results A total of 46,540 singleton pregnancies that underwent second-trimester Quad testing between 2016 and 2024 were followed for pregnancy outcomes. After excluding cases with uncertain final outcomes, medical or obstetric complications, fetal anomalies, and abortions (terminations before 24 weeks of gestation), 44,132 pregnancies remained for analysis, as shown in Fig. . Of these, 40,634 (92.1%) resulted in term deliveries (≥ 37 weeks), while 3,498 (7.9%) were preterm births, including 1,063 (2.4%) early preterm births (< 34 weeks). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are presented in Table . Maternal age and weight were slightly but significantly higher in the preterm birth group. Association between individual biomarkers and preterm birth On univariable logistic regression analysis, all four maternal serum biomarkers were significantly associated with preterm birth, as presented in Table . Elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), free β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), and inhibin-A (IhA) levels were associated with an increased risk of both preterm and early preterm birth, whereas unconjugated estriol (uE3) levels were inversely associated with these outcomes. Notably, all four biomarkers demonstrated a stronger effect size for early preterm birth than for overall preterm birth. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted including maternal serum biomarkers, maternal age, and parity. Maternal age and all four maternal serum biomarkers remained significantly associated with an increased risk of both preterm and early preterm birth, whereas parity was not. Importantly, exclusion of age and parity from the models did not significantly diminish the AUCs. Accordingly, in the interest of model parsimony, we present the final models including only the biochemical biomarkers, as presented in Table . On the contrary, during backward elimination in the logistic regression analysis, removal of uE3 from the model resulted in a slight but statistically significant reduction in the AUC; therefore, we retained uE3 in the final model. The predictive models based on the logistic regression analyses are as follows: log odds preterm birth = -2.495894 + 0.0252989(AFP MoM) + 0.0549719(hCG MoM) + 0.0521757(IhA MoM) -0.1005526(uE3 MoM). The model demonstrated relatively diagnostic performance in predicting preterm birth, with an area under the ROC curve of 0.564 (95% CI, 0.552–0.573), as shown in Fig. and Table . Internal validation of the model using 500 bootstrap replications indicated good calibration, with an E: O ratio of 1.003, a calibration-in-the-large (CITL) of 0.001, and a slope of 0.898, as presented in

The predictive models based on the logistic regression analyses are as follows: log odds preterm birth = -2.495894 + 0.0252989(AFP MoM) + 0.0549719(hCG MoM) + 0.0521757(IhA MoM) -0.1005526(uE3 MoM). The model demonstrated relatively diagnostic performance in predicting preterm birth, with an area under the ROC curve of 0.564 (95% CI, 0.552–0.573), as shown in Fig. and Table . Internal validation of the model using 500 bootstrap replications indicated good calibration, with an E: O ratio of 1.003, a calibration-in-the-large (CITL) of 0.001, and a slope of 0.898, as presented in Fig. . log odds early preterm birth = -2.615877 + 0.0390901(AFP MoM) + 0.0892294(hCG MoM) + 0.0610216(IhA MoM) -1.252047(uE3 MoM). The model demonstrated diagnostic performance in predicting early preterm birth, with an area under the ROC curve of 0.683 (95% CI, 0.664–0.699), as shown in Fig. and Table . Internal validation of the model using 500 bootstrap replications indicated good calibration, with an E: O ratio of 1.005, a calibration-in-the-large (CITL) of 0.000, and a slope of 0.944, as presented in Fig. . The diagnostic indices of the predictive models for preterm and early preterm birth (at cut-off prevalence 7.5% and 2.5%, respectively) are presented in Table . Discussion Quad test predictive model is useful to predict preterm birth, in particular early preterm birth. Each of the four biomarkers had diagnostic value in prediction of preterm birth. The chance of preterm birth is increased with a higher level of AFP, hCG, InA and with a lower level of uE3. However, diagnostic performance of individual biomarker was relatively low. Their combination yielded better diagnostic performance, providing AUC of 0.563 in prediction of preterm birth and AUC of 0.682 in prediction of early preterm birth. This predictive performance of the quad test appears relatively limited and, therefore, it should not be used as a standalone predictor. Among the individual biomarkers, based on the AUCs, AFP showed the most promise for predicting overall preterm birth, whereas uE3 exhibited the strongest association with early preterm birth. Nonetheless, it may serve as a cost-free adjunct for identifying women at increased risk of preterm and early preterm birth, thereby facilitating counseling and early detection, particularly in resource-limited settings. Unlike most previous studies [ – ], this study focused exclusively on spontaneous preterm birth, excluding indicated preterm births, which result from specific maternal or fetal conditions necessitating early delivery, such as early-onset preeclampsia with severe features, placenta previa with active bleeding, or placental abruption in early gestation. From a clinical perspective, assessing the risk of spontaneous preterm birth is more valuable than evaluating the overall risk of preterm birth, as women at higher risk of spontaneous preterm birth require targeted preventive measures, counseling, and management. Although non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) currently represents the most accurate screening method for fetal Down syndrome [ ], it is not widely adopted as the primary screening tool in many regions due to its high cost and limited availability. The quadruple (Quad) test therefore remains the standard screening modality in most regions, including in Southeast Asia. In settings where the Quad test is routinely performed for Down syndrome screening, its potential to provide additional information, such as identifying the risk of preterm birth, offers an important opportunity to maximize its clinical utility beyond chromosomal anomaly detection, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where cost-effective screening approaches are essential. Note that first-trimester biochemical markers for Down syndrome screening have also been used in many countries and may help stratify the risk of preterm birth [ , ]; however, their association with spontaneous preterm birth has not yet been explored. Research implication External validation in independent study populations is necessary to establish reproducibility. Furthermore, integrating quad test-derived risk with established predictors, such as cervical length, fibronectin, history of cervical insufficiency, or prior spontaneous preterm birth, should be explored to determine whether such combinations improve predictive performance. The pathophysiological mechanisms by which abnormal serum biomarkers increase the risk of spontaneous preterm birth, particularly early preterm birth, remain unclear and are needed to be further explored, although they are thought to be associated with placenta-mediated complications such as preterm birth (spontaneous or indicated), preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, placental abruption, and stillbirth [ ]. Clinical implication In settings where the quad test is routinely used for Down syndrome screening, it may also provide incidental information on preterm birth risk, particularly early preterm birth, without additional cost or effort. However, given its limited predictive value and lack of external validation, the quad test should not guide clinical intervention independently but may serve as an adjunct to established risk factors such as prior spontaneous preterm birth. In resource-limited settings, identifying women at higher risk through the quad test could facilitate counseling and promote earlier recognition and management of preterm

restriction, placental abruption, and stillbirth [ ]. Clinical implication In settings where the quad test is routinely used for Down syndrome screening, it may also provide incidental information on preterm birth risk, particularly early preterm birth, without additional cost or effort. However, given its limited predictive value and lack of external validation, the quad test should not guide clinical intervention independently but may serve as an adjunct to established risk factors such as prior spontaneous preterm birth. In resource-limited settings, identifying women at higher risk through the quad test could facilitate counseling and promote earlier recognition and management of preterm labor. This may be particularly valuable in low-income countries, where the prevalence of preterm birth is high and access to well-established predictive tools, such as cervical length measurement or cervical fibronectin testing, is limited. Strengths and weaknesses The strengths of this study include: (1) a large sample size based on a prospectively collected database, which enhances the reliability of the findings; (2) the results derived from routine, population-based clinical settings, rather than controlled research environments, thereby increasing the potential reproducibility of the findings in real-world practice; (3) a specific focus on spontaneous preterm birth, with the exclusion of indicated preterm birth, allowing the predictive model to be directly applied in preventive strategies for spontaneous preterm birth; and (4) internal validation of the predictive model using bootstrap techniques, demonstrating good calibration. The limitation of this study is that the population comprised Thai pregnant women from northern Thailand. Consequently, the predictive model requires external validation in populations of different ethnicities or from other geographical regions to confirm its generalizability. Additionally, although the sample size was sufficiently large to address the primary outcomes, the prevalence of very preterm birth (before 28 weeks of gestation) was too low to allow for subgroup analysis with high reliability. Conclusions The Quad test may serve as a predictor of spontaneous preterm birth, especially early preterm birth. Although its predictive performance is not very high, it may add value when combined with established risk factors, such as prior preterm birth, to promote awareness of early signs of uterine contractions for timely diagnosis and management of preterm labor. Furthermore, the model can be easily incorporated into existing Quad test software to report risks of both fetal aneuploidy and preterm birth, thereby enhancing the utility of routine screening without additional cost or effort.
