chunks.content: Background Preconception care is a primary preventive health service aimed at preparing women for pregnancy and improving maternal and infant health outcomes [ – ]. In accordance with global standards set by the World Health Organization (WHO) and other reputable authorities such as ACOG and CDC, there is a strong emphasis on integrating preconception counseling into routine health systems to address modifiable risk factors [ – ]. Furthermore, aligned with the national guidelines of the Ministry of Health of Türkiye, comprehensive care requires a holistic evaluation of risk dimensions, including genetic history, nutrition, and chronic diseases [ – ]. Identifying these risks helps women adopt manageable, healthy lifestyle behaviors [ – ]. Evidence shows that such counseling effectively improves birth outcomes and reduces risks, highlighting the need for widespread promotion [ – ]. However, traditional service delivery faces significant barriers, including a lack of organization, time constraints, and inadequate public awareness [ , , , ]. To overcome these barriers, web-based education has emerged as an accessible, interactive, and potentially cost-effective approach that may be used to reach women of reproductive age [ – ]. Studies indicate that digital interventions can successfully reduce health-related risk factors and promote positive behavioral changes in the preconception period [ – ]. While international literature demonstrates the positive impact of digital preconception care [ , , , ], there remains a significant gap regarding the implementation and effectiveness of such comprehensive web-based services in Türkiye. The present study was conducted to determine the effect of preconception care and counseling provided via the web-based software called Web Midwife Support designed by the researchers to use in the preconception period, on women’s awareness of risk and healthy lifestyle behaviors. Method Design and implementation of Web Midwife Support The web-based software called Web Midwife Support was created by developing the content, education system and design of the web-based education and conducting a pilot study. Creation of the web-based training content In the literature, it has been reported that while preconception counseling and care are provided, it is necessary to evaluate women holistically and to raise their awareness of risk through dimensions such as planning fertility with an evidence-based management, advanced maternal and paternal age, genetic and disease history of the family, physical activity, body mass index, nutrition, sexually transmitted infections and vaccination, chronic diseases, drugs, harmful habits and exposure, and psychosocial evaluation [ – ]. Within this context, the researchers prepared the content of the Web-Based Preconception Counseling and Care Program and the website based on evidence-based approaches [ – , ] in line with the literature, recommendations made by reputable organizations such as ACOG [ ], WHO [ ], RCOG [ ], CDC [ ] and ICM [ ], and results [ ] and suggestions of studies. The training was designed to consist of nine modules. Opinions of health professionals who were experts in their fields were also taken into account in creating the training content in accordance with the module titles. The web-based preconceptional care and counseling training program is shown in Supplementary Table 1. The videos created to be uploaded to the website were divided into training content subsections in a professional studio environment, using professional equipment. It took 6 min at least and 16 min at most to record each module video. In enriching these recorded contents with written expressions, animations, characters and visual elements, improving the resolution of the videos and editing the montage or effects, support was obtained from a professional video editor. In each module video, the main messages were given in line with the purpose and objectives of the presentation. The presentation videos were made as short as possible not to distract the participants’ attention, not to make them feel bored, and to keep their interest alive during the presentation. Design and development of web based education system To create, design and prepare the mobile compatible website, expert support and technical support and counseling services were received from a professional company.A one-year domain and hosting service named “ https://www.webebedestek.org/ ” was purchased from the software company and the web page was created with the name and logo of “Web Ebe Destek” (Türkiye equivalent of “Web Midwife Support”), which can be accessed through this system (Fig. ).The system consists of the following seven modules: “Role Management, User Management, Training Management, Form Management, User Training Screen, Contact Number Management, Module Management”. The YouTube platform was used to upload and watch video training content prepared for the website. “Web Midwife Support” YouTube channel “ https://www.youtube.com/@webebedestek ” was opened. The videos edited by the video editor were first uploaded to this platform by the researcher, and the visibility of the videos to everyone on this platform was hidden. Then, the IDs of the videos were taken and all the videos were uploaded to

be accessed through this system (Fig. ).The system consists of the following seven modules: “Role Management, User Management, Training Management, Form Management, User Training Screen, Contact Number Management, Module Management”. The YouTube platform was used to upload and watch video training content prepared for the website. “Web Midwife Support” YouTube channel “ https://www.youtube.com/@webebedestek ” was opened. The videos edited by the video editor were first uploaded to this platform by the researcher, and the visibility of the videos to everyone on this platform was hidden. Then, the IDs of the videos were taken and all the videos were uploaded to the website from the training creation screen. This method was chosen to provide the highest level of image quality. User names and passwords were created by the researchers through the system by selecting the user name, password, email, phone number and role authority for each person (Experimental-Control group). Women could access the website whenever they wanted with their own username and password. Thus, a system was created to prevent those who were not included in the sample or excluded from the study from entering the application, and the research-specific use of the web page was ensured. The system is designed in such a way that only the women in the experimental group can access the videos. However, if a user whether she is in the control or experimental group logs in for the first time, she fills in the informed consent form and the pre-test survey forms loaded on the system. Videos watched are colored “green” in the user panel of the website (Fig. ). The women watched training videos in module order, and they were not allowed to open a video before the previous one was watched. In addition, women were prevented from skipping a video to ensure that they watched all the training videos. The researcher monitored the User Training Detail Screen. The web platform was structured sequentially, preventing users from skipping content or progressing without finishing the active video. Consequently, in the final per-protocol analysis, the ‘uptake’ of the educational content was 100%, meaning all 42 experimental group participants successfully completed all nine training modules. Reminders were sent to the users who did not watch their videos regularly via the WhatsApp platform. The system gave the women the opportunity to watch videos over and over again, whenever they want, from any device (computer, tablet, smart phone) they want. The system was designed in such a way that the women in the experimental group were monitored on the User Training Screen to observe whether they watched the videos. To enable the users to receive preconception counseling and care services through the system, a help support dialog box was opened on the screen so that women could communicate 24/7 on issues they wanted to ask during and after the training. This button contributed to the interactive continuation of the education. A system scenario was created so that post-test survey forms would be accessed 8 weeks after the training module videos were watched. The development and technical refinement of the website and educational content were conducted between October 2022 and April 2023. During this period, the software was tested for usability and technical functionality through a preliminary application with 20 women (10 experimental, 10 control) who met the inclusion criteria. These women provided feedback that the platform was user-friendly and understandable; however, they were not included in the final study sample to ensure the integrity of the results. No changes were made to the study protocol following this preliminary phase. Study design, setting, participants and randomization The study is a pretest-posttest randomized controlled trial (RCT).The study population consisted of all the 18-49-year-old childbearing women who were registered in a premarital counseling unit of a community health center, and seven family health centers which were selected by drawing lots in a province in the Central Anatolia Region of Türkiye. The research was conducted between May-July, 2023. The sample size was calculated using PASS 14.0 software based on a reference study [ ]. To detect a significant difference in the primary outcome (Preconception Period Risk Awareness), with a significance level of 5% (α = 0.05), a minimum of 42 participants per group was required. This calculation assumed an expected mean difference of 10.3 and a standard deviation of 14.5, yielding an effect size of 0.70. Under these statistical parameters, the test power (1- β = 0.90) was calculated as 0.90367. To account for potential dropouts, the initial recruitment was increased by 20%, starting with 50 participants per group. Participants who met the inclusion criteria were assigned to either the experimental or control group (1:1 ratio) using a computer-generated randomization sequence via the random.org website [ ]. To ensure allocation concealment, the randomization sequence was generated by a researcher not involved in participant

Under these statistical parameters, the test power (1- β = 0.90) was calculated as 0.90367. To account for potential dropouts, the initial recruitment was increased by 20%, starting with 50 participants per group. Participants who met the inclusion criteria were assigned to either the experimental or control group (1:1 ratio) using a computer-generated randomization sequence via the random.org website [ ]. To ensure allocation concealment, the randomization sequence was generated by a researcher not involved in participant recruitment or data collection. Group assignments were revealed only after the baseline assessments were completed. To account for a potential 20% attrition rate, the initial recruitment goal was set at 50 participants per group. While the researchers and participants could not be blinded due to the nature of the web-based intervention, the study strictly adhered to CONSORT guidelines. The detailed numerical breakdown of participant recruitment, exclusions, and the final sample size ( n = 84) is presented in the Results section and illustrated in the CONSORT flow diagram (Fig. ). A clinical trial registration number (PRS ID: NCT06002451 ) was obtained for the study on August 13, 2023. Inclusion/exclusion criteria The inclusion criteria for the study were being literate and able to communicate in Turkish, being in the reproductive age group (18–49 years), not being pregnant at the time of recruitment, and having internet access via a computer, tablet, or smartphone. Conversely, the exclusion criteria were limited to conditions that would interfere with the study’s primary focus, specifically: having a history of receiving professional preconception counseling and care services, having a diagnosed psychiatric or psychological disorder, or being in the menopausal period. Additionally, participants who failed to actively engage with the web-based education system despite meeting the initial admission criteria were excluded from the final analysis. Outcomes The primary outcome of this study was the inter-group difference in the Preconception Period Risk Awareness Scale and Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors Scale-II scores between the experimental and control groups at the post-test (10th week). The a priori secondary outcomes included the intra-group (pre-test to post-test) changes in these scale scores within the experimental and control groups to evaluate individual longitudinal progress. Measures The primary outcomes of the study were the inter-group differences in preconception period risk awareness and healthy lifestyle behavior scores at 10 weeks post-intervention. These were assessed using the Preconception Period Risk Awareness Scale (PPRAS) and the Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors Scale-II (HLBS-II). The secondary outcomes included the intra-group pre-test and post-test changes within both the experimental and control groups. In addition to these primary and secondary measures, study data were collected using a Personal Information Form questioning the demographic and obstetric characteristics of the women. All quantitative assessments were conducted via the PPRAS and HLBS-II to evaluate the effectiveness of the web-based intervention. Personal information form The 15-item form is used to question the participating women’s demographic characteristics such as age, education level, income status, and obstetric characteristics. Preconception Period Risk Awareness Scale (PPRAS) The PPRAS developed by the researchers of the present study in line with preconception counseling and care is used to assess the risk awareness of women of reproductive age during the preconception period. The PPRAS includes 37 items and the following 8 sub-dimensions: fertility planning (items 1–3), advanced maternal and paternal age (items 4–6), genetic and disease history of the family (items 7–11), physical activity (items 12–14), nutritional status (items 15–17), sexually transmitted infections and vaccination status (items 18–25), chronic diseases (items 26–34) and psychosocial evaluation (items 35–37). Responses given to the items are rated on a five-point Likert type scale ranging from 1 to 5 (“Strongly disagree (1)”, “Disagree (2)”, Undecided (3)”, Agree (4)”, “Strongly agree (5)”. All the items in the chronic diseases subscale (items 26–34) are reverse scored. As the scores obtained from the scale increase so do the women’s risk awareness levels in the preconception period. The Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient was 0.90 for the overall PPRAS, indicating that the scale has a high degree of reliability. The Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient was 0.61 for the Fertility Planning subscale, 0.71 for the Advanced Maternal and Paternal Age Subscale, 0.78 for the Genetic and Disease History of the Family Subscale, 0.80 for the Physical Activity Subscale, 0.62 for the Nutritional Status Subscale, 0.85 for the Sexually Transmitted Infections and Vaccination Status Subscale, 0.88 for the Chronic Diseases Subscale, and 0.60 for the Psychosocial Evaluation Subscale [ ]. In the present study, the Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient for the overall PPRAS was calculated as 0.95. Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors Scale (HLBS-II) Walker et al. developed the HLBS-II in 1987 to assess an individual’s health-promoting behaviors related to his or her healthy lifestyle [ ]. The validity and reliability study

Paternal Age Subscale, 0.78 for the Genetic and Disease History of the Family Subscale, 0.80 for the Physical Activity Subscale, 0.62 for the Nutritional Status Subscale, 0.85 for the Sexually Transmitted Infections and Vaccination Status Subscale, 0.88 for the Chronic Diseases Subscale, and 0.60 for the Psychosocial Evaluation Subscale [ ]. In the present study, the Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient for the overall PPRAS was calculated as 0.95. Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors Scale (HLBS-II) Walker et al. developed the HLBS-II in 1987 to assess an individual’s health-promoting behaviors related to his or her healthy lifestyle [ ]. The validity and reliability study of the Turkish version of the HLBS-II was conducted by Bahar et al. (2008) [ ]. The HLBS-II includes 52 items and the following 6 sub-dimensions: Health Responsibility (items 3,9,15,21,27,33,39,45,51), Physical Activity (items: 4,10,16,22,28,34,40,46), Nutrition (items 2,8,14,20,26,32,38,44,50), Spiritual Development (items 6,12,18,24,30,36,42,48,52); Interpersonal Relations (items 1,7,13,19,25,31,37,43,49) and Stress Management (items 5,11,17,23,29,35,41,47) [ , ]. Responses given to the items are rated on a five-point Likert type scale ranging from 1 to 4 [never (1), sometimes (2), often (3), and regularly (4)]. The lowest and highest possible scores that can be obtained from the overall HLBS-II are 52 and 208, respectively. The total score obtained from the HLBS-II refers to the level of healthy lifestyle behaviors. The Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient of the HLBS-II is 0.92 suggesting that it has a high degree of reliability. The reliability coefficients of the sub-dimensions of the HLBS-II are as follows: Health responsibility: 0.77, Physical Activity: 0.79, Nutrition: 0.68, Spiritual Development: 0.79, Interpersonal Relations: 0.80, and Stress Management: 0.64. In the present study, the Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient for the overall HLBS-II was determined to be 0.94. Data collection Pre-intervention Research data were collected between May and July 2023. After obtaining informed consent, participants in both the experimental and control groups completed the baseline assessments via the web-based platform (Fig. ). These initial assessments, which included a Personal Information Form, the PPRAS, and the HLBS-II, are part of the sequential study flow detailed in the CONSORT flow diagram (Fig. ). Intervention Experimental group In the study, the women of reproductive age in the experimental group were provided with preconception counseling and care services for 10 weeks (two weeks of training and 8 weeks of follow-up). The 8-week follow-up and counseling process was conducted entirely online through the “Web Midwife Support” platform. No face-to-face meetings were held to maintain the digital nature of the intervention. During this period, participants utilized the 24/7 help-support dialog box to ask questions as needed. The researcher (a midwife) provided evidence-based answers and counseling to these inquiries on an on-demand basis.The experimental group watched training videos consisting of nine module training content for 2 weeks, in accordance with the training flow (Supplementary Table 1.). How the participants watched the training videos was monitored according to the training flow and they were sent reminder messages. They were enabled to communicate via the contact button that can be accessed 24/7 on the website, their questions regarding the scope of preconception counseling and care service were answered and referrals were made to experts if necessary. This messaging feature was designed strictly as an auxiliary, qualitative support tool to clarify immediate doubts and ensure participant engagement. Therefore, quantifying the frequency of these messages was not among the planned outcomes of this trial. Furthermore, to ensure participant safety, potential adverse events were continuously monitored throughout the 10-week intervention. This monitoring was conducted systematically via the aforementioned reminder messages and the 24/7 support feature, allowing participants to immediately report any physical or psychological distress. Control group The control group received no specific intervention and continued with their routine healthcare (usual care) during the 10-week study period. To ensure the integrity of the study, these participants were only permitted to log in to the web platform to complete the pre-test and post-test assessments; their access to the educational modules and interactive counseling support was strictly restricted until the study was completed. Post-intervention Ten weeks after the completion of the intervention, participants in both groups were re-administered the PPRAS and HLBS-II as a post-test via the website. To maintain ethical standards, women in the control group -who received no intervention during the study period-were granted full access to the educational materials and videos only after submitting their post-test data. The timing of these assessment phases and the final participant numbers are illustrated in Fig. . Statistical analysis The data obtained in the study were analyzed using the IBM SPSS (Statistical Package for Social Sciences) 23.0 program. A per-protocol (as-treated) analysis was utilized in this study rather than an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis. Participants who were initially randomized but failed to complete the full training modules, became pregnant, did not provide post-test data, or experienced internet access issues (n = 16) were excluded from

study period-were granted full access to the educational materials and videos only after submitting their post-test data. The timing of these assessment phases and the final participant numbers are illustrated in Fig. . Statistical analysis The data obtained in the study were analyzed using the IBM SPSS (Statistical Package for Social Sciences) 23.0 program. A per-protocol (as-treated) analysis was utilized in this study rather than an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis. Participants who were initially randomized but failed to complete the full training modules, became pregnant, did not provide post-test data, or experienced internet access issues (n = 16) were excluded from the final analysis. This ‘as-treated’ approach was specifically chosen to accurately evaluate the direct efficacy of the web-based intervention among participants who actively engaged with and received the full educational content. Descriptive statistical methods (numbers, percentage, arithmetic mean, standard deviation) were used to present the descriptive characteristics. Whether the data were normally distributed was checked through the kurtosis and skewness values. While the dependent samples t test was used in normally distributed dependent groups, the independent samples t test was used in normally distributed independent groups. While the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used in non-normally distributed dependent groups, the Mann Whitney U test was used in non-normally distributed independent groups. The chi-squared test was used for the inter-group comparisons of demographic characteristics of the participants in the experimental and control groups in categorical variables. Results Initially, 150 women were screened for the study. Among these, 50 were excluded for the following reasons: 14 did not meet the inclusion criteria, 16 refused to participate, and 20 were involved in the pilot study. Consequently, 100 women were randomized into the experimental ( n = 50) and control ( n = 50) groups. After accounting for participants who were lost to follow-up or did not complete the intervention, the study was completed with 84 participants (42 in each group), as detailed in the CONSORT flow diagram (Fig. ). The distribution of participants according to their sociodemographic and obstetric characteristics is presented in Tables and . These tables demonstrate that the participants in the experimental and control groups were similarly distributed across all variables at baseline. In accordance with the reporting standards for randomized controlled trials, no significance testing was performed for baseline characteristics, confirming that both groups were well-balanced before the intervention. Regarding the primary outcomes, the comparisons of the mean scores obtained from the PPRAS are presented in Table . At the baseline, no statistically significant differences were found between the experimental and control groups in any sub-dimensions or total scale scores (Experimental: 147.79 ± 21.11 vs. Control: 147.20 ± 20.80; p = 0.898). Following the intervention, the experimental group showed a significant increase in the total PPRAS score (182.29 ± 3.17; p < 0.001), while no significant change was observed in the control group (148.10 ± 20.71; p = 1.000). Intergroup comparisons at the post-test revealed that the experimental group achieved significantly higher awareness levels compared to the control group ( p < 0.001). Significant improvements ( p < 0.001) were observed in all sub-dimensions for the experimental group, including Fertility Planning (Experimental: 14.93 ± 0.26 vs. Control: 12.29 ± 2.17), Advanced Maternal and Paternal Age (14.79 ± 0.47 vs. 11.71 ± 1.89), Genetic and Disease History of the Family (24.69 ± 0.68 vs. 20.85 ± 3.51), Physical Activity (14.95 ± 0.31 vs. 12.22 ± 2.13), Nutritional Status (14.93 ± 0.26 vs. 13.22 ± 2.04), Sexually Transmitted Infections (38.55 ± 2.36 vs. 31.15 ± 6.68), Chronic Diseases (44.52 ± 0.92 vs. 33.10 ± 6.89), and Psychosocial Evaluation (14.93 ± 0.26 vs. 13.56 ± 1.73). Similarly, the results for the HLBS-II summarized in Table showed that baseline scores were similar between the groups (Experimental: 123.74 ± 24.09 vs. Control: 124.78 ± 22.91; p = 0.841). At the post-test, the experimental group’s total score increased significantly to 165.36 ± 16.25 ( p < 0.001), whereas the control group’s score remained stagnant (124.78 ± 22.78; p = 1.000). The difference between the groups at the follow-up was statistically significant in favor of the experimental group ( p < 0.001). Specifically, significant improvements in the experimental group were observed across all sub-dimensions ( p < 0.001): Health Responsibility (Experimental: 32.33 ± 3.27 vs. Control: 19.66 ± 5.52), Physical Activity (25.05 ± 4.14 vs. Control: 15.98 ± 4.82), Nutrition (31.12 ± 3.65 vs. Control: 20.98 ± 3.66), Spiritual Development (28.50 ± 4.13 vs. Control: 25.29 ± 5.12), Interpersonal Relations (25.95 ± 4.03 vs. Control: 24.24 ± 4.56), and Stress Management (22.40 ± 4.08 vs. Control: 18.63 ± 4.00). No side effects or adverse events were observed or reported in the participants during the study. Discussion The primary finding of this randomized controlled trial is that the web-based preconception counseling and care program, “Web Midwife Support”, significantly

0.001): Health Responsibility (Experimental: 32.33 ± 3.27 vs. Control: 19.66 ± 5.52), Physical Activity (25.05 ± 4.14 vs. Control: 15.98 ± 4.82), Nutrition (31.12 ± 3.65 vs. Control: 20.98 ± 3.66), Spiritual Development (28.50 ± 4.13 vs. Control: 25.29 ± 5.12), Interpersonal Relations (25.95 ± 4.03 vs. Control: 24.24 ± 4.56), and Stress Management (22.40 ± 4.08 vs. Control: 18.63 ± 4.00). No side effects or adverse events were observed or reported in the participants during the study. Discussion The primary finding of this randomized controlled trial is that the web-based preconception counseling and care program, “Web Midwife Support”, significantly improved both preconception risk awareness and healthy lifestyle behaviors among women of reproductive age. The effectiveness of our intervention aligns with the current healthcare trend, where web-based education is widely used in planning counseling and care services [ – ]. The use of these digital methods has become popular due to the rapid expansion of internet-based services, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic [ ]. Disseminating health-related information via the internet is generally considered the most appropriate way to reach populations [ , ]. Therefore, reaching women who need preconception care through such digital platforms and providing evidence-based support is a highly important and effective approach [ , , ]. The results of our study suggest that providing comprehensive but short training to women, and ensuring that they could receive preconception counseling and care freely whenever they wanted without making them feel bored, was an effective method to significantly improve their awareness of risk. This finding is supported by a web-based study conducted in Italy, which concluded that online advice improved health behaviors, increased folic acid use, and encouraged physician consultation among women planning pregnancy [ ]. Similarly, Withanage et al. [ ] determined that short and intensive primary care-based training effectively improves health knowledge and reduces pre-pregnancy risk factors. Furthermore, the significant increase in risk awareness observed in our study likely occurred because our training program was structured holistically. As demonstrated in a qualitative study [ ], there is a critical need for easily accessible, information-based web platforms to serve as primary sources of health information, which in turn directly improves women’s perceptions and awareness regarding pre-pregnancy health. A key strength of our intervention that contributed to increased risk awareness was the integration of live, 24/7 midwife support alongside the web-based modules, allowing women to be referred to relevant specialists when necessary. This design addresses a major limitation identified in previous research. For instance, a randomized controlled study using a web-based virtual health consultant (Gabby) found that while virtual agents are suitable for long-term care, they could not replace talking with a real healthcare provider [ ]. Our study bridges this gap by combining an innovative digital environment with real human interaction. Additionally, our findings regarding increased conscious awareness align with another randomized controlled study evaluating the ‘MyFamilyPlan’ application, which also positively affected women’s reproductive health discussions [ ]. However, it should be noted that because this 24/7 messaging feature was integrated primarily as a qualitative support tool, the specific frequency of messages and specialist referrals was not quantified in the present trial. Future research should systematically collect and analyze data on these live interactions to objectively measure their distinct impact on health outcomes. Regarding behavioral outcomes, the present study demonstrated that the preconception counseling and care program significantly improved the participants’ healthy lifestyle behaviors ( p < 0.05). Since unhealthy lifestyle behaviors have detrimental lifelong effects on reproduction, lifestyle interventions in the preconception period are crucial for improving fertility and the health of subsequent generations [ ]. Our results confirm that web-based education creates an appropriate environment for encouraging these health-promoting behaviors [ , , ]. Consistent with our findings, Je and Choi [ ] determined that a web-based preconception health program yielded significant improvements in the health promotion behaviors of couples ( p = 0.001), and integrating such systems can even improve prenatal care quality and self-efficacy [ ]. Finally, our study has a unique methodological value regarding the observation of these behavioral changes. Batra et al. [ ] noted that a limited one-week follow-up period might not be sufficient to observe meaningful changes in health behaviors. Our study eliminated this limitation in practice by providing module training for 2 weeks, followed by continuous preconception counseling and care services for 8 weeks, thereby allowing adequate and realistic time to monitor and achieve healthy lifestyle behavioral changes.Despite these strengths, this study has several limitations that warrant an in-depth consideration. First, the data on healthy lifestyle behaviors and risk awareness relied on self-reported scales, which may introduce reporting bias. Second, the study was conducted with a specific sample of women who had adequate digital literacy and internet access to use the “Web Midwife Support” platform; thus, the findings may not

study eliminated this limitation in practice by providing module training for 2 weeks, followed by continuous preconception counseling and care services for 8 weeks, thereby allowing adequate and realistic time to monitor and achieve healthy lifestyle behavioral changes.Despite these strengths, this study has several limitations that warrant an in-depth consideration. First, the data on healthy lifestyle behaviors and risk awareness relied on self-reported scales, which may introduce reporting bias. Second, the study was conducted with a specific sample of women who had adequate digital literacy and internet access to use the “Web Midwife Support” platform; thus, the findings may not be fully generalizable to populations with limited digital access or diverse socioeconomic backgrounds. Finally, while a 10-week follow-up was sufficient to observe behavioral and awareness changes, the study did not track long-term clinical obstetric outcomes (e.g., actual pregnancy rates, maternal morbidity, or birth outcomes). Future research should address these limitations by incorporating multi-center designs with longer follow-up periods to evaluate the actual clinical impact of such web-based interventions on pregnancy outcomes. Additionally, future studies could benefit from integrating objective clinical biomarkers alongside self-reported data to further validate the effectiveness of digital preconception care. Limitations of the study The fact that of the women of reproductive age, only those who had internet access at home or an internet connection on their mobile phone, and who had a tablet, computer or smartphone were included in the study was the limitation of the study. Thus, the findings obtained from the study are applicable only to the women surveyed and they cannot be generalized to all women. Another limitation of this study is the recruitment setting. Participants were recruited exclusively from a premarital counseling unit. This specific cohort may possess a higher intrinsic motivation, readiness, and awareness regarding preconception health compared to the general population. This potential selection bias should be carefully considered when generalizing the findings of this study to the broader population of all women of reproductive age. Conclusion In conclusion, the primary inter-group findings, along with the secondary pre-post improvements, provide promising evidence regarding the efficacy of the “Web Midwife Support” platform. This indicates that web-based preconception counseling is an effective, innovative approach to improving women’s awareness of preconception period risks and healthy lifestyle behaviors. By providing a foundational framework, this study can assist health personnel, particularly midwives, in integrating digital programs into field applications. Reviewing and enhancing preconception care services, which are currently not at the desired level in Türkiye and globally, remains a critical priority for developing new healthcare strategies. Within this context, it is recommended to conduct new web-based studies on preconception care. Furthermore, future research with larger samples should perform secondary data analyses to stratify results based on varying levels of platform ‘uptake’, specific module content, and scale subsets. Evaluating this dose-response relationship among different user profiles will provide deeper insights into the minimum optimal dose of digital education required to achieve significant behavioral changes. chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Since the 1980’s, the rate of cesarean delivery (CD) in the United States (US) has climbed dramatically to its current rate around 33% of all deliveries. Over a third of all CDs in the US are performed for labor arrest disorders, making labor arrest the most common indication for primary CD. The etiology of labor arrest is thought to be related to three primary factors – contraction strength or frequency, the size and position of the fetus, and the shape and space in the pelvis. Of these three etiologies, the most common and modifiable etiology of protracted labor is inadequate contraction strength or frequency, making this an important target for therapeutic intervention. Current standards for clinical management of prolonged labor include artificial rupture of membranes and administration of oxytocin to increase contraction strength and frequency. Even with these interventions, attempts to resolve prolonged labor often fail, ending in CD in up to 50% of these cases. Moreover, CD performed after prolonged labor has a higher risk of associated morbidity, including hemorrhage, infection, surgical injury, and poor neonatal outcomes. , Propranolol-hydrochloride has been investigated as a possible therapeutic agent in the management of labor since the 1960s, based on in vitro and in vivo evidence that propranolol increases uterine contractility. , As a nonselective β-adrenergic receptor blocker, propranolol blocks β2 adrenergic receptors that are expressed on the uterine myometrium, , thereby causing increased uterine smooth muscle contraction. Propranolol has been shown to cause increased contraction strength and frequency in pregnant patients at term. Clinical trials since the 1990s have demonstrated the safety of using propranolol during labor, but have shown mixed efficacy in the utility of propranolol as an adjunctive agent for labor induction or augmentation. – One randomized trial demonstrated a nearly 50% reduction in the rate of CD among patients with arrest of labor when given up to two doses of 2mg propranolol intravenously (IV) compared to placebo. However, subsequent studies have not corroborated these findings, and all of the existing studies of propranolol for labor augmentation have been limited by heterogeneous inclusion criteria, varied labor management protocols, and small sample sizes. , , This medication warrants further study to evaluate its effectiveness as an intervention for the treatment of arrested or prolonged labor. Our objective was to assess whether the addition of propranolol to standard labor interventions for patients with prolonged latent or active phase of labor would decrease the rate of CD. METHODS We conducted a double-blind placebo-controlled randomized trial at two hospitals within a large academic urban health system, the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania and Pennsylvania Hospital. The trial was conducted from July 2020 through June of 2022. Eligible patients were English-speaking and ≥16 years of age with a cephalic presenting singleton gestation ≥36 weeks who had a prolonged latent or active phase of labor. For the purposes of this study, we defined prolonged latent phase of labor as cervical dilation <6 cm after ≥8 hours of ruptured membranes (spontaneous or artificial) and oxytocin infusion. Prolonged active phase of labor was defined as cervical dilation ≥6 cm and <1 cm cervical dilation change over ≥2 hours with ruptured membranes and oxytocin infusion. These definitions of prolonged labor were established through expert consensus including a large group of practicing obstetricians and maternal-fetal medicine subspecialists in order to specifically identify patients whose labor courses were becoming abnormal, but had not yet met ACOG criteria for failed induction or arrest of active phase , in order to allow time to determine efficacy of the intervention before CD would be indicated. Exclusion criteria included: severe preeclampsia or a patient who was receiving a β blocker for any other indication, maternal heart rate <70 bpm, maternal blood pressure <90 mmHg systolic or <50 mmHg diastolic, any asthma, diabetes requiring insulin treatment during labor (given the concern regarding postnatal hypoglycemia with β blocker use), or a cardiac contraindication to β blockade. Patients who met eligibility criteria were approached on the labor unit by trained study personnel and written informed consent was obtained. The study medication was prepared in identical-appearing kits which included two 2mL vials and had an assigned study identification number by the Investigational Drug Service (IDS) via a computer-generated randomization scheme, and the medication kits were stored in a locked medication room on the labor unit. The randomization schema was maintained by IDS staff and not revealed to the investigators until after data analysis was completed. After obtaining written consent, one of the blinded, pre-randomized medication kits was obtained, andthe identification number was assigned to the patient. Each patient then received one dose of the blinded study medication in their kit, either 2mL propranolol (equivalent to 2mg) vs. 2mL placebo (normal saline), administered by the patient’s nurse as an IV push at a rate of 1mL/min. Each

The randomization schema was maintained by IDS staff and not revealed to the investigators until after data analysis was completed. After obtaining written consent, one of the blinded, pre-randomized medication kits was obtained, andthe identification number was assigned to the patient. Each patient then received one dose of the blinded study medication in their kit, either 2mL propranolol (equivalent to 2mg) vs. 2mL placebo (normal saline), administered by the patient’s nurse as an IV push at a rate of 1mL/min. Each patient was eligible for one possible repeat dose (available in the same assigned medication kit) of 2mL IV given ≥2 hours later if the patient remained on oxytocin infusion, made <2 cm of cervical dilation change on a subsequent exam, continued to meet inclusion criteria, and there were no plans to proceed with CD at that time. The study dosing regimen was selected based on previous clinical trials of propranolol use in labor, as well as current accepted practice of propranolol dosing regimens used in other clinical scenarios. Clinical team members were aware of patients’ participation in the trial but remained blinded to study group. All other aspects of labor management were at the discretion of the managing health care professional. At both hospital sites, labor management policies are consistent with ACOG guidelines for definitions of failed induction, arrest of dilation, and arrest of descent. Additionally, both sites use a standardized induction of labor protocol, which recommends active management of induction and labor, which includes interventions such as amniotomy at 4cm, oxytocin administration, and intrauterine pressure catheter use if a patient’s labor is not progressing. At both sites, hospital policy for oxytocin infusion includes initiation at 2 milliunits/minute and an increase of 2 milliunits/minute every 15 minutes until contractions are occurring every 2–3 minutes in a regular pattern, with a maximum of 40 milliunits/minute. In addition to routine maternal vital sign monitoring every 15–30 minutes throughout labor per hospital protocol, maternal heart rate and blood pressure were checked immediately prior as well as 5 minutes after administration of study drug. All patients had continuous fetal monitoring throughout labor and delivery. Per hospital protocol, all neonates who are exposed to a beta-blocker during labor undergo routine glucose screening after delivery via a heel-prick glucose check. Given the blinded nature of the study, the neonates of all patients enrolled in the study were considered beta-blocker exposed and had routine neonatal glucose screening. Patients were informed of this during the informed consent process. The primary outcome was CD. Secondary outcomes included duration of labor, maximum dose of oxytocin, indication for CD, shoulder dystocia, postpartum hemorrhage (defined as EBL>1,000mL), blood transfusion, endometritis, chorioamnionitis, and wound infection. Additionally, we assessed a composite maternal morbidity defined as any one of the following: venous thromboembolism, hysterectomy, intensive care unit admission, postpartum readmission up to 4 weeks, or maternal death. Additional secondary outcomes included neonatal hypoglycemia (defined as blood sugar level <50 mg/dL), neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admission > 48 hours, and a composite neonatal morbidity, defined as any 1 of the following: neonatal blood transfusion, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, intraventricular hemorrhage grade 3 or 4, need for neonatal therapeutic hypothermia, severe respiratory distress syndrome, necrotizing enterocolitis, sepsis, or death. Additionally, we planned an exploratory analysis in which we stratified the primary outcome by parity. Baseline data from our institution demonstrated a CD rate of 45% in patients with prolonged labor using the same definition for prolonged labor as utilized in this study. To obtain this estimate, a 3-month audit of the electronic health record was performed for deliveries at our institution. To determine our sample size, we considered a 15% absolute reduction in the rate of CD to be clinically meaningful. With an α of 0.05 and 80% power, we required 163 patients per group. Statistical analyses were performed using an intention-to-treat principle. Bivariate analyses were performed using chi-square and Fisher’s exact tests to compare categorical data. Student’s t-tests and Mann–Whitney U test were used to compare parametric and nonparametric data, where appropriate. A per-protocol analysis of the primary outcome was also conductedStatistical significance for the primary outcome was set at p<0.05. All data were analyzed using Stata version 15.1 (College Station, TX). Trained research staff collected all labor and delivery information, patient demographics, and maternal and neonatal outcome data. Information on race was collected to evaluate differences between groups. These data were collected and stored in an internet based clinical trial management system, Research Electronic Data Capture, REDCap. A data safety monitoring board (DSMB) was established to independently review the study protocol prior to study initiation, to evaluate the safety of the study throughout the enrollment period, and to conduct a pre-planned interim analysis at the mid-point of participant enrollment. At the time of the interim analysis, the DSMB recommended that the trial be stopped for futility. The determination for futility was made based on the assessment that even if goal enrollment was achieved, it would would not be statistically possible to demonstrate a significant difference in the primary outcome between study groups. In light of this, and the potential harm noted with an increased frequency in hemorrhage, the DSMB recommended cessation of the trial. RESULTS From July 2020-June 2022, a total of 9,002 laboring patients were screened for eligibility, of whom 850 met the definition for prolonged labor and 525 met the inclusion criteria and were eligible for enrollment ( ). Ultimately, 349 were approached for enrollment and 164 were consented and randomized with 84 in the propranolol group and 80 in the placebo group. Of these 164 patients, 154 received the first dose of study medication and just under half (n=64) received a second dose ( ). There were no cases of crossover between groups. displays demographic and clinical characteristics by study group. Our study population consisted of 60.5% Black and 34.6% White patients. The majority (83.5%) were nulliparous, most were overweight or obese, and 82.9% were undergoing an induction of labor. Seventy-five percent met criteria for enrollment by the prolonged latent phase of labor definition and 25% with the prolonged active phase of labor definition. Overall, the primary outcome of CD was similar between groups (57.1% propranolol vs. 57.5% placebo, RR 0.99 [0.76–1.29], ). When the primary outcome was stratified by parity, there remained no difference in CD. Results were also similar regardless of being enrolled in latent or active phase of labor and when analyzing results per-protocol (excluding the 10 patients who did not receive any study medication: 56.3% propranolol vs. 56.8% placebo, RR 0.99 [0.75–1.31]). demonstrates the differences in labor characteristics between groups. As noted in the table, there were no differences in length of labor, maximum dose of oxytocin utilized, or primary indication for CD. details indication for CD by phase of labor at enrollment. Table 4 details maternal and neonatal morbidity outcomes. There were no statistically significant differences in maternal or neonatal morbidity. The frequency of postpartum hemorrhage was higher for the propranolol group (20.2% vs. 10.0%, p=0.07, RR 2.02 [0.93–4.43]), but the difference was not statistically significant. The frequency of postpartum hemorrhage for participants who received only one dose of study drug were 15% in the propranolol group vs. 8.8% in the placebo group (p=0.35); frequencies for those who received two doses of study drug were 30.0% in the propranolol group vs. 11.8% in the placebo group (p=0.07). DISCUSSION In this multi-site, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial, there was no difference in CD between patients who received propranolol versus placebo for management of prolonged labor. There was also no difference in the rate of CD among subgroups of nulliparous or multiparous patients, or those enrolled in latent versus active phase of labor, though this trial was underpowered to detect differences in subgroups. While a prior trial from 1996 showed a nearly 50% reduction in CD among patients with arrested labor who received propranolol, our study did not corroborate these findings. The prior trial included a total of 96 patients with unchanged cervical dilation for ≥2 hours at ≥5cm dilation or “deceleration phase of at least 3 hours in nulliparas or 1 hour in multiparas,” and found a CD rate of 40% among those who received propranolol vs. 20% among those given placebo. Notably, significant benefit was only observed among participants with inadequate uterine contractility, and the trial used a lower dose oxytocin infusion (mean rate 8 mU/min (±8)), compared with a our trial (mean rate of 20.9 mU/min (±10)). It is therefore plausible that when oxytocin is titrated to its full potential to achieve adequate uterine contractions, as was done in our study, there is no further benefit conferred by the addition of propranolol. Two other previously published trials

or 1 hour in multiparas,” and found a CD rate of 40% among those who received propranolol vs. 20% among those given placebo. Notably, significant benefit was only observed among participants with inadequate uterine contractility, and the trial used a lower dose oxytocin infusion (mean rate 8 mU/min (±8)), compared with a our trial (mean rate of 20.9 mU/min (±10)). It is therefore plausible that when oxytocin is titrated to its full potential to achieve adequate uterine contractions, as was done in our study, there is no further benefit conferred by the addition of propranolol. Two other previously published trials also showed no difference in CD rate with propranolol administration for prolonged labor, , though these two trials included different populations. One included patients with arrest of active phase, but had differential use of oxytocin between study arms (28% in the propranolol group vs. 60% in the placebo group), and the other included many patients with a normal latent phase of labor and had an overall rate of CD of only 7%. Importantly, in our trial, all patients met criteria for prolonged labor despite active labor interventions including amniotomy, intrauterine pressure monitoring, and oxytocin titration. Therefore, our findings demonstrate that propranolol confers no additional benefit for the management of prolonged labor when standard labor interventions and oxytocin infusion are already being fully utilized. Other studies have not demonstrated an increased risk of postpartum hemorrhage with propranolol use. In one recent study evaluating propranolol as an adjunctive induction agent, there was a lower frequency of postpartum hemorrhage in the propranolol group (12.4% vs. 21.8%, p=0.05). While there was not a statistically significant difference in our trial, the higher frequency of postpartum hemorrhage in the propranolol group raises clinical concern. The exact etiology of how or why propranolol could lead to an increased risk of postpartum hemorrhage is unknown. It is plausible that when propranolol is utilized at the onset of labor, it may augment uterine contractility and ultimately uterine constriction thereby preventing hemorrhage, but perhaps when it is given after a lengthy and prolonged labor, when uterine contractility has already been exhausted, it may instead increase the risk of atony and hemorrhage. The relatively high rate of CD (>50%) among both nulliparous and multiparous patients in our trial demonstrates that our study included a group of patients with meaningfully abnormal labor curves who were at significant risk of requiring CD. Moreover, the lack of any suggestion of decrease in CD across any subgroup is compelling. We believe that our findings demonstrate a clear lack of benefit for propranolol in reducing CD among patients with prolonged labor who already received standard labor interventions. The strengths of this study are its rigorous design as a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial. Our study is nearly twice as large as prior trials evaluating propranolol for management of prolonged labor and more accurately reflects current evidence-based labor management. Furthermore, the inclusion of two separate hospitals with different clinical practices makes our findings more generalizable to other practice settings. Though our trial was stopped at the time of a planned interim analysis, we had a sufficient sample size to demonstrate futility in the primary outcome. Limitations of our trial include that labor management was at the discretion of health care professionals; however, both instutitions utilize an induction of labor protocol and a standardized approach to labor management. Additionally, the study was not powered to detect differences in the primary outcome among subgroups. Furthermore, we were not sufficiently powered to detect differences in secondary outcomes, which is likely limiting our ability to detect statistically significant differences in rates of postpartum hemorrhage and blood transfusion in unadjusted analyses. Labor management practices vary both institutionally and geographically, and it is possible that different labor management practices may influence the efficacy of this intervention. We found no evidence of benefit in the addition of propranolol for the management of prolonged labor. The trial was stopped for futility and concern for increased frequency of postpartum hemorrhage in the propranolol group. This medication should not be used for management of prolonged labor. documents.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin 227 Fetal Anomalies Diagnostic Imaging

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION The incidence of congenital heart disease (CHD) has been estimated at 6 to 12 per 1000 live births. According to the WHO, cardiac defects account for 42% of infant deaths and have become the leading cause of infant mortality. The fetal echocardiogram marks the primary tool for the evaluation and detailed diagnosis of fetal cardiovascular pathology from the late first trimester to term. Prenatal detection of CHD may improve the pregnancy outcome of fetuses with specific types of cardiac lesions. Accurate prenatal diagnosis offers potential clinical benefit with regard to infant outcome. Prenatal detection accuracy have varied widely for CHD. Some of this variation can be attributed to examiner experience, maternal obesity, transducer frequency, abdominal scars, gestational age, amniotic fluid volume, and fetal position. , Initially, fetal echocardiography included only a 4-chamber view (basic cardiac echocardiographic examination [BCEE]) of the heart, then outflow tract view (OTV) and 3-vessels trachea view (3VTV) were added to increase accuracy of fetal echocardiography. More recently, ECEE, which included the 4-chamber view, the right ventricular outflow tract, the left ventricular outflow tract, and the main pulmonary artery and its branches, was used as a specific protocol to identify some minimal defects in utero and provide more detail information on suspicious fetal heart. Several subspecialty organizations have published formal practice guidelines. – However, there was no consensus as how to choose from the 4 protocols for fetal CHD diagnosis according to different gestation period, different levels of risk, even though some comparison studies – have been done on the accuracy among different scan protocols. Buskens et al concluded a sensitivity of 4.5% with BCEE in a low-risk populations, whereas Oggè et al concluded a sensitivity of 60.3% with BCEE in a low-risk populations. Ott concluded a sensitivity of 14.3% with ECEE in a low-risk populations, whereas Abu-Rustam et al yielded a sensitivity of 65.8% with ECEE in a low risk. Tegnander et al yielded a sensitivity of 56.7% with BCEE + OTV in an unselected populations during the second trimester, whereas Zosmer et al yielded a sensitivity of 88.9% with BCEE + OTV in a high-risk population during the second trimester. Previous study had drawn a systematic review using 5 protocols detection of fetal CHD among unselected, low-, and high-risk populations, and they concluded that the pooled sensitivity of BCEE, BCEE + OTV/3VTV, ECEE, and BCEE + OTV + 3VTV were 52%, 65%, 89%, and 90%, respectively; however, they did not evaluate the sensitivity between prospective studies and retrospective studies, and only English articles were included in the study. Besides, they failed to make comparisons among different stages of pregnancy. Therefore, we decided to carry out a meta-analysis of prospective studies to make a more precise estimation. In the meta-analysis, we evaluated the accuracy of fetal diagnosis and compared sensitivities among different diagnostic protocols, different risk factors, and different stages of pregnancy. MATERIALS AND METHODS Literature Search Searches for all relevant published articles were performed in Chinese Biomedical Database (CBM), Medline, ISI Web of Knowledge, the Cochrane Library, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) from January 1, 1990 to August 13, 2015. The language was limited to English or Chinese. The eligibility of every study having >1 author during the search was assessed. We used the following keywords to collect relevant citations: (fetus OR fetal) AND (echocardiography OR echocardiogram OR ultrasonography) AND (congenital heart defect OR congenital heart defects OR congenital heart malformation OR congenital heart abnormality OR congenital heart abnormalities OR CHD) AND (prenatal diagnosis OR prenatal diagnoses OR prenatal screening). We further retrieved reference lists from included articles to avoid missing any relevant studies. Inclusionand Exclusion Criteria Two authors independently extracted the following information from included publications: the first author's name, publication year, country, maternal age, risk factors, gestational age, echo-views, number of fetus, and transducer frequency. If there were any disagreements, a consensus was agreed by discussion. Each study was screened for following inclusion and exclusion criteria: prospective studies were included; studies were selected for the review if they included at least 200 pregnant women; All neonates were postnatal examined or autopsy in cases of termination of pregnancy or perinatal death; provided the true positive (TP), true negative (TN), false positive (FP), and false negative (FN) results directly or indirectly, thus allowing the calculation of sensitivity and specificity. Additional data were requested from the original study investigators if necessary, such as positive likelihood ratios and negative likelihood ratios. Statistical Analysis We performed meta-analysis in a random-effect/fixed-effect model using Meta-disc software (Version 1.4) and Stata 11.0 software (Stata, College Station, TX). We used symmetric summary receiver-operating curve (SROC) to pool the result of diagnostic tests. Subgroup analysis was further conducted according to different sections, different gestations, and different risk factors. We conducted the heterogeneity test using χ 2 -based Q test and I

and false negative (FN) results directly or indirectly, thus allowing the calculation of sensitivity and specificity. Additional data were requested from the original study investigators if necessary, such as positive likelihood ratios and negative likelihood ratios. Statistical Analysis We performed meta-analysis in a random-effect/fixed-effect model using Meta-disc software (Version 1.4) and Stata 11.0 software (Stata, College Station, TX). We used symmetric summary receiver-operating curve (SROC) to pool the result of diagnostic tests. Subgroup analysis was further conducted according to different sections, different gestations, and different risk factors. We conducted the heterogeneity test using χ 2 -based Q test and I 2 test. The pooled sensitivity and 95% conﬁdence interval (CI) were calculated if there was no significant heterogeneity ( P > 0.05 and I 2 < 50%) existed. If not, a random-effect model was used. In our study, the I 2 value (0 ∼ 100%) over 50% indicated significant heterogeneity. The SROCs would show a curvilinear shape existed if a threshold effect appeared. We used funnel plots and the Deek test by Stata 11.0 software to evaluate the publication; a P value > 0.05 was considered as no obvious potential publication bias. RESULTS Characteristics of the Included Studies Initial searches identified 2456 English articles and 1456 Chinese articles. According to the inclusion and exclusion criteria mentioned above, 43 articles (18 Chinese article and 25 English articles) including 50 studies were eligible, with a total of 308,029 fetuses (Fig. ). A summary of included 50 studies is presented in Table , , – , – and the diagnostic test parameter of fetal echocardiography for the prenatal diagnosis of CHD is presented in Table . , – , – Meta-Analysis To explore whether any threshold effects existed in our study, we performed a spearman rank correlations of sensitivity against (1-specificity) to detect it. No obvious threshold effects exist in the meta-analysis according to the overall result (Spearman correlation coefficient: 0.041, P = 0.777). In general, the overall sensitivity and specificity of fetal echocardiography for the prenatal diagnosis of CHD had a moderate sensitivity of 68.5% (95% CI, 66.8%–70.2%) and the high specificity of 99.8% (95% CI, 99.7%–99.8%) (AUC = 0.9924). The SROC curve is shown in Figure with almost the same specificities of nearly 100%. We divided the included studies into 4 sections according to different echo-views: BCEE, ECEE, BCEE + OTV, and BCEE + OTV + 3VTV. We divided the eligible studies into 3 sections according to gestation order: the first trimester, the second trimester, the second to third trimester. And we also divided the eligible studies into 4 sections according to different risk factors: low risk, high risk, low and high risk, and unselected risk. The overall sensitivity of BCEE (Fig. A), BCEE + OTV (Fig. B), ECEE (Fig. C), BCEE + OTV + 3VTV (Fig. D) were 49.0%, 66.1%, 75.5%, and 83.7%, respectively. The overall sensitivity of ECEE, BCEE + OTV, and BCEE + OTV + 3VTV screening for fetal CHD was obviously higher compared with the echo-views of BCEE ( χ 2 = 133.14, 34.506, 99.337, all P < 0.05, respectively). When compared with BCEE + OTV, the overall sensitivity of ECEE was also obviously higher ( χ 2 = 18.168, P < 0.05). And when compared with BCEE + OTV and ECEE, the overall sensitivity of BCEE + OTV + 3VTV was also obviously higher ( χ 2 = 30.134, 9.447, P < 0.05, P = 0.002, respectively). Twenty-three articles diagnosed fetal CHD during the second trimester, 20 articles diagnosed fetal CHD during the second to third trimester, 2 articles diagnosed fetal CHD during first trimester to second trimester, 3 articles diagnosed fetal CHD during first trimester, only 1 article diagnosed fetal CHD during whole trimester, and 1 article not provided the gestation. According to different gestations, we performed a layering research and sensitivity analysis on the BCEE, ECEE, BCEE + OTV, BCEE + OTV + 3VTV. The overall sensitivity of the 4 protocols during the second trimester to third trimester were 65.6% (95% CI, 57.5%–73.0%), 60.3% (95% CI 51.7%–68.4%), 84.9% (95% CI 81.4%–88.0%), 80.7% (95% CI 74.5%–86.0%), respectively, and during the second trimester, the overall sensitivity of the 4 sections were 47.4% (95% CI 42.3%–52.5%), 68.0% (95% CI 63.4%–72.4%), 58.4% (54.4%–62.3%), 89.3% (81.7%–94.5%), respectively. When compared with the second trimester, the overall sensitivity of BCEE (Fig. ) and ECEE (Fig. ) screening for fetal CHD during the second to third trimester was obviously higher ( χ 2 = 14.585, 90.386, P < 0.05, respectively). However, when compared with the second trimester, the overall sensitivity of BCEE + OTV and BCEE + OTV + 3VTV screening for fetal CHD during the second to third trimester was not statistically significant ( χ 2 = 2.865, 3.548, P = 0.091, 0.06, respectively). To explore the sensitivity between the 4

(95% CI 63.4%–72.4%), 58.4% (54.4%–62.3%), 89.3% (81.7%–94.5%), respectively. When compared with the second trimester, the overall sensitivity of BCEE (Fig. ) and ECEE (Fig. ) screening for fetal CHD during the second to third trimester was obviously higher ( χ 2 = 14.585, 90.386, P < 0.05, respectively). However, when compared with the second trimester, the overall sensitivity of BCEE + OTV and BCEE + OTV + 3VTV screening for fetal CHD during the second to third trimester was not statistically significant ( χ 2 = 2.865, 3.548, P = 0.091, 0.06, respectively). To explore the sensitivity between the 4 scan protocols and 4 risk factors (low, high, low and high, unselected), we performed a layering research. In general, the overall sensitivity of BCEE, BCEE + OTV, ECEE, and BCEE + OTV + 3VTV for whole pregnancies were 49.0% (95% CI, 44.9%–53.2%), 66.1% (95% CI, 62.1%–70.0), 75.5% (95% CI, 73.2%–77.6%), and 83.7% (95% CI, 790%–87.7%), respectively. For pregnancies with low-risk factors and unselected factors, the overall sensitivity of BCEE (Fig. ) was 36.1% (95% CI, 29.7%–42.9%) and 55.7% 95% CI, 49.1%–62.2%), respectively. Only one article studied BCEE for pregnancies with high-risk factors, and only 1 article studied BCEE for pregnancies with low and high factors. For pregnancies with low-risk factors, high risk factors (Fig. ), low- and high-risk factors (Fig. ), the overall sensitivity of ECEE was 43.1% (95% CI, 38.5%–47.8%), 86.7% (95% CI, 83.2%–89.6%), and 89.5% (95% CI, 86.5%–92.0%), respectively. Only 2 articles , studied ECEE for pregnancies with unselected factors. For pregnancies with low-risk factors and unselected factors, the overall sensitivity of BCEE + OTV was 63.1% (95% CI, 57.1%–68.9%) and 67.2% (95% CI, 61.1%–72.8%), respectively. Only 1 article studied BCEE + OTV for pregnancies with high risk-factors, but no article for low- and high-risk factors. Three articles discussed BCEE + OTV + 3VTV for pregnant women with unselected risk factors, the overall sensitivity was 77.4% (95% CI, 69.7%–83.9%). Then a χ 2 test was performed between 4 scan protocols and different risk factors. Compared with pregnancies with low risk factors, the overall sensitivity of BCEE for whole pregnancies was obvious higher ( χ 2 = 10.605, P = 0.001). Compared with pregnancies with low-risk factors, the overall sensitivity of ECEE for whole pregnancies was also higher ( χ 2 = 133.827, P < 0.05), and for pregnancies with high-risk factors and low- and high-risk factors, the overall sensitivity of ECEE was obviously higher when compared with whole pregnancies ( χ 2 = 33.670, 54.686, P < 0.05, respectively). However, the overall sensitivity of BCEE + OTV for whole pregnant women was not statistically significant than pregnancies with low-risk factors and unselected risk factors ( χ 2 = 0.799, 0.069, P = 0.371, 0.793, respectively). Compared with pregnancies with unselected risk factors, the overall sensitivity of BCEE + OTV + 3VTV for whole pregnant women was not statistically significant ( χ 2 = 1.963, P = 0.161). Likewise, the overall sensitivity of BCEE was not statistically significantly than that of whole pregnancies ( χ 2 = 2.998, P = 0.083). Sensitivity Analysis and Meta-Regression There was substantial diversity across studies, the inconsistency ( I 2 ) was 94.5%, and sensitivity was 68.5% (95% CI, 66.8%–70.2%). One set of study data , , , – , – , , , were systematically removed, and the pooled results for the remaining studies were rechecked whether the results had a significant change, the inconsistency was still between 94.0% and 94.6%, then we removed them all, the inconsistency was still 85%, which suggested that the sensitivity analysis was robust. Then the sensitivity analysis was conducted for every study. If substantial heterogeneity is found to be present, then reasons for such heterogeneity can be explored by relating study level covariates to an accuracy measure. So a meta-regression was performed, out of all of the parameters, the risk level was significant sources of heterogeneity ( P = 0.012). However, none of the country, echo-view, transducer frequency, publication year, and gestation were statistically significant sources of heterogeneity ( P > 0.05). The meta-regression analysis results were shown in Table . Publication Bias We used funnel plot to detect whether the potential the publication bias of included studies existed in this study. In funnel plots, each dot represents a study included. All dots symmetric distribution on both sides of the line suggested there was no obvious publication bias. If not, which indicated that publication bias was existed. An absence of any asymmetric distribution of data points in the funnel plot and a quantified result of P = 0.061 in the Deek test indicated no potential significant publication bias in our meta-analysis (Fig. ). DISCUSSION The results of this meta-analysis indicate that prenatal echocardiography for CHD diagnosis had a moderate sensitivity and high specificity. The areas under
