Under these statistical parameters, the test power (1- β = 0.90) was calculated as 0.90367. To account for potential dropouts, the initial recruitment was increased by 20%, starting with 50 participants per group. Participants who met the inclusion criteria were assigned to either the experimental or control group (1:1 ratio) using a computer-generated randomization sequence via the random.org website [ ]. To ensure allocation concealment, the randomization sequence was generated by a researcher not involved in participant recruitment or data collection. Group assignments were revealed only after the baseline assessments were completed. To account for a potential 20% attrition rate, the initial recruitment goal was set at 50 participants per group. While the researchers and participants could not be blinded due to the nature of the web-based intervention, the study strictly adhered to CONSORT guidelines. The detailed numerical breakdown of participant recruitment, exclusions, and the final sample size ( n = 84) is presented in the Results section and illustrated in the CONSORT flow diagram (Fig. ). A clinical trial registration number (PRS ID: NCT06002451 ) was obtained for the study on August 13, 2023. Inclusion/exclusion criteria The inclusion criteria for the study were being literate and able to communicate in Turkish, being in the reproductive age group (18–49 years), not being pregnant at the time of recruitment, and having internet access via a computer, tablet, or smartphone. Conversely, the exclusion criteria were limited to conditions that would interfere with the study’s primary focus, specifically: having a history of receiving professional preconception counseling and care services, having a diagnosed psychiatric or psychological disorder, or being in the menopausal period. Additionally, participants who failed to actively engage with the web-based education system despite meeting the initial admission criteria were excluded from the final analysis. Outcomes The primary outcome of this study was the inter-group difference in the Preconception Period Risk Awareness Scale and Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors Scale-II scores between the experimental and control groups at the post-test (10th week). The a priori secondary outcomes included the intra-group (pre-test to post-test) changes in these scale scores within the experimental and control groups to evaluate individual longitudinal progress. Measures The primary outcomes of the study were the inter-group differences in preconception period risk awareness and healthy lifestyle behavior scores at 10 weeks post-intervention. These were assessed using the Preconception Period Risk Awareness Scale (PPRAS) and the Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors Scale-II (HLBS-II). The secondary outcomes included the intra-group pre-test and post-test changes within both the experimental and control groups. In addition to these primary and secondary measures, study data were collected using a Personal Information Form questioning the demographic and obstetric characteristics of the women. All quantitative assessments were conducted via the PPRAS and HLBS-II to evaluate the effectiveness of the web-based intervention. Personal information form The 15-item form is used to question the participating women’s demographic characteristics such as age, education level, income status, and obstetric characteristics. Preconception Period Risk Awareness Scale (PPRAS) The PPRAS developed by the researchers of the present study in line with preconception counseling and care is used to assess the risk awareness of women of reproductive age during the preconception period. The PPRAS includes 37 items and the following 8 sub-dimensions: fertility planning (items 1–3), advanced maternal and paternal age (items 4–6), genetic and disease history of the family (items 7–11), physical activity (items 12–14), nutritional status (items 15–17), sexually transmitted infections and vaccination status (items 18–25), chronic diseases (items 26–34) and psychosocial evaluation (items 35–37). Responses given to the items are rated on a five-point Likert type scale ranging from 1 to 5 (“Strongly disagree (1)”, “Disagree (2)”, Undecided (3)”, Agree (4)”, “Strongly agree (5)”. All the items in the chronic diseases subscale (items 26–34) are reverse scored. As the scores obtained from the scale increase so do the women’s risk awareness levels in the preconception period. The Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient was 0.90 for the overall PPRAS, indicating that the scale has a high degree of reliability. The Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient was 0.61 for the Fertility Planning subscale, 0.71 for the Advanced Maternal and Paternal Age Subscale, 0.78 for the Genetic and Disease History of the Family Subscale, 0.80 for the Physical Activity Subscale, 0.62 for the Nutritional Status Subscale, 0.85 for the Sexually Transmitted Infections and Vaccination Status Subscale, 0.88 for the Chronic Diseases Subscale, and 0.60 for the Psychosocial Evaluation Subscale [ ]. In the present study, the Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient for the overall PPRAS was calculated as 0.95. Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors Scale (HLBS-II) Walker et al. developed the HLBS-II in 1987 to assess an individual’s health-promoting behaviors related to his or her healthy lifestyle [ ]. The validity and reliability study

Paternal Age Subscale, 0.78 for the Genetic and Disease History of the Family Subscale, 0.80 for the Physical Activity Subscale, 0.62 for the Nutritional Status Subscale, 0.85 for the Sexually Transmitted Infections and Vaccination Status Subscale, 0.88 for the Chronic Diseases Subscale, and 0.60 for the Psychosocial Evaluation Subscale [ ]. In the present study, the Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient for the overall PPRAS was calculated as 0.95. Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors Scale (HLBS-II) Walker et al. developed the HLBS-II in 1987 to assess an individual’s health-promoting behaviors related to his or her healthy lifestyle [ ]. The validity and reliability study of the Turkish version of the HLBS-II was conducted by Bahar et al. (2008) [ ]. The HLBS-II includes 52 items and the following 6 sub-dimensions: Health Responsibility (items 3,9,15,21,27,33,39,45,51), Physical Activity (items: 4,10,16,22,28,34,40,46), Nutrition (items 2,8,14,20,26,32,38,44,50), Spiritual Development (items 6,12,18,24,30,36,42,48,52); Interpersonal Relations (items 1,7,13,19,25,31,37,43,49) and Stress Management (items 5,11,17,23,29,35,41,47) [ , ]. Responses given to the items are rated on a five-point Likert type scale ranging from 1 to 4 [never (1), sometimes (2), often (3), and regularly (4)]. The lowest and highest possible scores that can be obtained from the overall HLBS-II are 52 and 208, respectively. The total score obtained from the HLBS-II refers to the level of healthy lifestyle behaviors. The Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient of the HLBS-II is 0.92 suggesting that it has a high degree of reliability. The reliability coefficients of the sub-dimensions of the HLBS-II are as follows: Health responsibility: 0.77, Physical Activity: 0.79, Nutrition: 0.68, Spiritual Development: 0.79, Interpersonal Relations: 0.80, and Stress Management: 0.64. In the present study, the Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient for the overall HLBS-II was determined to be 0.94. Data collection Pre-intervention Research data were collected between May and July 2023. After obtaining informed consent, participants in both the experimental and control groups completed the baseline assessments via the web-based platform (Fig. ). These initial assessments, which included a Personal Information Form, the PPRAS, and the HLBS-II, are part of the sequential study flow detailed in the CONSORT flow diagram (Fig. ). Intervention Experimental group In the study, the women of reproductive age in the experimental group were provided with preconception counseling and care services for 10 weeks (two weeks of training and 8 weeks of follow-up). The 8-week follow-up and counseling process was conducted entirely online through the “Web Midwife Support” platform. No face-to-face meetings were held to maintain the digital nature of the intervention. During this period, participants utilized the 24/7 help-support dialog box to ask questions as needed. The researcher (a midwife) provided evidence-based answers and counseling to these inquiries on an on-demand basis.The experimental group watched training videos consisting of nine module training content for 2 weeks, in accordance with the training flow (Supplementary Table 1.). How the participants watched the training videos was monitored according to the training flow and they were sent reminder messages. They were enabled to communicate via the contact button that can be accessed 24/7 on the website, their questions regarding the scope of preconception counseling and care service were answered and referrals were made to experts if necessary. This messaging feature was designed strictly as an auxiliary, qualitative support tool to clarify immediate doubts and ensure participant engagement. Therefore, quantifying the frequency of these messages was not among the planned outcomes of this trial. Furthermore, to ensure participant safety, potential adverse events were continuously monitored throughout the 10-week intervention. This monitoring was conducted systematically via the aforementioned reminder messages and the 24/7 support feature, allowing participants to immediately report any physical or psychological distress. Control group The control group received no specific intervention and continued with their routine healthcare (usual care) during the 10-week study period. To ensure the integrity of the study, these participants were only permitted to log in to the web platform to complete the pre-test and post-test assessments; their access to the educational modules and interactive counseling support was strictly restricted until the study was completed. Post-intervention Ten weeks after the completion of the intervention, participants in both groups were re-administered the PPRAS and HLBS-II as a post-test via the website. To maintain ethical standards, women in the control group -who received no intervention during the study period-were granted full access to the educational materials and videos only after submitting their post-test data. The timing of these assessment phases and the final participant numbers are illustrated in Fig. . Statistical analysis The data obtained in the study were analyzed using the IBM SPSS (Statistical Package for Social Sciences) 23.0 program. A per-protocol (as-treated) analysis was utilized in this study rather than an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis. Participants who were initially randomized but failed to complete the full training modules, became pregnant, did not provide post-test data, or experienced internet access issues (n = 16) were excluded from

study period-were granted full access to the educational materials and videos only after submitting their post-test data. The timing of these assessment phases and the final participant numbers are illustrated in Fig. . Statistical analysis The data obtained in the study were analyzed using the IBM SPSS (Statistical Package for Social Sciences) 23.0 program. A per-protocol (as-treated) analysis was utilized in this study rather than an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis. Participants who were initially randomized but failed to complete the full training modules, became pregnant, did not provide post-test data, or experienced internet access issues (n = 16) were excluded from the final analysis. This ‘as-treated’ approach was specifically chosen to accurately evaluate the direct efficacy of the web-based intervention among participants who actively engaged with and received the full educational content. Descriptive statistical methods (numbers, percentage, arithmetic mean, standard deviation) were used to present the descriptive characteristics. Whether the data were normally distributed was checked through the kurtosis and skewness values. While the dependent samples t test was used in normally distributed dependent groups, the independent samples t test was used in normally distributed independent groups. While the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used in non-normally distributed dependent groups, the Mann Whitney U test was used in non-normally distributed independent groups. The chi-squared test was used for the inter-group comparisons of demographic characteristics of the participants in the experimental and control groups in categorical variables. Results Initially, 150 women were screened for the study. Among these, 50 were excluded for the following reasons: 14 did not meet the inclusion criteria, 16 refused to participate, and 20 were involved in the pilot study. Consequently, 100 women were randomized into the experimental ( n = 50) and control ( n = 50) groups. After accounting for participants who were lost to follow-up or did not complete the intervention, the study was completed with 84 participants (42 in each group), as detailed in the CONSORT flow diagram (Fig. ). The distribution of participants according to their sociodemographic and obstetric characteristics is presented in Tables and . These tables demonstrate that the participants in the experimental and control groups were similarly distributed across all variables at baseline. In accordance with the reporting standards for randomized controlled trials, no significance testing was performed for baseline characteristics, confirming that both groups were well-balanced before the intervention. Regarding the primary outcomes, the comparisons of the mean scores obtained from the PPRAS are presented in Table . At the baseline, no statistically significant differences were found between the experimental and control groups in any sub-dimensions or total scale scores (Experimental: 147.79 ± 21.11 vs. Control: 147.20 ± 20.80; p = 0.898). Following the intervention, the experimental group showed a significant increase in the total PPRAS score (182.29 ± 3.17; p < 0.001), while no significant change was observed in the control group (148.10 ± 20.71; p = 1.000). Intergroup comparisons at the post-test revealed that the experimental group achieved significantly higher awareness levels compared to the control group ( p < 0.001). Significant improvements ( p < 0.001) were observed in all sub-dimensions for the experimental group, including Fertility Planning (Experimental: 14.93 ± 0.26 vs. Control: 12.29 ± 2.17), Advanced Maternal and Paternal Age (14.79 ± 0.47 vs. 11.71 ± 1.89), Genetic and Disease History of the Family (24.69 ± 0.68 vs. 20.85 ± 3.51), Physical Activity (14.95 ± 0.31 vs. 12.22 ± 2.13), Nutritional Status (14.93 ± 0.26 vs. 13.22 ± 2.04), Sexually Transmitted Infections (38.55 ± 2.36 vs. 31.15 ± 6.68), Chronic Diseases (44.52 ± 0.92 vs. 33.10 ± 6.89), and Psychosocial Evaluation (14.93 ± 0.26 vs. 13.56 ± 1.73). Similarly, the results for the HLBS-II summarized in Table showed that baseline scores were similar between the groups (Experimental: 123.74 ± 24.09 vs. Control: 124.78 ± 22.91; p = 0.841). At the post-test, the experimental group’s total score increased significantly to 165.36 ± 16.25 ( p < 0.001), whereas the control group’s score remained stagnant (124.78 ± 22.78; p = 1.000). The difference between the groups at the follow-up was statistically significant in favor of the experimental group ( p < 0.001). Specifically, significant improvements in the experimental group were observed across all sub-dimensions ( p < 0.001): Health Responsibility (Experimental: 32.33 ± 3.27 vs. Control: 19.66 ± 5.52), Physical Activity (25.05 ± 4.14 vs. Control: 15.98 ± 4.82), Nutrition (31.12 ± 3.65 vs. Control: 20.98 ± 3.66), Spiritual Development (28.50 ± 4.13 vs. Control: 25.29 ± 5.12), Interpersonal Relations (25.95 ± 4.03 vs. Control: 24.24 ± 4.56), and Stress Management (22.40 ± 4.08 vs. Control: 18.63 ± 4.00). No side effects or adverse events were observed or reported in the participants during the study. Discussion The primary finding of this randomized controlled trial is that the web-based preconception counseling and care program, “Web Midwife Support”, significantly

No side effects or adverse events were observed or reported in the participants during the study. Discussion The primary finding of this randomized controlled trial is that the web-based preconception counseling and care program, “Web Midwife Support”, significantly improved both preconception risk awareness and healthy lifestyle behaviors among women of reproductive age. The effectiveness of our intervention aligns with the current healthcare trend, where web-based education is widely used in planning counseling and care services [ – ]. The use of these digital methods has become popular due to the rapid expansion of internet-based services, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic [ ]. Disseminating health-related information via the internet is generally considered the most appropriate way to reach populations [ , ]. Therefore, reaching women who need preconception care through such digital platforms and providing evidence-based support is a highly important and effective approach [ , , ]. The results of our study suggest that providing comprehensive but short training to women, and ensuring that they could receive preconception counseling and care freely whenever they wanted without making them feel bored, was an effective method to significantly improve their awareness of risk. This finding is supported by a web-based study conducted in Italy, which concluded that online advice improved health behaviors, increased folic acid use, and encouraged physician consultation among women planning pregnancy [ ]. Similarly, Withanage et al. [ ] determined that short and intensive primary care-based training effectively improves health knowledge and reduces pre-pregnancy risk factors. Furthermore, the significant increase in risk awareness observed in our study likely occurred because our training program was structured holistically. As demonstrated in a qualitative study [ ], there is a critical need for easily accessible, information-based web platforms to serve as primary sources of health information, which in turn directly improves women’s perceptions and awareness regarding pre-pregnancy health. A key strength of our intervention that contributed to increased risk awareness was the integration of live, 24/7 midwife support alongside the web-based modules, allowing women to be referred to relevant specialists when necessary. This design addresses a major limitation identified in previous research. For instance, a randomized controlled study using a web-based virtual health consultant (Gabby) found that while virtual agents are suitable for long-term care, they could not replace talking with a real healthcare provider [ ]. Our study bridges this gap by combining an innovative digital environment with real human interaction. Additionally, our findings regarding increased conscious awareness align with another randomized controlled study evaluating the ‘MyFamilyPlan’ application, which also positively affected women’s reproductive health discussions [ ]. However, it should be noted that because this 24/7 messaging feature was integrated primarily as a qualitative support tool, the specific frequency of messages and specialist referrals was not quantified in the present trial. Future research should systematically collect and analyze data on these live interactions to objectively measure their distinct impact on health outcomes. Regarding behavioral outcomes, the present study demonstrated that the preconception counseling and care program significantly improved the participants’ healthy lifestyle behaviors ( p < 0.05). Since unhealthy lifestyle behaviors have detrimental lifelong effects on reproduction, lifestyle interventions in the preconception period are crucial for improving fertility and the health of subsequent generations [ ]. Our results confirm that web-based education creates an appropriate environment for encouraging these health-promoting behaviors [ , , ]. Consistent with our findings, Je and Choi [ ] determined that a web-based preconception health program yielded significant improvements in the health promotion behaviors of couples ( p = 0.001), and integrating such systems can even improve prenatal care quality and self-efficacy [ ]. Finally, our study has a unique methodological value regarding the observation of these behavioral changes. Batra et al. [ ] noted that a limited one-week follow-up period might not be sufficient to observe meaningful changes in health behaviors. Our study eliminated this limitation in practice by providing module training for 2 weeks, followed by continuous preconception counseling and care services for 8 weeks, thereby allowing adequate and realistic time to monitor and achieve healthy lifestyle behavioral changes.Despite these strengths, this study has several limitations that warrant an in-depth consideration. First, the data on healthy lifestyle behaviors and risk awareness relied on self-reported scales, which may introduce reporting bias. Second, the study was conducted with a specific sample of women who had adequate digital literacy and internet access to use the “Web Midwife Support” platform; thus, the findings may not

study eliminated this limitation in practice by providing module training for 2 weeks, followed by continuous preconception counseling and care services for 8 weeks, thereby allowing adequate and realistic time to monitor and achieve healthy lifestyle behavioral changes.Despite these strengths, this study has several limitations that warrant an in-depth consideration. First, the data on healthy lifestyle behaviors and risk awareness relied on self-reported scales, which may introduce reporting bias. Second, the study was conducted with a specific sample of women who had adequate digital literacy and internet access to use the “Web Midwife Support” platform; thus, the findings may not be fully generalizable to populations with limited digital access or diverse socioeconomic backgrounds. Finally, while a 10-week follow-up was sufficient to observe behavioral and awareness changes, the study did not track long-term clinical obstetric outcomes (e.g., actual pregnancy rates, maternal morbidity, or birth outcomes). Future research should address these limitations by incorporating multi-center designs with longer follow-up periods to evaluate the actual clinical impact of such web-based interventions on pregnancy outcomes. Additionally, future studies could benefit from integrating objective clinical biomarkers alongside self-reported data to further validate the effectiveness of digital preconception care. Limitations of the study The fact that of the women of reproductive age, only those who had internet access at home or an internet connection on their mobile phone, and who had a tablet, computer or smartphone were included in the study was the limitation of the study. Thus, the findings obtained from the study are applicable only to the women surveyed and they cannot be generalized to all women. Another limitation of this study is the recruitment setting. Participants were recruited exclusively from a premarital counseling unit. This specific cohort may possess a higher intrinsic motivation, readiness, and awareness regarding preconception health compared to the general population. This potential selection bias should be carefully considered when generalizing the findings of this study to the broader population of all women of reproductive age. Conclusion In conclusion, the primary inter-group findings, along with the secondary pre-post improvements, provide promising evidence regarding the efficacy of the “Web Midwife Support” platform. This indicates that web-based preconception counseling is an effective, innovative approach to improving women’s awareness of preconception period risks and healthy lifestyle behaviors. By providing a foundational framework, this study can assist health personnel, particularly midwives, in integrating digital programs into field applications. Reviewing and enhancing preconception care services, which are currently not at the desired level in Türkiye and globally, remains a critical priority for developing new healthcare strategies. Within this context, it is recommended to conduct new web-based studies on preconception care. Furthermore, future research with larger samples should perform secondary data analyses to stratify results based on varying levels of platform ‘uptake’, specific module content, and scale subsets. Evaluating this dose-response relationship among different user profiles will provide deeper insights into the minimum optimal dose of digital education required to achieve significant behavioral changes. chunks.content: Introduction According to the definition by the International Continence Society (ICS), stress urinary incontinence (SUI) refers to the involuntary leakage of urine from the urethra during activities that cause a sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure, such as sneezing, coughing, or laughing ( ). Primiparous pregnancy is a major risk factor for the development of SUI, with the childbirth period being a key contributor ( , ). Epidemiological studies report that the incidence of postpartum SUI ranges from 16.41% to 25.00% ( ). The postpartum period represents a particularly critical stage for the onset and recognition of SUI. During this time, physiological changes in pelvic floor structure and function, coupled with the psychological adjustments associated with motherhood, can significantly influence how women perceive and respond to urinary symptoms. Many primiparas feel embarrassed and anxious about unpredictable urine leakage, compelling them to withdraw from routine social engagements and physical activities. This not only impedes their successful reintegration into social life but can also disrupt their postpartum recovery trajectories ( ). More critically, influenced by traditional beliefs or lack of awareness, some primiparas and their families mistakenly consider postpartum stress urinary incontinence as a ‘normal consequence of childbirth’, consequently enduring the condition silently rather than proactively seeking professional help, which often delays the optimal intervention timing ( ). Current evidence suggests that the period from 6 weeks to 6 months postpartum represents a critical window for the recovery of pelvic floor function. Initiating standardised rehabilitation interventions during this stage can effectively improve pelvic floor muscle dynamics and functional outcomes ( ). In this context, three-dimensional pelvic floor ultrasound has emerged as a primary imaging modality due to its accessibility, cost-effectiveness, high reproducibility, and ability to provide dynamic, spatially accurate visualization of pelvic floor structures and organ relationships ( ). In recent years, growing attention has been directed toward imaging-based evaluations of postpartum SUI. However, there remains a lack of systematic and user-friendly predictive models specifically designed for primiparous women in the early postpartum period. Therefore, the present study aims to integrate clinical risk factors with three-dimensional pelvic floor ultrasound parameters to identify independent predictors of postpartum SUI and to construct a nomogram prediction model. The goal is to provide evidence-based support for the early identification of high-risk individuals and to guide the implementation of individualized pelvic floor rehabilitation strategies in clinical practice. Materials and methods Study participants This study was a single-center retrospective study involving 447 primiparous women who delivered at Zhejiang Hospital between July 2022 and January 2024 and underwent postpartum follow-up and three-dimensional pelvic floor ultrasound examination at the outpatient clinic 6–8 weeks after delivery. The flow of participants through each stage of the study is presented in . Inclusion criteria were: 1. Women who gave birth at our hospital and returned for a follow-up examination 6–8 weeks postpartum; 2. Primiparous women with a single pregnancy; 3. Women capable of performing a proper Valsalva manoeuvre; 4. Women with complete clinical records. Exclusion criteria: 1. Those with congenital pelvic structural abnormalities; 2. Those who have undergone previous pelvic-related surgeries; 3. Those with large pelvic masses; 4. A history of chronic cough or long-standing constipation. 5. Those with a history of SUI or other Pelvic Floor Disorder (PFD) conditions prior to delivery; This study has been reviewed and approved by the Zhejiang Hospital Ethics Committee, with exemption from informed consent (ethics approval number: IRB-2024-049 K). Study design The diagnostic criteria for SUI were based on established clinical guidelines ( ) and included the following: 1. Involuntary leakage of urine from the urethral orifice during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure, such as sneezing, coughing, laughing, or physical exertion. The leakage resolves once the pressure subsides; 2. A positive result on either the cough stress test or the 1-h pad test. Three-dimensional pelvic floor ultrasound examinations were performed using a GE Voluson E10 colour Doppler ultrasound system equipped with a three-dimensional volume transducer, operating at a frequency range of 4–8 MHz. Prior to the examination, patients were instructed to void their bowels and bladder at least 15 min in advance and were trained to perform an effective Valsalva manoeuvre. During the examination, patients were placed in the lithotomy position and instructed to breathe naturally. After adjusting the machine settings, a sterile coupling agent was applied to the surface of the probe, and a disposable probe cover was used. The labia were gently separated, and the probe was positioned firmly against the perineum between the labia majora. A static mid-sagittal image of the pelvic floor was first obtained at rest, clearly visualising anatomical structures including the pubic symphysis, urethra, bladder neck, partial bladder, vagina, rectum, and anal canal ( ). Subsequently, patients were instructed to perform a maximal and effective Valsalva manoeuvre. Ultrasound images were collected during both the resting state and maximum Valsalva manoeuvre and

A static mid-sagittal image of the pelvic floor was first obtained at rest, clearly visualising anatomical structures including the pubic symphysis, urethra, bladder neck, partial bladder, vagina, rectum, and anal canal ( ). Subsequently, patients were instructed to perform a maximal and effective Valsalva manoeuvre. Ultrasound images were collected during both the resting state and maximum Valsalva manoeuvre and were stored separately for further analysis. Measurements of pelvic floor parameters were performed using the built-in software of the ultrasound system, and all measurements were taken at both rest and maximal strain for each subject. Observation target Clinical and obstetric data were obtained by reviewing the hospital’s electronic medical record system. The following information was collected at the time of maternal admission: age, height, weight, body mass index (BMI), smoking history, alcohol consumption history, presence of gestational hypertension [diagnosed according to the Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Gestational Hypertensive Disorders ( )], and presence of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) [diagnosed based on the criteria outlined by the Diabetes Branch of the Chinese Medical Association ( )]. Additional variables included total weight gain during pregnancy, gestational age at delivery, mode of delivery, neonatal sex, neonatal birth weight, use of assisted vaginal delivery (forceps), occurrence of vaginal tears and/or episiotomy, and whether the delivery was classified as precipitous ( ) or difficult ( ). All data were entered into Microsoft Excel and independently cross-checked by two researchers to ensure accuracy. Pelvic floor function was evaluated using three-dimensional pelvic floor ultrasound. The following parameters were recorded: 1) Bladder neck position at rest: The vertical distance between the bladder neck and the reference line in the resting state. Values above the reference line are recorded as positive; values below are recorded as negative. 2) Bladder neck position during maximal Valsalva manoeuvre: The vertical distance between the bladder neck and the reference line at maximal Valsalva. Positive and negative values are recorded as above. 3) Bladder neck mobility: Calculated as the difference between bladder neck positions at rest and during maximal Valsalva manoeuvre. 4) Urethral inclination angle at rest: The angle between the proximal urethra and the midline of the body in the resting state. 5) Urethral inclination angle during maximal Valsalva manoeuvre: The angle between the proximal urethra and the body’s midline during maximal Valsalva. 6) Urethral rotation angle: Defined as the difference between the urethral inclination angle at rest and during maximal Valsalva. 7) Posterior bladder angle at rest: The angle formed between the proximal urethra and the posterior wall of the bladder in the resting state. 8) Posterior bladder angle during maximal Valsalva manoeuvre: The angle between the proximal urethra and the posterior bladder wall during maximal Valsalva. 9) Levator hiatus area: The maximum cross-sectional area of the levator ani muscle hiatus during maximal Valsalva manoeuvre. All ultrasound examinations were performed by experienced sonographers using standardized protocols. Each parameter was measured at least three times, and the mean value was used for analysis to ensure measurement reliability. Statistical analyses All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 26.0, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages [ n (%)] and compared using the chi-square test. Continuous variables following a normal distribution were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and analysed using the independent samples t -test. Non-normally distributed continuous variables were presented as median (interquartile range) [M (P25, P75)] and compared using the Mann–Whitney U test. A p -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The dataset was randomly divided into a training set ( n = 312) and a test set ( n = 135) in a 7:3 ratio. The random sampling method is as follows: Number the samples according to the review time sequence and enter them into an Excel spreadsheet on a computer. Use the formula ‘=RANDBETWEEN (minimum value, maximum value)’ = VLOOKUP(lookup value, data, column index, match condition),” 312 training set sample sequence numbers (70% of the total sample) are randomly generated, while the remaining 135 samples (30% of the total sample) are assigned to the test set. All variables from the training set were initially included in a univariate logistic regression analysis to identify potential predictors. Variables with statistical significance in the univariate analysis were subsequently entered into a stepwise multivariate logistic regression model, using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) as the criterion for variable selection. Independent predictors identified in the final multivariate model were incorporated into the construction of a nomogram prediction model. The predictive performance of the nomogram was evaluated in both the training and test

Variables with statistical significance in the univariate analysis were subsequently entered into a stepwise multivariate logistic regression model, using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) as the criterion for variable selection. Independent predictors identified in the final multivariate model were incorporated into the construction of a nomogram prediction model. The predictive performance of the nomogram was evaluated in both the training and test sets using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and the Hosmer–Lemeshow (HL) goodness-of-fit test. Model discrimination was assessed by calculating the area under the ROC curve (AUC), while calibration was evaluated using calibration plots and the HL test. Variable coding notes: 1) Gestational diabetes mellitus: Yes = 1; No = 0 2) Gestational hypertension: Yes = 1; No = 0 3) Mode of delivery: Vaginal delivery = 1; Elective caesarean section = 2; Emergency caesarean section = 3 4) Assisted vaginal delivery (forceps): Yes = 1; No = 0 5) Episiotomy: Yes = 1; No = 0 6) Preterm birth: Yes = 1; No = 0 7) Difficult labour: Yes = 1; No = 0 Results This study ultimately included 447 subjects aged 19–40 years, with a mean age of 29.1 ± 3.1 years. Including 223 vaginal deliveries, 180 planned cesarean sections, and 44 intrapartum cesarean sections. Comparative analysis of general data from training sets and validation sets The cohort of 447 primiparous women was randomly divided into training and test sets at a 7:3 ratio, yielding 312 cases in the training set and 135 in the test set. No statistically significant differences were observed in clinical characteristics or ultrasound parameters between the sets ( p > 0.05), confirming their suitability for model development and validation. Univariate analysis of clinical data from the training set and various parameters from three-dimensional pelvic floor ultrasound Based on the presence or absence of SUI, participants in the training set were categorised into the SUI group ( n = 108) and the non-SUI group ( n = 204). Given the minimal prevalence of smoking and alcohol consumption ( n = 1 per group), these variables were not subjected to formal statistical testing as they lacked sufficient power for meaningful analysis. There were statistically significant differences ( p < 0.05) between the SUI group and the non-SUI group in the training set in terms of mode of delivery, use of assisted delivery techniques (forceps) during delivery, and the presence of episiotomy tears during delivery. There were statistically significant differences between the two groups in the following parameters ( p < 0.05): urethral tilt angle at rest, bladder neck position during maximum Valsalva manoeuvre, bladder neck mobility, urethral tilt angle during maximum Valsalva manoeuvre, urethral rotation angle, posterior bladder angle at rest, posterior bladder angle during maximum Valsalva manoeuvre, and levator ani muscle hiatus area ( ). Analysis of risk factors for postpartum SUI Variables demonstrating statistical significance ( p < 0.05) in univariate analyses were entered into a stepwise multivariable logistic regression model with the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) as the variable selection criterion to derive the final predictive model. The results showed that the use of assisted delivery techniques (forceps), bladder neck position during maximum Valsalva manoeuvre, urethral rotation angle, posterior bladder angle during maximum Valsalva manoeuvre, and levator ani muscle tear area were risk factors for early postpartum SUI (OR = 34.57, 0.81, 0.98, 1.04, 1.29, respectively, all p < 0.05; ). Development and evaluation of a nomogram prediction model The independent risk factors identified through stepwise logistic regression-namely, operative vaginal delivery (forceps), bladder neck position during maximal Valsalva, urethral rotation angle, retrovesical angle during maximal Valsalva, and levator hiatus area-were incorporated into a predictive nomogram model ( ). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis demonstrated excellent model performance, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.933 (95% CI: 0.906–0.961) in the training set, indicating a high level of discriminatory ability ( ). The Hosmer–Lemeshow (HL) goodness-of-fit test for the training set calibration curve yielded a χ 2 value of 10.281 (df = 8, p = 0.2458), suggesting good model calibration (as p > 0.05). Similarly, the HL test for the test set showed a χ 2 value of 7.456 (df = 8, p = 0.4884), further confirming the model’s calibration and stability when applied to an independent sample ( ). The ROC curve of the test set also indicated strong predictive performance, with a high AUC value demonstrating good generalisability. In both the training and test sets, the blue prediction curve consistently outperformed the “None” strategy (black curve) across most threshold levels, indicating that the model performs

Similarly, the HL test for the test set showed a χ 2 value of 7.456 (df = 8, p = 0.4884), further confirming the model’s calibration and stability when applied to an independent sample ( ). The ROC curve of the test set also indicated strong predictive performance, with a high AUC value demonstrating good generalisability. In both the training and test sets, the blue prediction curve consistently outperformed the “None” strategy (black curve) across most threshold levels, indicating that the model performs substantially better than random or uninformative prediction. Furthermore, the model’s performance surpassed that of the “All” strategy, underscoring its effectiveness in identifying individuals at high risk of postpartum SUI. Classic cases How to use the nomogram model: Based on the patient’s clinical data and pelvic floor ultrasound examination results, scores corresponding to each predictive indicator can be obtained. The sum of the scores for each indicator is the total score. Find the corresponding risk value on the total score line to determine the probability of SUI occurring in the postpartum woman. Example: The patient is a 27-year-old primipara who delivered vaginally with forceps-assisted delivery during labour. During the maximum Valsalva manoeuvre, the following measurements were taken: bladder neck position −3 mm; urethral rotation angle 92.8°; posterior bladder angle 158.01°; and levator ani muscle hiatus area 25.07 cm 2 . The total score was 220, which corresponds to a predicted risk of postpartum SUI of approximately >90% ( ). Discussion SUI is the most prevalent subtype of postpartum PFD in women ( ), significantly impairing physiological function as well as social and psychological wellbeing. However, the underlying pathophysiology of SUI remains incompletely understood. Current evidence suggests that weakened urethral sphincter function and compromised urethral support structures are the primary mechanisms, contributing to involuntary urine leakage during increased intra-abdominal pressure ( ). Early identification of SUI risk is essential for implementing personalised treatment strategies aligned with the principle of “prevention-first, prevention and treatment combined” ( ). Nonetheless, most existing predictive studies are retrospective and single-factor in nature, often yielding biased results despite identifying cut-off thresholds. In this study, we integrated clinical risk factors and three-dimensional pelvic floor ultrasound dynamic parameters into a multivariable analysis framework to construct a clinically applicable and visual nomogram model. This approach facilitates risk stratification and supports early and targeted interventions for postpartum SUI. Univariate analysis identified significant associations between postpartum SUI and several obstetric factors, including mode of delivery, use of assisted delivery (forceps), and presence of episiotomy or perineal laceration (all p < 0.05). Notably, multivariate logistic regression confirmed forceps-assisted vaginal delivery as an independent risk factor (OR = 34.57; 95% CI: 2.92–409.02), consistent with previous findings. Mechanistically, this can be attributed to: (1) the mechanical impact of the fetal head on the levator ani complex, which may stretch pelvic tissues up to 3.3 times their pre-pregnancy length ( ); (2) increased intra-abdominal pressure during the second stage of labour, combined with fetal descent, leading to trauma of the pelvic soft tissues, fascia, muscles, and nerves; and (3) direct damage to pelvic floor structures during episiotomy or operative delivery, particularly with forceps assistance, which compromises the integrity of the anterior pelvic compartment and predisposes to SUI ( ). A recent study of 92 primiparous women found that levator ani muscle injuries were significantly increased during vaginal delivery ( ). Although elective caesarean section may mitigate pelvic floor trauma and reduce SUI risk, it is associated with significantly higher rates of serious complications-such as cardiac arrest, infection, and haematoma-compared to vaginal delivery ( ). These findings underscore the importance of stratified clinical decision-making that balances maternal pelvic floor protection with surgical safety. Three-dimensional pelvic floor ultrasound has become a standard modality for evaluating SUI due to its accessibility, reproducibility, cost-effectiveness, and capacity to provide real-time, dynamic visualization of pelvic structures, particularly in the postpartum screening of primiparas. In the present study, several dynamic ultrasound parameters assessed during maximal Valsalva manoeuvre-including bladder neck position, urethral rotation angle, posterior bladder angle, and levator hiatus area-were identified as independent predictors of postpartum SUI. Notably, an increased anal sphincter tear area was significantly associated with a higher risk of SUI (OR = 1.29; 95% CI: 1.16–1.44), highlighting the importance of pelvic floor muscle integrity. Previous studies have demonstrated that enlargement of the levator hiatus is indicative of levator ani muscle injury, which compromises the structural support of the pelvic floor ( ). The levator ani muscle is the principal supportive structure of the pelvic floor; increased muscle thickness is associated with a smaller hiatus and enhanced pelvic support. However, excessive stretching or avulsion during childbirth may lead to compensatory enlargement of the levator hiatus, reduced fascial tension, and diminished pelvic support

Previous studies have demonstrated that enlargement of the levator hiatus is indicative of levator ani muscle injury, which compromises the structural support of the pelvic floor ( ). The levator ani muscle is the principal supportive structure of the pelvic floor; increased muscle thickness is associated with a smaller hiatus and enhanced pelvic support. However, excessive stretching or avulsion during childbirth may lead to compensatory enlargement of the levator hiatus, reduced fascial tension, and diminished pelvic support ( ). Consequently, a larger tear area correlates with an increased risk of stress incontinence during episodes of elevated intra-abdominal pressure. Additionally, bladder neck descent and an enlarged posterior bladder angle during Valsalva were also shown to be independent predictors of postpartum SUI, consistent with established pathophysiological theories ( ). According to the pressure transmission theory, sudden increases in intra-abdominal pressure may cause the bladder neck to descend below the pubococcygeal line, altering the posterior bladder angle and impairing the function of the proximal urethral sphincter. This results in the failure of urethral pressure to counterbalance intravesical pressure, thereby leading to incontinence ( ). The study by Turkoglu et al. ( ) also confirmed that BND has the highest sensitivity and specificity among the parameters for assessing SUI. Furthermore, in this study, a wider posterior bladder angle was significantly associated with an enlarged levator hiatus, suggesting a common pathophysiological mechanism in which weakened pelvic support structures contribute to structural deformation of the posterior bladder wall and vaginal fascia. Our findings also align with those of Liu et al. ( ), who developed a postpartum SUI prediction model based on pelvic floor ultrasound parameters. Their study identified bladder neck mobility and internal urethral orifice funneling as key predictive features. Similarly, our model emphasizes the importance of urethral dynamic parameters-including bladder neck position, rotation angle, and posterior bladder angle-as essential components in the early identification of women at risk for SUI. These characteristics are of particular importance in the clinical assessment of postpartum primiparas. Nomogram models are increasingly recognized as valuable tools in gynecological risk prediction, offering the advantage of integrating multiple risk factors into a user-friendly, visualized scoring system. These models enable clinicians to quantify individualized risk through intuitive point-based calculations ( ). The nomogram developed in this study innovatively incorporates both clinical variables (such as forceps-assisted delivery) and dynamic three-dimensional pelvic floor ultrasound parameters (bladder neck position, urethral rotation angle, and levator hiatus area during Valsalva). Compared with traditional models, our nomogram demonstrated superior diagnostic performance, with an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.933, and provides a clinically feasible and cost-effective strategy for early risk stratification and targeted intervention in postpartum SUI. Despite these promising results, our study has several limitations. Firstly, this study employed a retrospective design. Although urinary incontinence history was strictly determined based on diagnostic records in medical files, some symptomatic cases may not have been reported to clinicians or documented in detail. This may introduce a degree of selection bias into the results. Future research should adopt a prospective design and utilize validated standardized questionnaires at baseline to assess urinary incontinence status more accurately and comprehensively. Secondly, all data in this study originated from a single center, lacking external validation and thus limiting the generalizability of findings. Future research should conduct large-scale, multicentre studies to validate model efficacy. Thirdly, data collection was limited to the 6–8 weeks postpartum period, without long-term follow-up to assess the persistence or resolution of SUI symptoms over time. Furthermore, the potential effects of perinatal interventions-such as pelvic floor rehabilitation exercises-were not evaluated and may have influenced outcomes. Future research should involve multi-centre, prospective external validation cohorts to refine the model, incorporate additional clinical biomarkers or imaging parameters, and explore the integration of machine learning techniques to enhance the analysis of ultrasound features. Such advancements may further improve the predictive accuracy and clinical utility of postpartum SUI risk assessment models. Conclusion In summary, the nomogram model developed in this study, which integrates clinical risk factors with three-dimensional pelvic floor ultrasound dynamic parameters, demonstrates promising potential as a tool for predicting the risk of postpartum stress urinary incontinence in primiparous women. By facilitating early identification of individuals at higher risk, this model may contribute to improving clinical screening and guiding personalized interventions. Further validation in larger, multicentre cohorts incorporating additional relevant factors is warranted to confirm its generalizability and clinical utility.

documents.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin 233 Cesarean Delivery on Maternal Request

chunks.content: Introduction Cesarean section (CS) is a fundamental surgical intervention in obstetrics and is essential for reducing maternal and perinatal mortality in complicated pregnancies [ ]. Although CS was initially reserved for life-saving indications, its use has expanded globally due to factors such as perceived safety, convenience, and medico-legal pressures [ ]. As a result, global CS rates have more than doubled over the past 25 years, reaching 21.1%, which exceeds the World Health Organization’s recommended rate of 10–15% [ , ]. The increasing number of repeat cesarean deliveries (RCDs), accounting for 15–68% of all procedures, is a major contributor to this trend [ ]. While cesarean section (CS) is a life-saving intervention, it is associated with substantially higher maternal and neonatal risks compared with vaginal delivery. CS represents one of the most important risk factors for subsequent obstetric complications, including cesarean scar pregnancy, placenta accreta spectrum disorders [ – ]. In addition, postoperative infections are common, particularly surgical site infections (SSIs), endometritis, and urinary tract infections [ , ]. SSIs contribute significantly to maternal morbidity, leading to prolonged hospitalization, increased healthcare costs, greater antibiotic consumption, and potential long-term sequelae such as chronic pelvic pain, secondary infertility, and wound dehiscence [ , , ]. There is considerable variation in the epidemiology and reported rates of post–cesarean section (CS) maternal complications across settings, with a disproportionate burden observed in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). In countries such as Ethiopia, the incidence of post-CS surgical site infection (SSI) has been reported to range from 9.7% to 25.4%, further straining already resource-limited and fragile health systems [ , ]. Evidence from observational studies and randomized trials indicates that women with a history of prior CS experience significantly greater surgical morbidity compared with those undergoing a primary procedure. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses further demonstrate that the risk of maternal complications rises substantially with increasing numbers of prior CS [ , ]. Previous CS is consistently identified as a strong independent risk factor for postoperative morbidity, with nearly a threefold increase in infection risk, largely attributable to altered tissue planes, postoperative adhesions, distorted anatomy, and prolonged operative time [ , , ]. Repeat CS is also linked to greater surgical complexity, frequently requiring adhesiolysis and resulting in increased blood loss and longer procedures, which together heighten the likelihood of both intraoperative and postoperative complications [ ]. Moreover, the prevention and management of post-CS infections are becoming increasingly complex, as infection prevention and control strategies and preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis are challenged by evolving pathogen profiles and a growing burden of antimicrobial resistance, with studies reporting high levels of resistance among gram-negative and multidrug-resistant organisms in surgical site infections and variable adherence to guideline-recommended prophylaxis practices across settings [ – ]. There is still a dearth of reliable prospective data comparing primary and repeat CS outcomes in Ethiopia, despite the rising incidence of repeat CS and related maternal risks. The majority of current research is either single-center or retrospective, which restricts how broadly it can be applied [ ]. Moreover, few studies provide detailed microbiological characterization of SSIs or explore modifiable risk factors in this context. To address these gaps, the present prospective cohort study examined differences in the occurrence of post-cesarean surgical site infections and selected maternal outcomes between women undergoing repeat cesarean section (≥ 1 prior cesarean) and those undergoing their first cesarean section. Secondary objectives included describing the spectrum of bacteria isolated from SSI and the distribution of intraoperative and postoperative complications across exposure groups. A pre-planned subgroup analysis was conducted to explore whether the association between prior cesarean section and SSI differed across clinically important patient and procedural characteristics, aiming to identify potential modifiers of SSI risk, generate hypotheses for future research, and provide insights for tailoring context-specific preventive strategies in women undergoing repeat cesarean section. The findings are intended to inform context-appropriate preventive strategies and maternal health interventions in low-resource settings such as Ethiopia. Materials and methods Study design, rationale and durations This prospective cohort study was conducted from January 1 to December 31, 2022, in the obstetrics and gynecology units of three public hospitals in Southern Ethiopia: Arba Minch General Hospital (AMGH), Wolayita Sodo University Teaching and Referral Hospital (WSUTH), and Gidole Primary Hospital (GPH). The study followed STROBE guidelines for observational studies. A prospective cohort design was chosen to directly measure the incidence of surgical site infections (SSI) and other postoperative maternal outcomes among women undergoing repeat versus first-time cesarean sections. Prospective data collection minimized recall bias and allowed timely detection of complications during admission and post-discharge, ensuring comprehensive outcome assessment. The three hospitals serve populations ranging from 200,000 to 2 million and provide comprehensive obstetric care, including elective and emergency cesarean delivery, labor monitoring, and postoperative follow-up. A prospective cohort design was chosen to directly measure the incidence of surgical site infections (SSI) and other postoperative maternal outcomes among women undergoing repeat versus first-time cesarean sections. Prospective data collection minimized recall bias and allowed timely detection of complications during admission and post-discharge, ensuring comprehensive outcome assessment. The three hospitals serve populations ranging from 200,000 to 2 million and provide comprehensive obstetric care, including elective and emergency cesarean delivery, labor monitoring, and postoperative follow-up. Cesarean section rates during the study period were 27.3% at AMGH, 23.5% at WSUTH, and 24.9% at GPH. In all of the participating hospitals, surgical antibiotic prophylactic predominantly third generation cephalosporin routinely administered intravenously to nearly all women within 30–60 min before incision. For example in our cohort, 97.1% of women received surgical antibiotic prophylaxis (1 g of ceftriaxone) with an additional postoperative dose at 24 h. Population Target population The target population comprised all women with singleton term pregnancies who undergo cesarean delivery in public hospital obstetrics and gynecology (OB/GYN) units in Southern Ethiopia. Source and study population The source population included all women aged ≥ 18 years with singleton term pregnancies who were admitted for elective or emergency cesarean section to the OB/GYN units (labor wards and obstetric operating theaters) of Arba Minch General Hospital, Wolaita Sodo University Teaching and Referral Hospital, and Gidole Primary Hospital during the study period. The study population consisted of eligible women from the source population who underwent cesarean delivery during the study period and were enrolled prospectively according to the predefined sampling procedure. Participants were managed within routine OB/GYN clinical care and were classified based on their pre-existing exposure status, defined by the number of prior cesarean sections (first-time versus repeat cesarean section). No special or selected clinical groups were created. Exposure definition (first versus repeat Cesarean section) Exposure status was defined based on a documented history of prior cesarean delivery. Women with at least one previous cesarean section were classified as having a repeat cesarean section and were further categorized as having one or two prior cesarean sections or multiple repeat cesarean sections (≥ 3 prior cesarean sections). Women undergoing cesarean delivery for the first time were classified as first-time (primary) cesarean section. Women with first-time cesarean sections served as the reference group for comparative analyses to contextualize patterns of surgical site infections, intraoperative complexity, and postoperative maternal outcomes observed among women with repeat cesarean sections. This comparative framework has been used in prior observational studies to describe differences in maternal morbidity across cesarean delivery histories. In the present study, differences between exposure groups were assessed using multivariable analytical methods to account for measured maternal and obstetric characteristics, without implying causal inference [ , , ]. Eligibility criteria Inclusion Women aged ≥ 18 years with a Singleton pregnancy undergoing elective or emergency Cesarean section at the study hospitals, providing informed consent, and reachable for 30-day postoperative follow-up Exclusion Women with active infection at the time of surgery, concurrent surgery, referral from another facility after CS, incomplete medical records, inability to complete follow-up, critical illness, major psychiatric disorders, and age < 18 years. Adolescent group aged less than 18 years was excluded due to differences in obstetric risk profiles, and they are rare cases for representation in the repeat CS in this group Sample size calculation The sample size was calculated using the two-population proportion formula [ ] in OpenEpi. In this calculation, p₁ represented the incidence of SSI in the baseline population and p₂ the incidence among women with a prior cesarean section. We assumed a significance level of 5% (Zα = 1.96) and a power of 80% (Zβ = 0.84). A baseline incidence of SSI following cesarean section was taken as 11% [ ]. Previous studies have reported that repeat cesarean delivery increases the risk of SSI by 1.2–2-fold [ , , ]. For this study, we planned to detect an increase of 1.47 (i.e., from 11% to 16.2% as a clinically meaningful estimate within that reported range). With a 1:1 ratio of exposed to non-exposed groups, the minimum required sample size was 1,376 women (688 per group). To account for potential loss to follow-up or incomplete data, a 10% contingency was added, yielding a final required sample size of 1,514 participants (757 per group). However, during the one-year study period, the total participants enrolled in the study were n = 1,506 (a total of 753 per group). A 1:1 allocation was chosen to maximize statistical power, reduce variance of effect estimates, and provide stable multivariable analyses. Equal allocation also reflects the approximate distribution of primary and repeat CS cases in the participating hospitals, ensuring both statistical efficiency and practical feasibility. A 10% contingency was added to the sample size calculation to account for potential loss to follow-up or missing data. However, participants with incomplete critical records, such as missing key exposure or outcome variables, were excluded from the analysis to maintain data integrity. Other minor missing data were addressed analytically using appropriate statistical techniques, ensuring that the study retained methodological rigor while minimizing bias. Sampling procedure and participant enrollment Given the large number of eligible cesarean deliveries across the three study hospitals during the study period, we employed a stratified, systematic sampling approach with fixed-ratio allocation to enroll a feasible subset of participants for prospective follow-up and detailed data collection. To ensure sufficient numbers in both groups for meaningful comparison, the total planned sample ( n = 1,506) was allocated in a 1:1 ratio between women undergoing first-time cesarean section and those with a history of repeat cesarean section, based on a priori sample size calculations. Sampling was stratified by hospital and exposure status (first CS vs. repeat CS). Within each hospital–exposure stratum, a sampling frame was created using chronologically ordered lists of all eligible cesarean deliveries. The sampling interval (k) was calculated by dividing the number of eligible cases in each stratum by the allocated sample size, resulting in an interval of approximately two across sites. A random starting point was selected using a lottery method, after which every kth eligible woman was enrolled until the pre-defined stratum quota was reached. When a selected woman was ineligible or declined participation, the next eligible case in the sequence was enrolled without altering the sampling interval [Additional file 2: Supplementary Table S1] [ ]. Study outcomes and measurement The primary outcome of the study was the incidence of surgical site infection (SSI) among women undergoing cesarean section, defined according to the National Healthcare Safety Network of the Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) [ ]. Secondary outcomes included intraoperative complications (blood transfusion, dense adhesions, placenta previa, and type of anesthesia used), Postoperative complications (postoperative systemic antibiotic prophylaxis (SAP) usage, length of hospital stay, and hospital readmission for any reason), and microbiological characteristics of SSI (cutlture positivity rate, bacterial profile and infection type (monobacterial, vs. polymicrobial). Covariates/risk factors and potential confounders Potential risk factors were grouped into demographic, obstetric/clinical, and procedural factors. Demographic variables included age, residence, body mass index, and alcohol or tobacco use. Obstetric and clinical factors comprised parity, referral status, and labor before CS, duration of labor, membrane rupture and duration, number of vaginal examinations, recent hospitalization, and underlying medical conditions. Procedural factors included CS urgency (emergency vs. elective), incision type (Pfannenstiel vs. vertical), intraoperative events (blood transfusion), surgical hand scrub method, preoperative skin preparation (aqueous povidone-iodine, iodine + alcohol, chlorhexidine-alcohol), skin closure type, operation duration, surgeon grade, antibiotic prophylaxis (type, timing, dose), and anesthesia type. These variables were selected for their clinical relevance and potential to confound the relationship between CS type and surgical site infection. Operational definitions The presence of pre-existing medical conditions was defined as the presence or absence of any of the following: hypertension, anemia, diabetes mellitus, malaria or acute febrile illness, or the presence of any chronic systemic disease like HIV, renal disease, heart disease, or liver disease [ ]. Repeat caesarean section (CS) was defined as any caesarean delivery performed in a woman who has had at least one previous CS [ ]. Multiple repeat CS was defined as three or more previous CS deliveries [ ]. Participants enrollment and prospective follow-up procedure Eligible women scheduled for cesarean section (CS) during the study period were consecutively approached preoperatively and provided written informed consent. For those unable to read or write, the consent form was read aloud in the local language, with a literate witness confirming the decision. Participants were assured that their care would not be affected by participation, and confidentiality was strictly maintained using unique study identifiers. A total of 1,506 women were enrolled in a 1:1 ratio into repeat or first-time CS cohorts and prospectively followed for 30 days post-CS delivery to monitor surgical site infections (SSI) and other maternal outcomes. Follow-up included daily ward visits during admission, review of hospital records, and scheduled outpatient or telephone contacts after discharge. Baseline and follow-up data were collected using a pretested tool. Differences between

Data collection procedures Data source, collection tools, and methods Data were collected prospectively from women undergoing cesarean section at three public hospitals in southern Ethiopia through direct patient interviews, clinical examinations, and review of medical, anesthesia, and operation records. A pretested semi-structured questionnaire, case report form, and standardized SSI checklist were used to capture socio-demographic, behavioral, obstetric, clinical, and surgery-related information. Trained multidisciplinary teams—including obstetricians, gynecologists, midwives, and a microbiologist at two sites—conducted data collection to ensure accuracy and methodological rigor. Baseline and intraoperative data included socio-demographics, obstetric and medical history, CS type (elective/emergency), and anesthesia, duration of surgery, blood loss, surgeon experience, antimicrobial prophylaxis, and intraoperative complications. Participants were followed prospectively for 30 days post-CS for SSI and other maternal outcomes through daily ward visits, hospital record review, scheduled outpatient visits, and telephone follow-up. SSI was defined and classified according to CDC criteria, and standardized assessment checklists were applied to all suspected cases [ , ]. Microbiological assessment Microbiological procedures involved aseptic collection of wound swabs and aspirates from suspected infections, transport under controlled conditions, and culture on blood, MacConkey, mannitol salt, and chocolate agar. Isolates were identified using conventional microbiological techniques, including Gram staining, biochemical tests, and reference standards per Bergey’s Manual [ ]. Laboratory quality assurance included use of reference strains (Pseudomonas aeruginosa ATCC 27853, Escherichia coli ATCC 25922), daily oversight by the principal investigator, and strict adherence to standard operating procedures [ ]. Quality assurance To ensure data quality, comprehensive training was provided before study initiation on data collection tools, surveillance methods (including participant recruitment, consent procedures, and follow-up), data recording, and microbiological techniques. A pretest was conducted on 5% of the sample at Chencha Hospital, which was not part of the main study. The questionnaire was initially developed in English, translated into the local language, and then back-translated to English to ensure accuracy. Laboratory test reliability was maintained through rigorous quality control measures, including the use of reference strains Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ATCC 27853) and Escherichia coli (ATCC 25922) procured from the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI). Data checks for completeness, clarity, and consistency, and standard operating protocols were strictly followed for all laboratory procedures. Data management and statistical analysis Data were entered into EpiData and analyzed using SPSS v25.0. Continuous variables were summarized as means ± SD or medians (IQR), depending on distribution, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Comparisons between repeat and first-time CS groups were performed using t-tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for continuous variables and χ² or Fisher’s exact tests for categorical variables. Baseline characteristics and case-mix factors including demographic, obstetric/clinical, procedural, and hospital-related variables were compared between groups. A pre-planned subgroup analyses were conducted to explore whether the association between prior cesarean section and SSI differed across clinically important patient and procedural characteristics. Subgroups were selected based on evidence from previous studies and biological plausibility, including hospital type, type of cesarean section (elective vs. emergency), BMI, underlying medical conditions, and preoperative skin preparation method. Poisson regression with robust variance was used to estimate relative risks (RR) and adjusted relative risks (aRR) with 95% confidence intervals, modeling SSI as a binary outcome with repeat CS as the primary exposure. Covariates included in the adjusted model were selected based on bivariable analyses ( p < 0.25) or clinical relevance and comprised: maternal age, residence, BMI, CS frequency, history of prior hospitalization, multiple vaginal examinations, labor before CS, prolonged labor > 24 h, urgency of CS, type of anesthesia, and preoperative skin preparation. Model assumptions—including multicollinearity, linearity, over dispersion, and goodness-of-fit—were assessed. Only participants successfully followed for the full 30-day postoperative period were included; sensitivity analyses suggested minimal bias from losses to follow-up. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, and results are reported as aRR (95% CI) to quantify the independent effect of repeat CS on SSI and related maternal outcomes. Results Participant flow and study population During the study period, 3,587 women undergoing cesarean section across three public hospitals in Southern Ethiopia (GPH ( n = 460); AMGH ( n = 1,043); WSUSTH ( n = 2,084) were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 3,485 (97.2%) were eligible, and 102 (2.8%) were excluded due to pre-existing infection, referral/concurrent surgery, incomplete records, inability to complete follow-up, or critical/psychiatric conditions. A total of 1,506 women were enrolled, equally divided between first-time CS ( n = 753) and repeat CS ( n = 753). Hospital-specific enrollment for primary /first-time CS was; GPH ( n = 128), AMGH ( n = 238), WSUSTH ( n = 387); and repeat CS was GPH ( n = 83), AMGH ( n = 239), WSUSTH ( n = 431). All participants completed 30-day postoperative follow-up and included in the final analysis (Fig. ). Baseline characteristics of participants by exposure group At baseline, the two cohorts were broadly comparable in socio-demographic characteristics. Women undergoing repeat CS were older on average than those with a first CS (30.1 ± 5.6 vs. 26.9 ± 5.0 years, p < 0.001). Nearly half of the participants resided in urban areas (47.2%) and half in rural areas (52.8%). All women in the first CS group were primiparous, whereas the repeat CS group was predominantly multiparous or grand multiparous. Antenatal care attendance was high, with 67% having ≥ 4 visits, particularly in the first CS group. Most CS were emergent (76.9%), and 76.4% of women were in labor at the time of surgery. Mean BMI was slightly higher in the repeat CS group (25.9 ± 4.3 vs. 24.8 ± 3.7, p < 0.001), but obesity prevalence was identical (4.9%). Membrane rupture was documented in 55.8% of women, with prolonged rupture (> 18 h) in 16.5%. One-third (33.9%) had at least one comorbidity, including anemia, hypertension/pre-eclampsia, diabetes, or other conditions. Prior hospitalization was reported in 16.7%, more frequently in the repeat CS group. Spinal/regional anesthesia was the predominant technique (81.7%), with general anesthesia slightly more common in repeat CS (20.6% vs. 15.9%). The majority of incisions were transverse (Pfannenstiel, 95%), and iodine–alcohol was the most common skin preparation (50.2%), although chlorhexidine–alcohol was more frequently used in repeat CS (Supplementary Table S2). Comparison of incidence, severity and microbiology of SSI by exposure group Among 1,506 women who underwent cesarean delivery, the overall incidence of surgical site infection (SSI) was substantially higher in women undergoing repeat CS (20.3%) compared to first-time CS (6.8%), corresponding to a nearly threefold increased risk (RR 2.98, 95% CI 2.20–4.03; p < 0.001). Deep incisional infections occurred more frequently after repeat CS (30.1 vs. 9.8%; RR 3.07, 95% CI 1.28–7.36; p = 0.012). Time to SSI onset was significantly longer following repeat CS (15.9 ± 2.9 days) compared with first-time CS. When considering microbiologically confirmed infections at the population level, the incidence of bacterial SSI was also markedly higher in repeat CS (17.3 vs. 6.8%). In repeat CS group higher incidence of monobacterial SSI (14.5 vs. 5.6%), Gram-negative SSI (10.8 vs. 2.5%), and polymicrobial SSI (3.7 vs. 1.2%)(Table ). Association of repeat CS with incidence of SSI (adjusted analysis) In bivariable analysis, several factors were associated with an increased risk of surgical site infection (SSI), including maternal age ≥ 30 years, repeat cesarean section (CS), prior hospitalization, multiple vaginal examinations, emergency surgery, general anesthesia, and type of preoperative skin antisepsis. After adjusting for potential confounders in multivariable Poisson regression with robust variance, repeat CS remained significantly associated with SSI, nearly tripling the risk of SSI compared with first-time CS (aRR = 2.94, 95% CI: 2.20–3.93, p < 0.001). Maternal age ≥ 30 years was associated with a 56% higher risk (aRR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.06–2.29, p = 0.02), and prior hospitalization increased SSI risk by 56% (aRR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.18–2.10, p = 0.002). Emergency cesarean delivery was also independently associated with higher risk (aRR = 1.76, 95% CI: 1.06–2.91, p = 0.03). Regarding preoperative skin antisepsis, chlorhexidine–alcohol was associated with the lowest SSI incidence, whereas aqueous povidone-iodine more than doubled the risk (aRR = 2.12, 95% CI: 1.41–3.19, p = 0.001), and iodine plus alcohol increased risk by 49% compared with chlorhexidine-based antisepsis (aRR = 1.49, 95% CI: 1.01–2.18, p = 0.04). Other variables, including BMI, multiple vaginal examinations, labor before CS, prolonged labor, and general anesthesia, were not statistically significant after adjustment(Table ).
