Regarding preoperative skin antisepsis, chlorhexidine–alcohol was associated with the lowest SSI incidence, whereas aqueous povidone-iodine more than doubled the risk (aRR = 2.12, 95% CI: 1.41–3.19, p = 0.001), and iodine plus alcohol increased risk by 49% compared with chlorhexidine-based antisepsis (aRR = 1.49, 95% CI: 1.01–2.18, p = 0.04). Other variables, including BMI, multiple vaginal examinations, labor before CS, prolonged labor, and general anesthesia, were not statistically significant after adjustment(Table ). Subgroup analysis of repeat CS and SSI Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore whether the association of repeat CS on SSI could be modified by hospital type, emergency status, BMI, PROM, comorbidity, skin antisepsis, and number of prior CS and to generate hypothesis. The association between repeat cesarean section (CS) and SSI varied by hospital type, surgical urgency, and clinical factors. Repeat CS was associated with higher SSI risk in referral/teaching hospitals (aRR = 3.10, 95% CI: 1.90–5.05) and during emergency surgery (aRR = 3.10, 95% CI: 2.20–4.35). The risk increased with the number of prior CS, showing a dose–response effect (1–2 prior CS: aRR = 2.00; ≥3 prior CS: aRR = 3.20). Effect modification was also evident for preoperative skin antisepsis, with the highest risk observed for povidone-iodine (aRR = 3.80) and lowest for chlorhexidine–alcohol. 3.80, 95% CI 2.60–5.60) and iodine-alcohol (aRR 2.10, 95% CI 1.40–3.15) associated with higher risk compared to chlorhexidine-alcohol (Table ). Intra and post-operative maternal complication by exposure Secondary outcomes varied significantly by cesarean type. Repeat CS was associated with longer operative times with mean with standard deviation of (59.0 ± 11.0 vs. 40.1 ± 9.0 min, p < 0.001), greater use of general anesthesia (20.6% vs. 15.9%, p = 0.018), and higher rates of intraoperative complications, including significant bleeding or blood transfusion (23.9% vs. 13.9%, p < 0.001), dense adhesions (4.8% vs. 0.4%, p < 0.001), and placenta previa (2.0% vs. 0.7%, p = 0.030). Postoperatively, repeat CS patients received more prophylactic antibiotics (97.6% vs. 58.9%, p < 0.001) and had longer hospital stays (3.8 vs. 1.3 days, p < 0.001) (Table ). Microbiology of SSI (culture positivity and bacterial profile) by exposure Among 204 postoperative wound samples obtained from women with suspected SSI after cesarean section, 181 were culture-positive, giving an overall culture positivity rate of 88.7%. Culture confirmation in repeat and primary CS group was 85.0% and 100% respectively. Most infections were monobacterial (83.4%), while polymicrobial infections accounted for 16.6% of culture-confirmed SSIs. A total of 213 bacterial isolates were recovered. Gram-negative bacteria were the most frequent overall (46.9%), particularly in repeat CS (52.9%), dominated by Klebsiella pneumoniae (23.0%), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (12.2%), and Escherichia coli (11.7%) (Table ). Discussion In this prospective cohort study, the incidence of surgical site infection (SSI) following cesarean section (CS) was 13.5% (95% CI: 11.9–15.4), reflecting a substantial burden of postoperative infection in public hospitals in southern Ethiopia. This estimate is consistent with prior reports from Ethiopia and other LMICs [ , ]. While comparable to pooled national estimates for Ethiopia (9.7% to 25.4%) and individual study from Harer Ethiopia, lower than the 25.4% reported from Debretabor north Ethiopia [ ]. This study demonstrated that women with repeat CS were significantly more likely to develop SSI compared with women without prior cesarean surgery (20.3% vs. 6.8%), reflecting nearly a threefold elevated risk (RR 2.98, 95% CI 2.20–4.03; p < 0.001). Similar evidence has been reported in other cohort studies, where a history of prior cesarean was associated with increased risk of postoperative infection and complications following cesarean delivery [ , , ]. For examples observational study conducted at the University Clinical Center of Kosovo reported approximately 7.4-fold for SSI development in those with previous CS [ ]. The pattern in existing literature aligns with a growing body of epidemiologic evidence indicating women with priory history of CS would likely to developed post-operative morbidity, this could be partly explained by factors such as scar tissue formation, altered local tissue perfusion, adhesions, and prolonged operative time [ , , , ] and impair vascular perfusion, facilitating bacterial colonization [ , ]. Furthermore women with repeat CS experienced a higher proportion of deep incisional SSIs, which are generally associated with more extensive tissue involvement and greater morbidity, whereas superficial SSIs predominated among first-time CS. This pattern aligns with previous studies reporting deeper wound involvement in women with prior abdominal surgery, potentially due to altered tissue planes and scar formation that may predispose to deeper bacterial invasion [ , ]. The prolonged time to onset of SSI observed in the repeat CS group further suggests a difference in the underlying disease process; delayed presentation has been reported in other surgical cohorts where subclinical contamination or slower

repeat CS experienced a higher proportion of deep incisional SSIs, which are generally associated with more extensive tissue involvement and greater morbidity, whereas superficial SSIs predominated among first-time CS. This pattern aligns with previous studies reporting deeper wound involvement in women with prior abdominal surgery, potentially due to altered tissue planes and scar formation that may predispose to deeper bacterial invasion [ , ]. The prolonged time to onset of SSI observed in the repeat CS group further suggests a difference in the underlying disease process; delayed presentation has been reported in other surgical cohorts where subclinical contamination or slower development of infection occurs in poorly vascularized or scarred tissues [ ]. Our subgroup analyses further demonstrated a dose–response relationship between the number of prior cesarean sections and the risk of SSI. Women with multiple repeat CS (≥ 3) had nearly a fourfold higher risk of infection compared with first-time CS while those with one or two prior CS had an intermediate risk (Table ). This pattern was consistent across hospital types, emergent procedures, comorbidity status, and preoperative skin antisepsis, highlighting that the cumulative effect of prior surgery contributes independently to SSI risk [ , ]. Nevertheless the subgroup analysis further highlights that the magnitude of SSI risk associated with repeat cesarean section varies according to patient, procedural, and hospital-related factors where repeat Cs conducted in emergency procedure, in referral and teaching hospital, patient with high BMI, underlying conditions, and using aqueous povidone-iodine for preoperative skin preparation increased the risk of developing SSI suggesting that hospital-level factors, including case complexity, resource availability, increased exposure and less preparation of operative time, or extended exposure may modify the effect of prior CS [ , ], .These findings underscore the need to treat repeat CS as a high-risk surgical event requiring enhanced perioperative planning and vigilant postoperative monitoring [ ]. These observations generate hypotheses that hospital-level factors, case complexity, operative duration, and preoperative preparation may modify the effect of prior CS on SSI. Collectively, these findings highlight the importance of considering repeat CS as a potentially higher-risk surgical event and the need for enhanced perioperative planning and vigilant postoperative monitoring. Interestingly, while repeat cesarean sections had a higher overall SSI incidence and more severe infections, culture positivity was higher in first CS-associated SSIs (100%), likely reflecting the predominance of superficial infections limited to skin and subcutaneous tissue. This aligns with previous reports showing that superficial SSIs are mainly caused by commensal skin flora such as Staphylococcus spp [ , ]. In contrast, SSIs after repeat CS were more often deep, monobacterial Gram-negative infections (52.9% vs. 31.7%), dominated by Klebsiella pneumoniae (23.0%), and polymicrobial infections, which are harder to culture, partially explaining the lower culture positivity despite higher overall SSI risk. Several mechanisms could contribute to this shift. Prolonged operative times have been consistently associated with an increased risk of SSI across surgical types, including gynecologic procedures, likely due to longer exposure of tissues to environmental and endogenous bacteria [ ]. Inadequate timing or suboptimal prophylactic antibiotic coverage has also been linked to higher SSI rates following CS, underscoring the importance of achieving effective antimicrobial concentrations at incision [ ]. Additionally, antibiotic exposure can alter bacterial flora and select for resistant organisms, potentially increasing the relative prevalence of Gram-negative pathogens in surgical wounds [ ]. These factors—longer operations, altered flora, and antibiotic selection pressure—may be particularly relevant in repeat CS where adhesions and tissue changes complicate surgery. Collectively, these findings suggest that empirical therapy for SSIs in repeat CS should consider coverage for Gram-negative particularly in settings with high emergency CS rates or prevalent antimicrobial resistance, complementing traditional findings where Gram-positive skin flora predominate [ , , ]. Nevertheless, this study provides an important insight by demonstrating a high proportion of Gram-negative isolates from SSIs among women who received preoperative surgical prophylaxis, specifically third-generation cephalosporins. This finding suggests that standard prophylaxis may be increasingly compromised by the emergence and circulation of extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)–producing pathogens in Ethiopian clinical settings, likely driven by sustained selection pressure from frequent and broad-spectrum antibiotic use. Supporting this, evidence from southern Ethiopia reports high rates of ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae in surgical site infections, with many Gram-negative isolates resistant to ceftriaxone and other β-lactam antibiotics [ ]. Unfortunately, since antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AMST) were not included in the study, the role of ESBL-producing pathogens remains speculative and cannot be directly confirmed. Women undergoing repeat CS also appeared to experience more complex perioperative courses, including longer operative times, increased use of general anesthesia and postoperative antibiotics, and higher rates of intraoperative complications such as bleeding and adhesions (Table ). These patterns are consistent with previous mechanistic and empirical findings, which suggest that surgical scarring, adhesions from prior procedures, and more complex operative conditions contribute to the increased perioperative risks observed in repeat

and other β-lactam antibiotics [ ]. Unfortunately, since antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AMST) were not included in the study, the role of ESBL-producing pathogens remains speculative and cannot be directly confirmed. Women undergoing repeat CS also appeared to experience more complex perioperative courses, including longer operative times, increased use of general anesthesia and postoperative antibiotics, and higher rates of intraoperative complications such as bleeding and adhesions (Table ). These patterns are consistent with previous mechanistic and empirical findings, which suggest that surgical scarring, adhesions from prior procedures, and more complex operative conditions contribute to the increased perioperative risks observed in repeat cesarean deliveries [ , , ]. However, other previous studies did not find the elevated requirement for blood transfusion [ ]. , the incidence of peripartum hemorrhage and blood transfusion in women with four or more CS compared to those with three or more. Postoperatively, these women had prolonged hospital stays and higher rates of extended antibiotic use, indicating increased resource utilization and heightened exposure to nosocomial pathogens [ ]. Given the association between repeat cesarean delivery and increased SSI risk, broader efforts to safely reduce unnecessary primary cesarean sections may have important downstream benefits for maternal morbidity. Strategies such as careful labor induction protocols, shared decision-making around mode of delivery, and evidence-based labor management have been suggested to lower cesarean birth rates in low-risk populations without compromising perinatal outcomes [ , ]. This study also found that emergency procedures were independent predictors of SSI following cesarean delivery (Table ), reflecting the challenges of urgent surgery, such as limited preparation time, prolonged labor exposure, and potentially more complex operative conditions. These findings are consistent with previous reports [ ]. This underscores the need for targeted perioperative strategies in emergent cases, including optimized antibiotic prophylaxis and careful intraoperative technique. Our findings indicate that preoperative skin antisepsis is a key, modifiable determinant of surgical site infections in cesarean delivery. Specifically, aqueous povidone-iodine was associated with more than a twofold higher risk of SSI compared with chlorhexidine-based preparations, while iodine plus alcohol increased risk by nearly 50%. This demonstrates that the choice of antiseptic has a substantial impact on postoperative infection rates (Table ). These findings align with randomized trials demonstrating the superior efficacy of alcohol-based chlorhexidine over aqueous or combined iodine-based preparations in abdominal and obstetric surgery [ , ]. They also support current World Health Organization recommendations, which advise alcohol-based chlorhexidine as the preferred antiseptic for cesarean delivery, with alternatives such as aqueous povidone-iodine reserved for settings where chlorhexidine is unavailable [ ]. This represents an actionable opportunity to reduce postoperative infections, particularly in higher-risk populations, including women undergoing repeat or emergency cesarean deliveries. Optimizing skin preparation protocols could therefore serve as a high-impact, evidence-based intervention to improve maternal surgical outcomes [ ]. According to systematic review of skin closure techniques in gynecologic surgery noted advanced closure systems such as Dermabond Prineo could be associated with improved wound outcomes and potentially lower infection rates compared with traditional methods, although evidence varies across surgical contexts (elective versus emergent procedures) [ ].This supports the notion that perioperative procedural factors, beyond intrinsic patient characteristics, contribute to SSI risk and represent targets for prevention strategies. Patient-related characteristics, including age and prior hospitalization, further influence susceptibility to SSI. Older age may reflect changes in tissue healing and immune response, whereas a history of hospitalization could indicate prior exposure to healthcare-associated pathogens or baseline comorbidities, even if not overtly recorded. The attenuation of associations with BMI, prolonged labor, and multiple vaginal examinations after adjustment suggests that these factors interact with other patient or procedural determinants, rather than acting as independent risk modifiers [ , , ]. Although recent systematic reviews have linked skin incision technique to postoperative SSI risk and aesthetic outcomes [ ] our study did not find such associations, nor with other predictors like BMI, prolonged labor, or multiple vaginal examinations. This may reflect limited statistical power in certain subgroups, residual confounding from unmeasured factors such as operative technique, antibiotic timing, or nutritional status, and variations in clinical practice and perioperative care across study sites. Limitations Despite key strengths, including the prospective comparative design and integration of epidemiological and microbiological data providing a comprehensive assessment of SSI incidence, severity, and causative organisms in first-time and repeat CS, several limitations should be acknowledged. The findings are associational relationship should be made with caution. First, the study was conducted in three hospitals within a single region, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other settings with different patient populations, surgical practices, or resource availability. Second, microbiological procedure were not included the most sensitive molecular techniques which may have led to underestimation of pathogen detection and diversity. First, the study was conducted in three hospitals within a single region, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other settings with different patient populations, surgical practices, or resource availability. Second, microbiological procedure were not included the most sensitive molecular techniques which may have led to underestimation of pathogen detection and diversity. The other important limitation of this study is the potential for selection bias in the microbiological analysis, as cultures were performed only for aerobic microorganisms using conventional culture and biochemical methods among clinically suspected patients. This may underrepresent other important pathogens, subclinical infections. Given the lack of antimicrobial susceptibility testing was also the key limitation of this study, future studies incorporating molecular-based approaches are highly warranted to evaluate the effectiveness of surgical antibiotic prophylaxis in the context of evolving bacterial profiles, emerging resistance and inform antimicrobial stewardship program. Finally, as this is an observational study, the simultaneous assessment of exposures and outcomes limits the ability to establish causal links between risk factors and SSI. Residual confounding by unmeasured patient, procedural, or hospital-level factors cannot be ruled out. Conclusion Surgical site infection (SSI) remains a common complication following cesarean section, affecting approximately one in seven women, with a markedly higher incidence in repeat CS compared to first-time CS. women undergoing repeat CS was more likely to develop deep/incisional type of post-operative SSI with a predominance of Gram-negative and polymicrobial infections type, whereas superficial infections predominated in first-time CS. In addition, the observed higher frequency of prolonged operative time, use of general anesthesia, and intraoperative complications such as bleeding, adhesions, and placenta previa among women undergoing repeat cesarean section suggests greater surgical complexity and highlights the need for strict infection prevention measures, appropriate preoperative skin antisepsis, optimized intraoperative practices, and careful postoperative monitoring, particularly in emergency procedures. Given the observational design, causal inferences are limited, and future randomized studies are warranted to confirm these associations and evaluate strategies to reduce SSI. chunks.content: Introduction Perhaps best summarized by the phrase “no margin, no mission,” Catholic health systems face conflicting pressures to maintain their mission-oriented identity while staying financially viable in the competitive, profit-driven American health care landscape. Trends in consolidation and acquisition have accelerated in recent decades as health systems—both Catholic and non-Catholic—seek to expand their market power and financial strength ( ; ; ; ). The number of Catholic-owned or affiliated hospitals grew by 28% between 2001 and 2020, and today almost one-fifth of U.S. nonprofit hospitals are Catholic ( ). Catholic hospitals are also larger, with more beds on average, than their non-Catholic counterparts ( ; ). Especially in rural areas, patients may have to travel long distances, if that is feasible, to access non-Catholic hospitals ( ; ). Catholic hospitals adhere to the Ethical and Religious Directives (ERDs), a list of 77 specific directives that govern hospital operations and clinical care ( ). The ERDs emphasize Catholic health care’s commitment to serving poor and vulnerable populations, including the uninsured, racial/ethnic minorities, immigrants, Medicaid beneficiaries, and rural populations ( ; ; ). In addition, Catholic hospitals are expected to provide pro-natalist obstetrics care to support “the sanctity of human life from its very beginning.” However, the ERDs also explicitly forbid Catholic hospitals to provide services such as abortion, contraception, and sterilization that “render procreation impossible” ( ). Previous research has found Catholic hospitals were more likely to provide charity care and community benefit services compared to non-religious nonprofit hospitals ( ; ), and more likely to offer stigmatized services (e.g., HIV/AIDS, psychiatric care) compared to public and for-profit hospitals ( ). Some studies also suggest that Catholic hospitals may be more likely to provide obstetrics care and operate a neonatal intensive care unit ( ; ). Given the increasing trend of obstetric unit closures and consolidation, especially in rural areas, this suggestive evidence warrants further investigation ( ; ; ). However, research has also found that organizational structure, management, and patient experience within modern Catholic hospitals have become increasingly similar to their non-Catholic counterparts ( ; ; ). This convergence aligns with broader trends in the health care industry, where acquisitions often lead to significant operational changes at acquired facilities ( ; ; ). For example, Andreyeva et al. found that operating expenses declined after previously independent hospitals in New York state joined a health system, and these declines were primarily driven by a decrease in the number of employees concentrated in support functions. However, patient volume remained unchanged, suggesting that large systems were able to increase efficiency—reduce inputs while maintaining the same level of output ( ). New Contribution A recent literature review found that, despite the significant role of Catholic providers within the U.S. health care system, there are relatively few studies on this topic ( ). Previous research on Catholic health care is mainly descriptive in nature and limited by the potential for selection bias and unobserved confounding. In this study, we advance the literature by applying rigorous quasi-experimental methods to analyze the impact of competing institutional logics within Catholic health systems. By comparing changes in hospital operations following acquisitions by different ownership types, we empirically assess how Catholic health systems navigate competing mission-driven and financial tensions differently than their non-Catholic counterparts. Primary hospital operation outcomes are mission-oriented services (e.g., chaplaincy, charity care) and obstetrics care—services that are typically not profitable, but Catholic systems may be more likely to provide given their religious doctrine ( ; ). Secondary hospital operation outcomes are measures of utilization, operating expenses, and employment, which may change with the financial pressures associated with health system acquisitions ( ; ). Given the expansion of Catholic health care, our findings will inform current state policy debates on institutional conscience rights and government oversight in health care acquisitions. For example, several states are considering bills with additional protections or requirements related to the “institutional conscience” rights of Catholic hospitals in the wake of the Dobbs vs. Jackson Women’s Health Organization Supreme Court decision ( ). In addition, we make novel contributions in organizational theory by using the case of Catholic system acquisitions to illustrate how mission-driven organizations balance competing institutional logics, which can be defined as the organizing principles associated with different aspects of society that guide organizational behavior ( ; ). Conceptual Model In recent decades, there has been increasing interest in extending neo-institutional theory to study the multiple (and oftentimes, competing) institutional logics that drive organizational behavior, especially during times of organization change ( ; ; ). Catholic acquisitions present an interesting case to study the impact of applying multiple institutional logics—for example, religious and financial logics— within newly acquired hospitals. Not only do Catholic hospitals adhere to the ERDs, an explicit set of rules and values governing their operations, they also have organizational resources and incentives to follow these directives. When a hospital is acquired by a Catholic health system, hospital leadership and staff typically go through a series of trainings to ensure alignment with the system’s Catholic values, brand identity, and operating model. Catholic systems also have a “Director of Mission Integration” who uses established tools, such as the Catholic Ministry Identity Assessment, to oversee the consistent implementation of the ERDs in practice ( ; ; ). Moreover, Catholic health care systems often rely on support and funding from local communities and the Catholic Church ( ; ; ). By consistently applying the shared rules and values outlined in the ERDs, Catholic hospitals signal to stakeholders—patients, the Catholic Church, and the broader community—that the organization remains faithful to its identity and is “deserving” of resources. This context informs our first hypothesis: Hypothesis 1: Hospitals are more likely to preserve or expand mission-oriented services and obstetrics care after joining Catholic systems compared to non-Catholic systems. At the same time, the U.S. health care landscape has become increasingly competitive and profit-driven in recent years, contributing to accelerated merger/acquisition trends to expand providers’ market power and financial stability ( ; ; ). Policymakers and regulators are increasingly scrutinizing hospital acquisitions due to concerns over profit-driven incentives and potential reductions in access to care, especially in rural and underserved areas ( ; .). Today, four of the 10 largest U.S. health care systems are Catholic, including the single largest nonprofit system, CommonSpirit Health ( ). To remain competitive and financially viable, health systems—both Catholic and non-Catholic—must operate efficiently and look for opportunities to cut costs, especially within newly acquired hospitals ( ; ). This context informs our second hypothesis: Hypothesis 2: Post-acquisition, hospitals implement cut-cutting measures, including lower operating expenses and decreased employment, while maintaining or increasing utilization. These effects are similar after both Catholic and non-Catholic system acquisitions. Methods Data and Study Sample We integrated five data sources to construct a 14-year (2009–2022) unbalanced panel dataset of U.S. hospitals. Our primary data source was the American Hospital Association (AHA) survey, a comprehensive survey of U.S. hospitals is completed annually by hospital administrators and contains information on hospital location, system membership, size, entity type (government, for-profit, or nonprofit), utilization, expenses, employment, and service lines. Consistent data collection and survey processes are used to facilitate accurate time-series analyses ( ). The inclusion of a unique, stable hospital identifier allows hospitals to be linked over time and analyzed longitudinally. 78% of hospitals in our sample had data for all 14 years (2009–2022). Hospital closures and openings mean that some hospitals were added or removed from the dataset each year. The survey typically achieves high response rates (above 75%). If a hospital was open, but did not respond to the survey in a given year, AHA imputes missing values using a structured estimation process based on historical data and peer hospitals, creating a high degree of continuity across years ( ; ). We use several secondary data sources to check and confirm data on the acquisition of hospitals by health systems, including the LevinPro HC database that tracks health care mergers and acquisitions, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Hospital Change of Ownership dataset, and Health Care Pricing Project data on hospital acquisitions ( ). We also used the Compendium of U.S. Health Systems maintained by the Agency for Health care Research and Quality to identify religiously-affiliated health systems. We then manually validated if each religiously-affiliated system was Catholic using hospital and health system websites, press releases, and local diocesan lists of affiliated organizations. The initial dataset included 86,571 total hospital-years. To construct the analytic sample, we excluded hospitals that were part of a health system throughout the study period ( n = 49,854). It is necessary to exclude these “already-treated” hospitals to maintain a clean control group and ensure the validity of difference-in-differences (DID) estimates ( ). In addition, we excluded hospitals that switched in or out of a system more than once ( n = 1,033), were part of both Catholic and non-Catholic systems over the study period ( n = 181), and had less than 2 years of data before or after joining a system (

The final analytic sample included 2,722 unique hospitals and 33,552 hospital-years from 2009 to 2022. During the study period, there was a total of 707 first-time system acquisitions of previously independent hospitals, 76 (11%) by Catholic systems, and 631 (89%) by non-Catholic systems. Measures Treatment Variable Treatment is defined as the first year a previously independent hospital was acquired by a health system (a central organization that owns and/or manages health provider facilities or health-related subsidiaries). We only analyzed first-time acquisitions to ensure that any observed changes could be clearly attributed to the impact of joining a particular health system, without potential for contaminating effects from previous acquisitions. To explore if treatment effects differed depending on whether the acquiring health system was Catholic vs. non-Catholic, we further identified two treated sub-groups: “Catholic-acquired” (hospitals whose first acquisition was by a Catholic system) and “non-Catholic-acquired” (hospitals whose first acquisition was by a non-Catholic system). For all analyses, the control group was consistently defined as hospitals that were independent throughout the study period (“never-acquired” hospitals). Primary Outcomes Our primary hospital operation outcomes were measures of mission-oriented services and obstetrics care. Mission-oriented services were dichotomous variables indicating the provision of the following four services at the end of the fiscal year: (a) chaplaincy, defined as religious ministering and pastoral counseling services for hospital patients, their families, and staff; (b) charity care, defined as health care services provided free of cost or on a sliding scale for uninsured and underinsured persons, including free clinics subsidized by the sponsoring health care organization; (c) community outreach, defined as a hospital program that systematically interacts with the community to identify those in need of services, alerting persons and their families to the availability of services, locating needed services, and enabling persons to enter the service delivery system; and (c) linguistic/translation, defined as services to make health care more accessible to non-English speaking patients. Considering Catholic hospitals’ stated commitment to ensuring access to obstetrics care, alongside the recent trend of obstetric unit closures, we also examined changes in obstetrics care following acquisitions by Catholic and non-Catholic systems. An obstetrics unit was defined as a hospital unit that provided care, examination, treatment, and other services to women during pregnancy, labor, and postpartum. Other obstetrics care outcomes included obstetric bed count and proportion of obstetric beds to total hospital beds. Secondary Outcomes Secondary hospital operation outcomes included measures of utilization, operating expenses, and employment. Bed count was defined as number of beds set up and staffed at the end of the fiscal year. Bed count could be both a predictor of acquisition and/or change significantly post-acquisition. Therefore, we normalized the subsequent outcomes by bed count to eliminate heterogeneity purely due to differences in hospital size. Utilization measures per bed included: total inpatient admissions and number of inpatient days with Medicaid as the primary payer and, separately, Medicare. We measured the following three types of operating expenses per bed: (a) total expenses, defined as all operating expenses during the fiscal year, including payroll, employee benefits, and all other expenses; (b) payroll expenses, which included all salaries and wages; and (c) employee benefit expenses, which included social security, group insurance, retirement benefits, workman’s compensation, and unemployment insurance. Employment was measured as the number of full-time equivalents (FTEs) per bed on payroll, which accounted for both full-time and part-time employees. Doctors of Medicine (MDs) included physicians and dentists. Nurses included registered, licensed practical, and vocational nurses. Support staff included assistive nursing personnel, technicians (radiology, laboratory, pharmacy), respiratory therapists, and all other employees. Covariates Our analyses controlled for Medicaid payer mix (defined as proportion of total inpatient days with Medicaid as the primary payer) for both conceptual and analytical reasons. We have conceptualized Medicaid payer mix as a confounder, given it may impact both treatment assignment (hospital acquisition) and study outcomes (mission-oriented services, obstetrics care, etc.). Our statistical tests confirmed this variable was associated with lower odds of hospital acquisition (see Supplemental Appendix A ) and also changed differentially over time between the treatment and controls groups in the pre-period (e.g., non-parallel pretrends, see Supplemental Appendix B ). Therefore, we have included Medicaid payer mix as a covariate to more precisely isolate

Analysis Our main analytical strategy aimed to estimate differences in hospital response to acquisitions by Catholic and non-Catholic systems. We also used a targeting regression to examine which types of hospitals were targeted for acquisition by Catholic and non-Catholic systems (additional details and results of the targeting regression are presented in Supplemental Appendix A ). For our main analyses, we used a staggered DID specification to compare changes in trends at independent hospitals that were acquired by Catholic and non-Catholic systems (treated groups) vs. trends for independent hospitals that were never acquired (control group). Using a DID approach in which the “event” is the year of hospital acquisition, we compared changes in hospital operation measures between the 8 years before (“pre-period”) and 8 years after (“post-period”) acquisition, relative to trends in these measures among never-acquired hospitals over the same time period. Our model is as follows: (1) γ ht = β 1 ( post * Catholic − acquired ) ht + β 2 ( post * non − Catholic − acquired ) ht + γ X ht + θ h + θ t + ∈ h t ϒ ht denotes the outcome of interest for hospital h in year t . β 1 and β 2 capture the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) after joining Catholic and non-Catholic systems, respectively. X ht denotes the time-varying hospital covariate, Medicaid payer mix. The model includes hospital fixed effects (θ h ) to adjust for time-invariant hospital characteristics that may be correlated with the outcome (e.g., geographic location), and year fixed effects (θ t ) to adjust for national shocks (e.g., economic conditions, COVID-19 pandemic). Standard errors were clustered at the hospital level. We “winsorized” each continuous outcome, meaning outlier observations below the first percentile and above the 99th percentile were replaced with the 1st and 99th percentile values, respectively, given these values were likely not feasible. Our preferred specification utilized the Borusyak et al. imputation-based DID approach, which is particularly well-suited to our empirical setting given its efficient handling of both time- and group-based heterogeneous treatment effects ( ). Regarding time-based heterogeneity, hospital acquisitions occurred at different points over the study period (are “staggered”), so dynamic treatment effects may vary based on calendar year and/or relative time post-acquisition. Recent literature has highlighted limitations of using traditional two-way fixed effects estimators with staggered treatment timing ( ; ; ). By constructing imputed untreated outcomes for each treated unit (using pre-treatment data and the never-treated control group), the Borusyak et al. method accommodates complex patterns in treatment timing. This approach mitigates concerns with staggered timing and enhances both the precision and efficiency of our estimates ( ). In addition, the Borusyak et al. approach allows us to assess the statistical significance of group-based heterogeneous effects (here, Catholic vs. non-Catholic system acquisitions), a capability not directly available with other estimation procedures that do not use an imputation approach. Last, the Borusyak et al. method requires a stronger parallel trends assumption compared to alternative approaches, which enhances the credibility of causal effects if such assumptions are met. In our model, the identifying variation was based on the staggered timing of hospital acquisitions and the comparison of acquired and never-acquired hospitals in each relevant time period. To interpret β 1 and β 2 as the causal effect of system acquisition on outcome ϒ ht , we must assume that the outcome trends of the acquired hospitals would have been parallel to the outcome trends of the never-acquired hospitals in the absence of treatment. We assessed pre-treatment trends both formally (using joint pretrends tests) and graphically (using event study plots) and confirm the parallel trends assumption was met for all study outcomes. In Supplemental Appendix Table B1 , we present p -values from formal statistical tests of jointly significant pretrends for each outcome. Joint p -values of >.05 support the parallel pretrends assumption, as we are unable to reject the null hypothesis of no differences in trends between treatment and control groups prior to acquisition. Discussion In recent decades, health system acquisitions have become a defining feature of the U.S. health care landscape, often driven by financial pressures and the need for operational efficiency. While prior research has highlighted the cost-cutting strategies commonly associated with acquisitions, less is known about the role of Catholic-owned systems—which constitute 4 of the 10 largest U.S. health systems—in shaping post-acquisition outcomes ( ; ). This study leverages a national sample of U.S. hospitals over a 14-year period to provide new insights into the operational impacts of Catholic and non-Catholic health systems’ acquisitions. In doing so, we provide rigorous empirical evidence to inform ongoing state policy debates related to the expansion of Catholic health care and also make novel theoretical and methodological contributions. We found that hospitals were more likely to provide some mission-oriented services, including chaplaincy and charity care, after being acquired by a Catholic vs. non-Catholic system (relative to the control group of never-acquired hospitals). However, there was no change in the likelihood of offering community outreach or linguistic/translation services after being acquired by a Catholic or non-Catholic system. In addition, hospitals acquired by non-Catholic systems were less likely to operate an obstetric unit and had lower obstetric bed count relative to never-acquired hospitals, while hospitals acquired by Catholic systems had no significant change in obstetric services after acquisition. These results generally support Hypothesis 1 and align with previous literature finding Catholic ownership was associated with providing more mission-oriented services ( ; , ; ). Our results provide mixed support for Hypothesis 2. Aligning with expectations, changes in operating expenses and employment were generally similar after both Catholic and non-Catholic acquisitions. These results align with previous research showing reductions in operating costs, primarily by reducing employees in support functions, after previously independent hospitals join a health system ( ). In addition, these findings align with previous literature highlighting growing similarities between Catholic and non-Catholic hospitals in managerial/operating strategies ( ) and quality measures ( ). However, contrary to Hypothesis 2 expectations, we found differential changes in some utilization outcomes (e.g., admissions per bed) after Catholic vs. non-Catholic acquisitions. Future research should investigate the organizational behavior driving these heterogeneous utilization results. We take multiple steps to assess the validity of our estimates. First, we formally test and are unable to reject the null hypothesis of no differences in pretrends at treated (acquired) hospitals compared to the control group (never-acquired hospitals), implying the former were not on track to experience the observed changes absent treatment. Second, we confirm the robustness of our results to multiple study design and specification checks, increasing our confidence in the causal interpretation of findings. Health Policy and Practice Implications Our findings provide practical evidence on the effects of health system ownership for policymakers and health care leaders. Health care consolidation faces increasing public scrutiny given the growing role of for-profit entities and industry incentives for profit-maximization, often prompting calls for enhanced government oversight ( ; .). Catholic health system acquisitions present an interesting dynamic, as our findings show they have the potential to preserve or even expand some mission-oriented services. However, this also raises key questions about equitable access to services prohibited by Catholic doctrine, such as abortion and contraception. In the wake of the Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization Supreme Court decision, access to comprehensive reproductive health care is particularly important. Future research should explore the impact of Catholic ownership on access to comprehensive reproductive health care, especially in areas where Catholic hospitals have significant market share. In addition, our study makes novel theoretical and methodological contributions. Using the case of Catholic system acquisitions, we demonstrate how conflicting institutional logics interact and evolve over time within newly acquired hospitals. In some cases, mission-oriented logics outweigh financial logics—for example, expanding charity care at acquired hospitals. Aligned with institutional theories and organizational identity, the explicit nature of the ERDs and human/financial resources dedicated to their consistent implementation may play a role in the preservation of mission-oriented services ( ; ; ). Furthermore, this study utilizes an advanced imputation-based DID estimator, which is particularly well-suited for settings with staggered treatment timing and heterogeneous treatment effects. By employing this method, we provide robust causal inference and greater precision in estimating group-specific effects (e.g., Catholic vs. non-Catholic acquisitions). This approach advances the econometric literature by addressing limitations of traditional two-way fixed effects models and demonstrates the importance of

Limitations This study has several limitations. First, although Catholic systems are the largest provider of religiously-affiliated care in the United States, they still only operate a minority of total hospitals. The relatively small number of Catholic acquisitions compared to non-Catholic acquisitions (76 vs. 631 hospitals) may reduce statistical power, leading to wider confidence intervals and potentially limiting the detection of significant effects. Second, this study examined hospital-level operations and does not utilize clinical data to verify the actual use or quality of services provided, which limits our ability to assess patient-level impacts. Third, our analytic sample compares first-time acquisitions with never-acquired hospitals to ensure a clean comparison and valid identification of post-acquisition effects. While this design enhances internal validity, it narrows generalizability by excluding hospitals with prior health system affiliations. Fourth, this analysis focuses on quantitative outcomes, leaving qualitative aspects of hospital operations, such as leadership decisions or cultural integration, unexplored. Finally, unobserved factors such as market conditions or leadership changes may confound some results despite the inclusion of covariates and fixed effects. Conclusion This study uses rigorous quasi-experimental methods, informed by organizational theory, to examine how health care providers balance conflicting institutional pressures. We find that, while acquisition effects broadly align with the cost-containment strategies observed in prior research, there were heterogeneous effects based on system ownership. Some mission-oriented services, such as chaplaincy and charity care, were more likely to be provided after Catholic vs. non-Catholic acquisitions. In addition, non-Catholic systems were more likely to cut obstetric services at newly acquired hospitals. Taken together, these results suggest that system ownership plays a role in shaping hospital priorities post-acquisition and highlights the importance of disaggregating effects by ownership type. As health system consolidation continues, policymakers and health care leaders should consider the implications of these differing approaches, particularly in balancing financial sustainability with equitable access to care. chunks.content: Background Description of the condition In recent years, improved access to early diagnosis, new therapies, and enhanced support systems have increased survival rates among women with gynaecological cancers, including endometrial, cervical, ovarian, vaginal, and vulvar cancers [ , ]. However, many survivors experience long‐term complications that impair quality of life, with sexual dysfunction being a main issue [ , , ]. Diagnosing sexual dysfunction in cancer survivors is challenging, often under‐reported or overlooked, and requires open patient‐clinician communication, physical examination, and psychological assessment according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM‐5) criteria [ , , , , ]. The DSM‐5 defines sexual dysfunction as a disturbance in sexual pleasure and the physiological or psychological processes involved in sexual response, including disorders of interest/arousal, genitopelvic pain/penetration, and orgasm [ ]. In gynaecological cancer survivors, sexual dysfunction arises from both psychological effects, such as distress and altered self‐image, and physiological changes due to the disease or its treatment's adverse effects [ ]. Women with cervical, endometrial, and vulvar cancers may be at greater risk due to more frequent and direct exposure to pelvic surgery and radiotherapy [ , ]. For instance, radical hysterectomy can disrupt the pelvic nerve plexus and blood vessels, reducing arousal, lubrication, and neuromuscular co‐ordination, while radiotherapy may cause mucosal damage, fibrosis, and vaginal canal stiffness [ , , , ]. It may also weaken pelvic floor muscles, reducing their contractile strength and endurance [ ]. Cancer therapies, including chemotherapy, can also induce early menopause, with reduced oestrogen levels contributing to decreased libido, vaginal dryness, and pelvic floor laxity [ , , , , , ]. The pelvic floor, comprising muscles, ligaments, and fascia, plays a central role in sexual function, and cancer‐related damage may lead to high‐tone dysfunction, poor co‐ordination, laxity, and vaginismus [ , , ]. If unaddressed, sexual dysfunction may worsen psychological distress, disrupt relationships, and diminish overall well‐being [ ]. Description of the intervention and how it might work A wide range of interventions have been investigated for the treatment of sexual dysfunction in gynaecological cancer survivors. Candidate pharmacological options include oestrogen hormone replacement therapy (HRT), testosterone therapy, and certain antidepressants [ , ]. In contrast, non‐pharmacological strategies that address the psychological and physical aspects of sexual health encompass several categories [ , , ]. These include psychotherapeutic or psychoeducational interventions such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), couple‐based therapy, and mindfulness‐based techniques; mechanical interventions like vaginal lasers, dilators, lubricants, or clitoral therapy devices; and complementary and alternative therapies, including acupuncture and natural supplements such as maca, Korean red ginseng, and Ginkgo biloba extracts [ , , , , , , , , , , , ]. Among non‐pharmacological strategies, pelvic floor muscle therapy interventions represent an especially important and accessible option. These interventions, which have been investigated more in the context of female sexual dysfunction in general rather than in gynaecological cancer survivors in particular, target pelvic floor function and musculoskeletal support through modalities such as repeated voluntary contractions, resistance training, mobilisation, electrical stimulation, and muscle control [ ]. Pelvic floor muscle therapy interventions may be delivered individually or in combination. They can be categorised as follows [ , , , , ]. Pelvic floor muscle strength training (PMST) (e.g. Kegel exercises), involving voluntary, repetitive contractions of the pelvic floor muscles. Pelvic floor muscle resistance training (PMRT), consisting of strength‐building exercises using body weight, resistance bands, or other forms of resistance. Electrical stimulation of the pelvic floor muscles, using low‐grade electrical currents to stimulate pelvic floor muscle activity or modulate pain. This includes such methods as transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), sacral neuromodulation (SNM), dorsal genital nerve stimulation (DGNS), and percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS). Pelvic floor manual therapy, which consists of hands‐on techniques targeting soft tissues, fascia, and trigger points, as well as external mobilisation and myofascial release. Pelvic floor muscle biofeedback, which uses sensors to provide real‐time feedback on muscle activity. Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain how pelvic floor muscle‐focused interventions may improve sexual function in this population. Strengthening pelvic floor muscles through PMST or PMRT may enhance muscular support, co‐ordination, and neuromuscular control, potentially improving arousal, lubrication, and orgasmic function [ , , , , ]. Strengthening the levator ani muscle has been shown to improve pelvic structural support and to reduce strain on the surrounding ligaments [ ]. Additionally, increased pelvic blood flow and enhanced tissue mobility through manual techniques (e.g. myofascial release, trigger point therapy) may promote healing and revascularisation of damaged tissues, reduce pain, and further enhance arousal and lubrication [ , ]. Interventions like biofeedback and electrical stimulation, which have been investigated especially in women with sexual dysfunction and concurrent urinary incontinence or vulvodynia, can retrain pelvic floor control [ , , ]. ]. Strengthening the levator ani muscle has been shown to improve pelvic structural support and to reduce strain on the surrounding ligaments [ ]. Additionally, increased pelvic blood flow and enhanced tissue mobility through manual techniques (e.g. myofascial release, trigger point therapy) may promote healing and revascularisation of damaged tissues, reduce pain, and further enhance arousal and lubrication [ , ]. Interventions like biofeedback and electrical stimulation, which have been investigated especially in women with sexual dysfunction and concurrent urinary incontinence or vulvodynia, can retrain pelvic floor control [ , , ]. Electrical stimulation may also help modulate chronic pelvic pain following surgery or radiotherapy, while biofeedback promotes muscle awareness and co‐ordination, facilitating proper muscle recruitment and relaxation during intercourse, thereby decreasing vaginismus [ , , , ]. Together, these interventions may increase vaginal receptivity, improve pleasure for both partners, strengthen the couple's relationship, and support broader physical and mental well‐being, all of which positively affect sexual health. Why it is important to do this review Although often overlooked, sexual dysfunction is a common issue among gynaecological cancer survivors and can significantly impact their well‐being and quality of life both before and after treatment [ , ]. Addressing this issue should therefore be considered an integral part of holistic survivorship care, further helping to strengthen the relationship between survivors and healthcare professionals [ , ]. Despite its importance, no current clinical guidelines recommend specific interventions for the management of female sexual dysfunction in this group. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) acknowledges pelvic floor muscle interventions as a potential option, but this is based on weak evidence derived from the general population rather than gynaecological cancer survivors [ ]. While some studies have evaluated the use of such interventions in breast cancer survivors, findings have been inconsistent [ ]. Given the challenges faced by all women with sexual dysfunction, whether cancer‐related or not, it is reasonable to explore the potential efficacy and safety of pelvic floor muscle therapy in gynaecological cancer survivors. These interventions may offer an accessible and acceptable non‐pharmacological alternative, particularly for individuals who are often overburdened by prior or ongoing cancer treatments and are therefore reluctant to pursue pharmacological options. Compared to psychotherapeutic interventions, which may carry stigma for some patients due to their discomfort discussing sexual health with mental health professionals, or mechanical strategies like vaginal dilators, which may be less tolerated in the presence of strictures, pelvic floor muscle therapy could theoretically be more appealing [ , ]. Similarly, complementary and alternative medicine approaches sometimes lack a solid evidence base. The patient‐centred and holistic nature of pelvic floor muscle interventions may also increase adherence, which is essential for treatment success [ ]. Although trials have assessed the efficacy of pelvic floor muscle training in improving sexual dysfunction among gynaecological cancer survivors, and despite the perceived advantages of these interventions, the contribution of stronger pelvic floor muscles to sexual function in gynaecological cancer survivors remains uncertain [ , , , ]. While generally considered safe, these interventions can, in some cases, cause adverse effects such as pelvic floor muscle hypertonicity, spasms, fatigue, or pain, either during or independent of vaginal penetration [ ]. A better understanding of their benefits and risks could contribute meaningfully to comprehensive survivorship care [ ]. Previous Cochrane reviews have either focused on mechanical interventions, such as vaginal dilators for women undergoing pelvic radiotherapy for cervical or uterine cancer, or provide outdated evidence on pharmacological and non‐pharmacological options across broader cancer survivor populations [ , ]. Meanwhile, other relevant systematic reviews may not focus on gynaecological cancer survivors, examine prevalence rather than interventions, may combine self‐measured sexual function outcomes with those measured via validated tools, or omit risk of bias or certainty of evidence assessments [ , , , ]. These steps are particularly crucial in the field of sexual health, where outcomes are often reported by intervention recipients [ ]. Taking this into account, we aim to inform patients, clinicians, researchers, and policymakers about which pelvic floor muscle interventions, if any, are safe and beneficial for improving sexual function in gynaecological cancer survivors. Objectives To assess the effects of pelvic floor muscle therapy for sexual dysfunction in gynaecological cancer survivors. Methods We will follow the methodology of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions for conducting this review [ , , ], and the PRISMA 2020 statement for its reporting [ ]. We have applied the guidance from both sources to develop this protocol's Background and Methods sections. Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include randomised controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the effect of pelvic floor therapy interventions on gynaecological cancer survivors with sexual dysfunction. Methods We will follow the methodology of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions for conducting this review [ , , ], and the PRISMA 2020 statement for its reporting [ ]. We have applied the guidance from both sources to develop this protocol's Background and Methods sections. Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include randomised controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the effect of pelvic floor therapy interventions on gynaecological cancer survivors with sexual dysfunction. We will also include cluster‐RCTs and cross‐over trials (including only data from before the cross‐over). Given that we expect to find only a few RCTs addressing our review question, and that non‐randomised studies of interventions will be available which address our criteria directly and without critical bias, we will also include non‐randomised studies of interventions [ , ]. We will particularly include non‐RCTs, quasi‐randomised or pseudo‐randomised studies (i.e. studies that allocate participants to interventions using a method of allocation that is not truly random, such as by date of birth, medical record number, or alternation), and prospective cohort studies demonstrating strong methodological design [ , ]. A strong design would require prospective outcome measurement (i.e. clear temporal directionality) and efforts to control for selection and confounding biases [ , ]. We will include conference abstracts, and will contact their investigators for additional information regarding the study's conduct or results as needed. We will apply no restrictions on the year of dissemination or language. Types of participants We will include gynaecological cancer survivors. As per the definitions of the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and the American Cancer Society, we will define a cancer survivor as anyone “from the time of cancer diagnosis through the balance of life” and “no matter where they are in the course of their disease” [ , ]. This definition is also endorsed by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network [ ]. Agreeing with the statement from the National Coalition of Cancer Survivorship, we understand and fully respect that anyone affected by cancer can “identify with the term they feel best describes their experience” or with no label at all. However, we will use the term ‘cancer survivor’ (or simply ‘survivor’) throughout this review, as it is the most widely used and scientifically accepted term [ , , ]. Based on the relevant classification of the International Federation of Obstetrics and Gynaecology (FIGO), we will include participants with the following gynaecological cancers. Vulvar cancer Vaginal cancer Cervical cancer (i.e. cancer of the cervix uteri) Uterine cancer (i.e. cancer of the corpus uteri, e.g. endometrial cancer) Cancer of the ovary, fallopian tube, and peritoneum (i.e. the membrane surrounding them) Gestational trophoblastic disease (i.e. tumours developing from cells that would normally create the placenta). We will include studies with survivors of cancers other than gynaecological ones only if the subset of individuals with gynaecological cancers exceeds 75% of the study's overall population, or if we can access separate data on participants with gynaecological cancer through published study records or direct correspondence with the authors. We will not apply any restrictions in terms of locations or settings. Recognising the distinct epidemiology of each gynaecological cancer (e.g. cervical cancer typically affects younger women, whereas vulvar cancer more often occurs in older patients) and their differential impact on pelvic floor and sexual function, we will perform subgroup analyses by cancer type. Additionally, given the different mechanisms through which treatments can impair pelvic floor and overall sexual function (e.g. nerve damage from surgery versus vaginal stenosis and fibrosis from radiotherapy), and differences in clinical management, we will also subdivide our included population by treatment modality (e.g. surgery, radiotherapy, or combined treatments), if possible. We will include all survivors, both those with cancer and those free of it (i.e. free from the disease after treatment or free from recurrence). We will also include participants at any cancer stage (i.e. early‐stage cancer, advanced‐stage or metastatic cancer, or end‐stage cancer requiring only palliative care), either before, during, or after any anticancer treatment [ ]. To investigate the potentially modifying effect of the emotional or physical impact of cancer stage, we will examine the effect of interventions on participants with advanced or end‐stage cancer (stage III or IV) versus early‐stage cancer (stage I or II). Participants should have been sexually active before their cancer diagnosis. We will include all women experiencing relevant symptoms as per the definition of sexual dysfunction (recorded within studies either through self‐report or validated scales) [ ]. Although the DSM‐5 requires the presence of symptoms for at least six months for sexual dysfunction to be diagnosed, we will also include studies of women experiencing symptoms for less than six months, as many advanced gynaecological cancers may progress faster [ , ]. Since it is not always feasible to reliably distinguish between women

or IV) versus early‐stage cancer (stage I or II). Participants should have been sexually active before their cancer diagnosis. We will include all women experiencing relevant symptoms as per the definition of sexual dysfunction (recorded within studies either through self‐report or validated scales) [ ]. Although the DSM‐5 requires the presence of symptoms for at least six months for sexual dysfunction to be diagnosed, we will also include studies of women experiencing symptoms for less than six months, as many advanced gynaecological cancers may progress faster [ , ]. Since it is not always feasible to reliably distinguish between women with new‐onset sexual dysfunction following a cancer diagnosis and those with pre‐existing dysfunction, we will include both populations. Sexual dysfunction may worsen or become clinically apparent only after cancer diagnosis or treatment, leading to potential misclassification. Given that pre‐existing sexual dysfunction may modify the efficacy or safety of physical therapy interventions, we will also separately examine women with pre‐existing versus new‐onset sexual dysfunction, where data are available. Types of interventions This review will focus on pelvic floor muscle therapy, which encompasses interventions aiming to improve sexual function by focusing on the optimal function of the pelvic floor muscles. These will include the following. PMST (i.e. voluntary, repetitive pelvic floor muscle contractions, such as Kegel exercises). PMRT (i.e. strength‐building exercises using any form of resistance). Pelvic floor muscle electrical stimulation (i.e. methods using low‐grade electrical currents stimulating pelvic floor muscles like TENS, SNM, DGNS, and PTNS). Pelvic floor manual therapy (i.e. hands‐on techniques targeting soft tissues, fascia, and trigger points, with the aim of mobilisation and myofascial release; we will not consider vaginal dilators since their aim is the mechanical stretching of the vaginal canal rather than muscular mobilisation and myofascial release). Pelvic floor muscle biofeedback (i.e. the use of sensors that provide real‐time feedback on pelvic floor muscle activity); although biofeedback contains a psychological component and is often considered a ‘mind‐body’ intervention, we will include it due to its physical therapy component and its perceived ability to increase pelvic neuromuscular control and awareness. Our review will encompass the following comparisons. Pelvic floor muscle therapy intervention(s) versus no pelvic floor muscle therapy (i.e. survivorship care including no pelvic floor muscle therapy interventions). Pelvic floor muscle therapy intervention(s) versus other pelvic floor muscle therapy intervention(s). We will consider interventions eligible if they were applied at any point after cancer diagnosis, as per the definition of a cancer survivor. We will allow nutritional advice and aerobic or core stability exercises as potential co‐interventions, as they may often be combined with pelvic floor muscle therapy, and plan to record any such co‐interventions meticulously. We will also allow combinations of pelvic floor muscle therapy interventions. We will allow an educational component of these interventions only if it focuses on pelvic floor muscle therapy (and potential supplemental physical exercise or nutrition). This means we will allow if providers train recipients on how to properly perform certain interventions (e.g. Kegel exercises) or educate recipients on accepted co‐interventions like nutrition and aerobic or core stability exercises. Physical therapists or other healthcare professionals could deliver or supervise the interventions or educate participants. The interventions may be applied with or without professional supervision, or with the assistance of artificial intelligence (AI) supervision. We will exclude studies examining combinations of pelvic floor muscle therapy with pharmacological or non‐pharmacological interventions other than those described in this section. We will also exclude studies comparing pelvic floor muscle therapy with pharmacological interventions. In line with the appropriate guidance, we also want to ensure the minimum number of comparisons that serve the review's objective [ ]. Outcome measures Critical outcomes Our critical outcomes are as follows [ , ]. Sexual function, defined as the absence of difficulty moving through the stages of sexual desire, arousal, and orgasm, as well as subjective satisfaction with the frequency and outcome of individual and partnered sexual behaviour. It may be measured by any validated self‐ or clinician‐administered instrument such as the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), the Derogatis Inventory of Sexual Functioning (DISF‐SR), and others, within 12 months after the initiation of the intervention [ , ]. For consistency, we will prioritise the FSFI over other instruments. Namely, if the same study reports the FSFI and additional instruments, we will only use the FSFI. We will include alternative scales in the review only to ensure that we do not entirely exclude studies where the FSFI is unavailable. We will take care not to analyse together scales whose higher scores indicate better sexual function (e.g. FSFI) with those whose higher scores indicate worse function (e.g. the Golombok Rusk Inventory of Sexual Satisfaction (GRISS)). Self‐reported new‐onset or worsening pain associated with vaginal penetration (i.e. dyspareunia) within three months [ ]. Important outcomes We will analyse the following important outcomes, which will

the same study reports the FSFI and additional instruments, we will only use the FSFI. We will include alternative scales in the review only to ensure that we do not entirely exclude studies where the FSFI is unavailable. We will take care not to analyse together scales whose higher scores indicate better sexual function (e.g. FSFI) with those whose higher scores indicate worse function (e.g. the Golombok Rusk Inventory of Sexual Satisfaction (GRISS)). Self‐reported new‐onset or worsening pain associated with vaginal penetration (i.e. dyspareunia) within three months [ ]. Important outcomes We will analyse the following important outcomes, which will be measured within 12 months after the initiation of the interventions, unless otherwise stated. Sexual distress, defined as frustration, anxiety, and worry regarding sexual activity and measured by any validated self‐ or clinician‐administered instrument such as the revised Female Sexual Distress Scale (FSDS‐R), the original version of the Female Sexual Distress Scale (FSDS), and others. We will prioritise the FSDS‐R over other scales [ , ]. Satisfaction with intimacy/relationship, as measured by any validated intimacy/relationship satisfaction scale, such as the Couples Satisfaction Index (CSI), the Relationship Assessment Scale (RAS), and others. We will prioritise scales assessing satisfaction with sexual aspects of intimacy (e.g. CSI) over those assessing intimacy (e.g. RAS), and over more general scales like the Quality of Marriage Index (QMI) [ , , ]. Quality of life, measured by any relevant instrument validated for either cancer survivors or the general population, such as the Quality of Life Index for Cancer Survivors (QOL‐CS), the WHO Quality of Life Index (WHOQOL), and others [ , ]. We will prioritise scales specific to cancer survivors (e.g. QOL‐CS). Frequency of intercourse (i.e. the number of sexual encounters, either self‐reported or recorded within diaries or logs, per time unit (e.g. times per week, month, or year)). Early intervention discontinuation due to poor tolerability (e.g. due to pain or discomfort, difficulty adhering to or properly applying the intervention, injuries, or other self‐reported adverse effects), assessed within three months. To “allow for modification of adaptations to changes in desire”, the recommended minimum duration of studies measuring efficacy outcomes of female sexual function is six months [ ], therefore we chose to measure our critical and important efficacy outcomes within 12 months after the initiation of the interventions. We will measure safety outcomes within three months, since they are more relevant early after starting the intervention. We will exclude studies only if we ensure that the outcomes of interest have not been measured, rather than not reported. In other words, if an outcome of interest is not reported, we will first ensure that it was not measured at all by the study investigators. Search methods for identification of studies In collaboration with the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Information Specialist, we will search for RCTs, quasi‐RCTs, non‐RCTs, or prospective cohort studies on the use of pelvic floor muscle therapy interventions for sexual dysfunction in gynaecological cancer survivors. We will apply no language or date restrictions to the search. Electronic searches We will search for relevant studies in the following electronic databases [ , ]. Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), which includes trial reports from the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) and trial registrations from ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), using the Ovid platform; from inception to present MEDLINE (Epub Ahead of Print, In Process and Other Non‐Indexed Citations), using the Ovid platform; from 1946 to present Embase, using the Ovid platform; from 1980 to present PsycINFO, using the Ovid platform; from 1806 to present ClinicalTrials.gov (clinicaltrials.gov/) and WHO ICTRP (trialsearch.who.int/) trial registries for ongoing trials, web platform; from inception to present The search strategies are available in the Appendix ( ). Searching other resources We will check the reference lists of retrieved studies, relevant reviews, and conference proceedings from major conferences to identify additional studies. Additionally, we will search relevant grey literature sources, including the first 200 records from the Google Scholar database. We will also search the Epistemonikos database (www.epistemonikos.org/), a multilingual database of health evidence and the largest source of systematic reviews. Furthermore, we will consult experts in the field to identify ongoing or existing studies. To ensure the integrity of the included studies, we will check PubMed (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov) for studies of concern and retracted studies, including expressions of concern, errata, corrigenda, and retractions. We will exclude any identified problematic studies from the review. Data collection and analysis We will select studies, collect study data, import the data into RevMan [ ], and analyse them according to methods described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ , , , , ]. We will exclude any identified problematic studies from the review. Data collection and analysis We will select studies, collect study data, import the data into RevMan [ ], and analyse them according to methods described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ , , , , ]. Selection of studies After deduplicating the records retrieved from the search using EndNote [ ], sets of independent review authors (AB, DG, A Saitis, MN, and A Syristatidi) will screen the titles and abstracts of the unique records and exclude those that do not fulfil the review's eligibility criteria. We will retrieve the full texts of the remaining records and independently screen them for eligibility. We will exclude studies not meeting the criteria and explicitly document the reasons for doing so in the 'Characteristics of excluded studies' table. We will use Rayyan online software for all screening processes [ ]. If the eligibility of a study remains unclear even after accessing its full‐text record, we will contact the study authors for further clarification. Another review author (DV or MP) will resolve disagreements during both stages. If potentially eligible studies are published in languages not spoken by the review team, we will seek assistance from colleagues with relevant language skills or through the Cochrane Engage platform. We will summarise the full study selection process in a PRISMA flow chart [ ]. Data extraction and management Sets of review authors (AB, DG, A Saitis, MN, and A Syristatidi) will independently extract study characteristics and outcome data from the reports of each included study. A predefined spreadsheet will first be piloted among team members. Within each set of review authors, one review author will extract data from the records, and the other will validate the imported values against the extraction form. We will resolve any disagreements through discussion; if discrepancies persist, we will consult a third review author (DV or MP). In the case of multiple reports of a single study, we will use the main report as the reference and will supplement it with data from the secondary reports. We will email the authors of the included studies for additional data or methodological details as needed. If we receive no response or insufficient data, we will send them a reminder within 20 days after the first contact [ , ]. The data extraction form will contain the following items. General information and study details Identifiers of the report and study Names of the review authors extracting data and the extraction date Funding sources for the study Declarations of interest of the primary investigators Country, including the income level group (i.e. low, lower‐middle, upper‐middle, and high) according to the World Bank countries classification based on Gross National Income per capita Study design (i.e. RCT, non‐randomised/quasi‐randomised controlled trial, prospective cohort) Study centre(s) Healthcare setting (public or private) Study period Corresponding author's contact details Study registration information Study methods Study design: parallel, cluster, or cross‐over trial for RCTs;
